title: It Was a Brutal House of the Dragon Season 3 Finale for Rhaenyra. But She’s Still the Hero
summary: It's tempting to say the Queen has taken a heel turn in Season 3. But she's still the hero—if likely a tragic one.
full_text:
This article contains spoilers for the House of the Dragon Season 3 finale.
House of the Dragon is not making a habit out of quiet finales. Viewers who grumbled over the anticlimax of Season 2 must have been pleased with Sunday’s Season 3 finale, which one-upped the previous episode’s Sunfyre resurrection and brûléeing of many soldiers loyal to Rhaenyra with a Battle of Tumbleton that torched the city; left thousands of casualties Black, Green, and civilian; and ended both Ormund Hightower’s (James Norton) kingmaking ambitions and his life. Major character deaths weren’t even limited to the battlefield: RIP Helaena, for one, too good for Westeros and for her family. I’ll miss Phia Saban’s quietly resolute performance.
You wouldn’t be wrong to place the blame for the battle’s carnage as well as Helaena’s spiky suicide on Rhaenyra (Emma D’Arcy). It’s she who, after some handwringing, orders Daemon (Matt Smith) to lay siege to Tumbleton and “root out every Hightower and kill them to the last man.” She also has a captive, pregnant, hunger-striking Helaena violently force-fed. Anti-Rhaenyra sentiment is festering, even within the Red Keep. Until this season, she has been Dragon’s default hero, bravely defending her right to succeed her father against a Green faction whose loyalty to Aegon II (Tom Glynn-Carney) basically comes down to misogyny, despite wrenching personal losses. But now that she sits the Iron Throne, the show is making us—like the starving peasants she has yet to materially help—question whether she is truly the great leader she’s convinced she can be. I don’t know that she is, or that anyone could be in similar circumstances. She’s still the hero of this story, though, even if she turns out to be a tragic one.
The finale opens with Rhaenyra waking to the news that Aegon is alive, and that his return—with a still-quite-lethal Sunfyre, no less—after she declared him dead makes him some kind of messiah. Understandably, she panics, cursing the memory of Viserys (Paddy Considine) for putting her in such a terrible situation. “His prophecy has tested me again and again, and I have met its every challenge!” she complains to Daemon. He takes the opportunity to remind her of her Targaryen supremacy. So, how should she wield it? “The only quality the realm understands is strength,” Daemon says. It’s enough to get him dispatched to Tumbleton.
Baela (Bethany Antonia) urges Rhaenyra to have Lord Corlys (Steve Toussaint) rescued from the Hightowers’ clutches while Black forces are in town. He is, after all, the Hand of the Queen, and he’s sacrificed mightily for her cause. Also: “It was your fault” the Sea Snake was captured in the first place, Baela says. When Rhaenyra seems less than enthusiastic about helping him, Baela really goes off on her. “If a person is useful to you, you wield them,” she accuses. “But if not, you abandon them.” This may be true. A few scenes later, Rhaenyra abruptly banishes her paramour Mysaria (Sonoya Mizuno)—through a minion, no less. (Mysaria does get a nice severance package.) But doesn’t a responsible sovereign have to be ready to throw her friends and family under the bus in service of what she believes to be the greater good of the kingdom? I mean, wasn’t that the takeaway of six seasons of Matt Smith’s other show, The Crown? Of course, as with Elizabeth’s real-life refusal to let her sister marry a divorced man, the question of whether it’s actually prudent for the monarchy to deprioritize saving Corlys is a different matter.
It isn’t just Baela who rips into Rhaenyra in her own home. Helaena’s force-feeding comes after a heated encounter with the Queen. “You cannot think I would harm you,” says Rhaenyra, who must still see herself as a merciful person. (That she has thugs shoving gruel down Helaena’s throat seconds later suggests an alarming lack of self-awareness.) Helaena’s retort: “Do you think life is nothing more than not being dead? Our father would hate you for this.” She’s right. But Rhaenyra is also correct when she points out to her half-sister that Viserys’ dithering over succession is what put them in this predicament in the first place. Then again, there’s truth to Helaena’s scathing final blow: “All the things you care about are ugly. This place is ugly. You, yourself, are ugly.”
Helaena is Dragon’s Cassandra; her supernatural prescience and big-picture perspective make her perhaps the wisest character this side of Game of Thrones’ Bran the Broken. (This makes the embroidered portrait of Rhaenyra on a bloody Iron Throne that is, in effect, her suicide note, particularly foreboding.) If you take “the things you care about” and “this place” to mean power and King’s Landing—or Westeros at large—she’s reiterating a core theme of A Song of Ice and Fire. Like anyone vying for a throne, Rhaenyra is playing a brutal, yes, game. Would it be a more just or humane game, though, if she forfeited? Would it have a better long-term outcome?
Rhaenyra doesn’t think so. And unlike Aegon or Aemond (Ewan Mitchell), whose kingly ambitions don’t seem grounded in anything more than entitlement and will to power, she is actually taking Westeros’ future into consideration when she clings to her birthright. Not only does she ascend the Iron Throne with the intention of helping the small folk, but she also sincerely believes in the Song of Ice and Fire prophecy—a prophecy that Thrones viewers know will, whether self-fulfilling or not, both lead to great destruction and, ultimately, prove instrumental in saving humanity from extinction via White Walker. This is why we see her, in the finale, demand to be anointed by the High Septon (Gary Raymond) and order Alyn (Abubakar Salim) to kill him when he refuses. She isn’t betraying the Seven, exactly, because her fealty is to the prophecy and to her Valyrian ancestors. She believes she’s answering a higher calling.
Tragedy lies in the gulf between beliefs or intentions and reality. In the Battle of Tumbleton, it’s Daemon rejecting Gwayne (Freddie Fox) and Daeron’s (Benjamin Evan Ainsworth) plea for peace, taking offense at Corlys’ further attempts at diplomacy, exhorting his army to avoid excessive casualties because “the Queen’s moral standing must remain absolute”—and then presiding over a grisly mass slaughter against an enemy that makes terrified children cannon fodder. Because he is carrying out her order to decimate the Hightowers, in defiance of Corlys’ plan for victory without bloodshed, Rhaenyra is just as responsible for these atrocities as Daemon. A tragic hero has the most noble aims but, due to some intrinsic character flaw or external factor (a sexist society, say, or misplaced faith) ends up doing the wrong thing for the right reasons. Rhaenyra seems to be heading in this unfortunate direction, but she’s no villain. We’ll find out in the show’s last act whether her heroism proves to be triumphant or tragic.

title: Who Lived and Who Died in the Battle of Tumbleton in the House of the Dragon Season 3 Finale
summary: The Battle of Tumbleton resulted in some significant losses
full_text:
Warning: This post contains spoilers for the House of the Dragon Season 3 finale.
It's been a good six episodes since Rhaenyra Targaryen (Emma D'Arcy) at long last seized the Iron Throne and proclaimed herself Queen of the Seven Kingdoms in House of the Dragon Season 3. But it wasn't until Sunday night's finale that we truly got a glimpse into why Westerosi history books dubbed her "Rhaenyra the Cruel."
After learning her half-brother and former king Aegon II (Tom Glynn-Carney) had resurfaced in a literal blaze of glory supplied by his previously presumed dead dragon Sunfyre, Rhaenyra's desperation to assert herself as the realm's rightful ruler was palpable. So, she finally picked a definitive side in the ongoing struggle between Daemon (Matt Smith) and Mysaria (Sonoya Mizuno) to win her trust. Rather than continuing to work to legitimize her rule through support for the common people per Mysaria's counsel, Rhaenyra opted for the show of brute force Daemon has been all too eager to lead the charge on. As he put it, "The only quality the realm understands is strength."
However, Rhaenyra did have one caveat for giving Daemon the go-ahead to attack Ormund Hightower (James Norton) and his forces at Tumbleton: "The realm is watching. Do not make a monster out of me."
Unfortunately, when dragons are involved, all-out carnage seems like more of an inevitable outcome than an active choice. So it shouldn't have really come as a surprise to anyone involved when the assault on Tumbleton quickly spiraled into a fiery onslaught that turned the city's smallfolk into collateral damage.
As for all our major players, here's everyone who lived and who died in the Battle of Tumbleton.
Who lived
Daemon Targaryen
The Rogue Prince lived to fight another day, but not without taking a nearly lethal beatdown at the hands of Ser Jon Roxton (Joplin Sibtain). By the end of the episode, Daemon appeared to be more cowed than we've ever seen him. And if the horrified expression on his face was any indication, he's all too aware of how badly he bungled Rhaneyra's order not to let the battle make her look like an evil tyrant.
Corlys Velaryon
Corlys (Steve Toussaint) may have lost a finger to Ormund, but he managed to largely stay out of the fray at Tumbleton after Gwayne (Freddie Fox) handed him over to Daemon as part of an attempted peace offering. Unfortunately, his son Alyn (Abubakar Salim) seems to have already grown comfortable filling Corlys' role as Hand of the King back at King's Landing.
Gwayne Hightower
That final shot of a somewhat scorched Gwayne crawling through the ruins of Tumbleton in search of Daeron (Benjamin Evan Ainsworth) let us know everyone's favorite Hightower had managed to make it through yet another fiery dragon rampage.
Daeron Targaryen
Although we didn't get confirmation Daeron survived the blast of dragonfire that sent him and Gwayne flying through the streets of Tumbleton, we also didn't see him die on screen. In the A Song of Ice and Fire universe, that's pretty much a guarantee he'll be back next season. Plus, we haven't even gotten to see him ride his dragon Tessarion yet.
Hugh Hammer
Hugh (Kieran Bew) survived the violence, but we can't imagine he won't be out for vengeance for the death of his wife, Kat (Ellora Torchia), and the remaining members of her family. Who exactly he'll decide is at fault for their untimely demise is still up in the air, though.
Ulf the White
Ulf (Tom Bennett) may have bad blood with the highborns of both Team Green and Team Black, but his decision to carry out that vendetta by going rogue and raining dragonfire down on Tumbleton directly resulted in a massacre of the city's common folk (likely including some of the very same people with whom he spent the previous night drinking a local tavern dry). At this point, it's pretty clear Ulf could care less about anyone but himself.
Jon Roxton
Considering he almost took down Daemon, Ser Jon is clearly no slouch when it comes to combat. But now that Lord Ormud is dead, he'll have to chart his own path forward.
Oscar Tully
We didn't really get to see the young lord of the Riverlands in action during the battle, but he did quickly pop back up at the end of the episode to prove he was still kicking.
Alysanne Blackwood
Like Oscar (Archie Barnes), Alysanne (Annie Shapero) was slaying Hightowers off-screen for most of the clash. But even if she had died, Alysanne's already made a lasting name for herself as the one who delivered the killing blow to Ser Criston Cole.
Who died
Roderick Dustin
The leader of the Winter Wolves was ordered not to die before Tumbleton's main gate fell. Ser Roderick (Tommy Flanagan) more than accomplished his task, even managing to deliver an incapacitating blow to Ormund before meeting a smiling end engulfed in Silverwing's dragonfire.
Ormund Hightower
After showing his true colors by forcing children to the frontlines of Tumbleton's battlements to serve as human shields, Ormund brought about his own demise with his brutal treatment of a hungover Ulf just as the battle began. In the end, all of Ormund's bluster about the the unworthiness of the Targaryens didn't stop a dragon from killing him.
Kat
It was unclear exactly how Kat actually died since she didn't have any visible wounds or appear to be injured in any way when Hugh found her body. But we're taking Hugh's scream of anguish as a sign that Kat is no longer with us.
Additional deaths
Heleana Targaryen
Heleana (Phia Saban) didn't die at the Battle of Tumbleton, but her death is certainly significant. In a callback (or rather, call-forward) to King Tommen Baratheon throwing himself from a high tower of the Red Keep in Game of Thrones, pregnant Heleana chose to jump to her death out of a very similar window in the castle rather than continue to live as Rhaenyra's prisoner. It's difficult to imagine a world in which Alicent (Olivia Cooke) and Rhaenyra's relationship will come back from this one.
High Septon Eustace
Rather than continue to put up with his refusal to anoint her as Queen of the Seven Kingdoms, Rhaenyra came to the conclusion that her best course of action was to put the High Septon (Simon Chandler) to the sword instead. Unfortunately, we have a feeling that move isn't going to play so well with her many subjects who adhere to the Faith of the Seven.

title: Bitcoin Red Team founder turns to Chinese AI: ‘It absolutely guts me’
summary: Bitcoin Red Team has now found 1,288 critical and high-level vulnerabilities in the Bitcoin ecosystem as of Saturday.
full_text:
Bitcoin Red Team founder turns to Chinese AI: ‘It absolutely guts me’
Bitcoin Red Team has now found 1,288 critical and high-level vulnerabilities in the Bitcoin ecosystem as of Saturday.
A Bitcoin security researcher says he has been forced to go back to using open-source Chinese AI models after finding himself restricted from analyzing further codebases by OpenAI, highlighting a growing concern that the most capable AI tools aren’t being made available to defenders.
In an X post on Tuesday, AnchorWatch CEO Rob Hamilton said he had begun integrating OpenAI’s Trust & Cyber capabilities into his Bitcoin Red Team work on Saturday, only to find his access restricted the following morning.
“It absolutely guts me as a patriotic American to have to do this, but I will be going back to using Chinese open source models to conduct my research to protect Bitcoin infrastructure,” he added.
Bitcoin Red Team, a group of volunteers, has been using AI tools and human review to scan hundreds of open-source Bitcoin-related repositories for vulnerabilities, with efforts accelerating days after the Coldcard hardware wallet hack, which has seen over $100 million in Bitcoin stolen.
Last month, crypto executives told Cointelegraph that many of crypto’s biggest players are still waiting to gain access to powerful new AI models to strengthen their code from attacks, with only a select few having been able to get it.
“I am now prevented from being able to continue the investigation in a further effort to make sure their code changes are sufficient, as well as understand if there are other issues that have yet to be discovered,” said Hamilton.
“Black hats will not hit these issues. The white hats will. We’ve hit a local minima in policy,” said Hamilton. “Intelligence is unrestricted for those who don’t follow rules, and those who engage in harm reduction are left on the sidelines.”
Related: Crypto firms still seeking frontier AI access; only select few have it

title: Australia orders Cryptolink Bitcoin ATMs offline over ‘basic reporting’ failures
summary: Australia’s financial watchdog has suspended Cryptolink’s registration for three months, adding to a crackdown that previously saw the Bitcoin ATM operator fined $56,340.
full_text:
Australia orders Cryptolink Bitcoin ATMs offline over ‘basic reporting’ failures
Australia’s financial watchdog has suspended Cryptolink’s registration for three months, adding to a crackdown that previously saw the Bitcoin ATM operator fined $56,340.
Australia’s anti-money laundering watchdog has suspended the operation of Cryptolink’s Bitcoin ATMs for three months, citing “ongoing concerns” about its compliance with anti-money laundering obligations.
Australia has the highest number of crypto ATMs of all countries in the Asia-Pacific region. Australian authorities have been cracking down on the criminal use of crypto ATMs since at least late 2024.
AUSTRAC CEO Brendan Thomas said Monday the company’s Virtual Asset Service Provider (VASP) registration has been suspended for three months starting Sunday, meaning its crypto ATMs will not be allowed to operate during that time.
AUSTRAC said Cryptolink failed to meet basic reporting requirements, particularly threshold transaction reports, and did not respond to AUSTRAC’s request for information.
“As part of our continued focus on digital currency as a money laundering risk, AUSTRAC has ongoing concerns about the company’s ability to manage high-risk transactions through its CATMs,” said Thomas.
The action follows an enforceable undertaking that Cryptolink entered into with AUSTRAC in October 2025, after its Cryptocurrency Taskforce identified alleged breaches including late transaction reporting and shortcomings in Cryptolink’s risk assessments. AUSTRAC also issued a $56,340 infringement notice, which Cryptolink paid.
Cryptolink has 96 ATMs in Australia, allowing customers to exchange cash for Bitcoin. Most of its ATMs are located in major cities including Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane.
Cointelegraph reached out to Cryptolink for comment.
Related: Bitcoin Depot stock crashes 71% premarket after Chapter 11 filing

title: Space Agencies Are Trying to Keep Astronauts From Losing Their Sight
summary: A device currently being used to help octogenarians do self-administered eye exams could be part of future space missions to monitor astronauts’ ocular health.
full_text:
The European Space Agency is trying to understand why astronauts lose their eyesight in space, in the hope they can figure out how to treat—or even prevent—the condition as looming longer spaceflights heighten the risk of permanent vision damage.
The agency has commissioned British eye-scanning startup Siloton to develop a solution ahead of the international Artemis flights to the moon and other deep space missions. The health tech uses quantum technology to shrink core components used in eye-testing equipment found at optometrists to fit on a photonic chip smaller than a coin.
Founded by physicists in 2020, Siloton is currently working with the UK’s National Health Service to enable patients with retinal conditions to self-scan at home. “The ESA pretty much has the same requirements,” says cofounder and chief technology officer Euan Allen. “It's just in a totally different environment.”
Spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS) is a collection of eye and brain changes caused by spending prolonged periods in a low-gravity environment, and it impacts around 70 percent of astronauts on the International Space Station, according to NASA. One of the starkest cases is that of NASA astronaut John Phillips, who launched to the ISS in 2005 with 20/20 vision, and splashed down six months later with his vision at 20/100—what’s considered a moderate visual impairment. While he was in space, bodily fluid, uninhibited by gravity, built up in his head, squashing his eyeballs, swelling his optic nerve, and pushing his retina forward.
While returning to Earth can reverse some of the damage, space agencies are concerned by both the operational risk of astronauts losing their vision mid-mission, as well as the longer-term health impacts. “The eye condition SANS is a serious health risk facing astronauts on long missions,” says Rebecca Evernden, director of the UK Space Agency. Medical engineers want to develop their understanding of the condition and the factors causing it so that they can manage any ocular damage, and eventually treat it or even stop it from becoming a problem.
Scientists are already monitoring how spaceflight impacts the human eye on the ISS using a modified version of the device found in optometry offices that measures the thickness of layers at the back of the eye. However, the device is bulky and requires real-time remote guidance from experts on the ground. As astronauts journey further into deep space, lengthening communication delays with Earth will mean this is no longer feasible.
Siloton’s device would allow astronauts to scan their retinas more frequently by automating some of the process so that examinations do not need ground support. The ESA hopes that will generate more data on any ocular degeneration, and possibly provide early warning signs that changes in the eye may be occurring—even before they result in vision change.
Other technical challenges include getting around using batteries to power the device because they pose such a big fire risk. In spacecraft, where space is at a premium, designers will also have to decide where the binocular-sized equipment would live and how to position and keep an astronaut’s head in place without gravity (typically, that’s done by having a chin rest).
But that’s a walk-in-the-park compared with getting a retiree whose sight is failing to cooperate, says Allen. “We're very confident, because we're trying to do that with 80-year-old patients who already have some level of visual imparity,” says Allen, “whereas these will be highly trained astronauts who are much younger and have full function of their eyes.”
”I think lots of the stuff that we're doing for space will bleed through and make our home device better, and vice versa as well,” he adds. “All this research and development work, in principle, is making our products that are going to go into the NHS much better.”

title: 前以太坊基金成員開嗆V神：基金會不能幫你找市場契合度，優秀的創辦人該自己扛責任
summary:
前以太坊基金成員指出，真正優秀的創辦人早就清楚方向與短板，向基金提出的是具體且有邊界的請求。 （前情提要：以太 […]

〈前以太坊基金成員開嗆V神：基金會不能幫你找市場契合度，優秀的創辦人該自己扛責任〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
前以太坊基金成員指出，真正優秀的創辦人早就清楚方向與短板，向基金提出的是具體且有邊界的請求。
（前情提要：以太坊新提案 EIP-8361 曝光：質押率達 50% 收益）
（背景補充：以太坊下個升級「Pectra」有什麼料？質押者救濟機制與錢包）
前以太坊基金創業支援成員 Abbas Khan 近日在社群媒體表示，離開以太坊基金後可以直言：真正優秀的創辦人很清楚，基金無法替專案找到產品市場契合（PMF）。
Khan 指出，那些成功建立專案的團隊通常已經明確了方向、短板與需求，向基金提出的是具體且有邊界的請求。部分創辦人曾寄望於以太坊的轉發或基金支援來解決分發與 PMF 問題，但「沒有基金會能讓你成功，做產品、找分發、驗證 PMF，責任在你自己」。
以太坊基金的「支援」與「成就」是兩回事
Khan 也承認，早期以太坊基金缺乏創辦人支援團隊的批評確實合理，相關功能後來也有所改善。但他強調「支援建設者」與「期望基金會成就你」是兩回事。
基金會應該提供的是資源對接、入門專案與指導等基礎幫助，但無法替團隊建構專案或決定命運。這番話也提醒正在 Web3 領域創業的團隊——資金與資源可以來自外部，但產品方向必須由創辦人自己驗證。
Web3 創業的 PMF 在哪？
目前以太坊生態正經歷基礎設施升級的密集期。EIP-8361 新提案力阻 ETH 通膨危機，SharpLink CEO 也公開反對EIP-8363 砍質押收益。這些升級直接影響質押者的收益結構，也間接影響依賴質押收益生存的早期專案的現金流。
對創辦人來說，PMF 不只是產品好不好用，更是產品是否切中了市場的真實需求。以太坊生態的競爭日益激烈，a16z 最新募資 150 億美元瞄準 AI 與加密領域，日本首相岸田文雄也公開支援 Web3，期待更多專案加入。但資金湧入不代表每個專案都能找到立足點。
Abbas Khan 的觀察點出了 Web3 創業的核心真相：基金會能幫你開啟門，但要走進去並留下痕跡，還得靠自己驗證產品與市場的契合度。

title: CryptoQuant：CME 避險基金轉多：比特幣期貨罕見出現淨多頭
summary:
CryptoQuant 創辦人 Ki Young Ju 指出，芝商所（CME）避險基金的比特幣期貨持倉已翻轉為 […]

〈CryptoQuant：CME 避險基金轉多：比特幣期貨罕見出現淨多頭〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
CryptoQuant 創辦人 Ki Young Ju 指出，芝商所（CME）避險基金的比特幣期貨持倉已翻轉為淨多頭，在基差交易（carry trade）機制下多年持續偏空的格局中，這是一次罕見的訊號。
（前情提要：BTC需求萎縮至「負65萬枚」是7年罕見！CryptoQuant：最終清洗才剛開始）
（背景補充：芝商所 CME Group 聯手納斯達克推出首款「加密指數期貨」，一口氣打包 BTC、ETH、SOL..等七大幣種）
芝商所（CME）的比特幣期貨市場出現多年未見的反轉訊號。CryptoQuant 創辦人兼執行長 Ki Young Ju 在 X 上發布一張持倉趨勢圖，指出避險基金在 CME 的比特幣期貨部位已經翻轉為淨多頭，這種情況在基差交易（carry trade）主導的機構操作模式下極為罕見。來源連結
Hedge funds on CME flipped net long BTC futures.
This is rare. The basis trade keeps them structurally short. That's why this chart's been red for years. You can't carry trade into a net long.
The suits are betting on upside. pic.twitter.com/hG1musewVx
— Ki Young Ju (@ki_young_ju) August 10, 2026
為什麼「避險基金轉多」很特別
傳統上，參與 CME 比特幣期貨的避險基金以基差交易（cash-and-carry arbitrage）為主：在現貨市場買入比特幣，同時在期貨市場放空，鎖定展期收益。這種策略在機制上就會讓期貨端的持倉長期偏向空方，所以 Ki Young Ju 所貼出的持倉圖過去幾年幾乎一直維持紅色（空頭佔優）。
要讓這類機構在期貨端形成淨多頭，代表他們不再只是收展期費，而是直接押注比特幣價格上漲。這不是套利，是方向性看多。
時間點與市場背景
這篇貼文發布在 8 月 10 日，距離本週初的美國經濟資料與市場波動不遠。同一時間，市場上也有幾個平行的資金動向值得注意：
- 美國現貨比特幣 ETF 上週流入 8.53 億美元，創下 4 月以來的單周新高。
- 有比特幣巨鯨礦工在過去 20 天累計向 Binance 轉入超過 6,494 枚 BTC，套現壓力浮現。
- Coinglass 資料顯示，若 BTC 突破 6.7 萬美元，主流 CEX 空單清算規模可達 4.12 億美元。
避險基金從「收展期費的空頭」變成「押注上漲的多頭」，通常不會是單筆偶發交易，而是策略層面的調整。這意味著機構層面開始重新評估比特幣的風險報酬比，尤其是在現貨 ETF 持續吸金、CME 本身也不斷擴大加密衍生品的產品線之際。
下一步觀察什麼
CME 的持倉資料是延後公布的，這張圖顯示的是近期最新一期資料的趨勢。值得追蹤的重點有三：

title: Travelodge staff gave domestic abuser key to his victim's room
summary: A woman tells the BBC her attacker kicked her hotel room door "off its hinges" after reception gave him the key.
full_text:
Travelodge staff gave domestic abuser key to his victim's room
- Published
A domestic violence victim has told BBC Breakfast how she was attacked in her hotel room after Travelodge reception staff gave a key to her abuser.
The woman, whom the BBC is calling Lucy, said she was "failed" by the chain and described it as one of the "most traumatic nights of my life" after the man kicked the door off its hinges.
She contacted the BBC after hearing about the sentencing of Kyran Smith, who sexually assaulted a woman in her bed at a Travelodge in Maidenhead in 2022.
Speaking about Lucy's case, Travelodge said that while incidents like this were "very rare", customer safety and security was, and remained, a priority with staff undergoing recent training.
Lucy said she was staying at the hotel in October 2025 for "a night away from the fear" following a period of abuse that left her "frightened and exhausted".
"He walked into the hotel and told the receptionist that his girlfriend was upstairs having a seizure. He asked what room I was in and what floor I was staying on," she said.
The receptionist handed him a key before directing him upstairs to Lucy's room, she said.
"I couldn't believe it. The one place I thought he could never get to, he had somehow reached. I felt sick with panic. My safe place disappeared in an instant," she added.
She said he physically attacked her and tried to grab her phone.
After Lucy convinced her attacker to leave, he returned, "banging, shouting and becoming more aggressive".
"I was absolutely terrified. I froze, hoping he would stop. Instead, he kicked the hotel room door off its hinges and forced his way back inside."
She said she ran downstairs "shaking, crying and begging for help", adding: "I thought someone would protect me."
Instead, Lucy was offered another room in the hotel.
Travelodge said it had investigated what happened and found the attacker had given Lucy's full name and room number at reception.
However, a spokesperson said an established policy – to never confirm to a third party that a guest was staying at one of its hotels – was not followed and "this should not have happened".
Lucy is one of a number of people who have contacted the BBC following the sentencing of Smith, who was jailed for seven and a half years in February.
After sentencing, Travelodge said there had been "immediate changes to our room access security policy to ensure that any additional or replacement room keys are only issued with explicit permission from the person (or people) staying in the room".
- Travelodge probes further room access reports 
  - Published30 March
- Travelodge boss was sent email by sex assault victim 
  - Published1 April
- Travelodge accused of not accepting wrongdoing 
  - Published27 July
Another woman, Jo from Leeds, contacted BBC News following coverage of the Maidenhead attack.
In July, she woke in her room to an unknown man standing at the end of her bed, and screamed for help.
"It was just horrible, it was horrendous. Terrifying. I was shaking so badly," she said.
Her friend who was staying in the room heard him say, "I'm sorry, they gave me this key," she said.
Jo considered staying elsewhere following the reports of the attack in 2022, but was reassured by Travelodge's chief executive Jo Boydell, who previously said: "The safety and security of customers in our hotels is extremely important and we want everyone to be safe, and feel safe, in our hotels."
Jo said: "What happened to us shouldn't have happened. And the assurances [Travelodge] gave are not accurate. The systems are failing."
In response, Travelodge said an investigation found "our updated room access security policies, which were in place at the time, were not correctly followed, which is not acceptable.
"We have retrained the hotel team on our current room security and check-in procedures."
Andy Smith, who has travelled the country with his band and stays in dozens of Travelodge hotels a year, said he had been given keys to other people's rooms recently.
"On Friday, we went up to the room and there was a guy already asleep in there in a state of undress," he said.
It followed another incident about 18 months ago where another man had gained access to his room by telling reception staff he was checking in under a common name such as "Mr Smith", Smith said.
"I think he just chanced it. Because my name's Smith, I think it's just the pure luck of it. I mean, why wouldn't anyone be asking for ID or anything, like a booking reference or an email address. It's beggar's belief."
Travelodge responded by saying "any case of an unauthorised person entering a guest's room is a significant cause for concern and we want to be clear that these incidents should not have happened".
A spokesperson for industry group UKHospitality said recent incidents were "extremely serious" and it understood the concerns from guests.
It was working with its members to create guidance on customer security which would be published shortly, the spokesperson said.
"Developed with sector experts, we have continued to engage with ministers on this important work and received positive feedback from government on the work taking place to further bolster guest security," they said.
Travelodge said it had commissioned an independent review led by a barrister "to examine our room access security policies and escalation procedures".
"While the independent review is progressing, we have also conducted an internal review and have since made changes to our room access security policy and incident escalation procedures supported by training for all of our customer-facing colleagues."
Lucy said the night of her attack had "changed me forever", and she was now unable to stay in hotels because of the fear and anxiety she feels.
"Hotels need safeguarding procedures... because one mistake can have devastating consequences," she said.
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

title: Risk of patient safety 'bonfire' with Health Bill changes, Lib Dems say
summary: The party says the government's plans to modernise the NHS risk another major  hospital scandal.
full_text:
Risk of patient safety 'bonfire' with Health Bill changes, Lib Dems say
- Published
The Liberal Democrats have urged Andy Burnham to stop the "bonfire of patient safety" as part of the government's plans to modernise the NHS.
Healthwatch England (HWE), an independent body which represents the views of patients at their local health and social care providers, is set to be scrapped under the NHS Modernisation Bill.
The Health Service Safety Investigation Bureau (HSSIB), which carries out patient safety investigations, is also being abolished.
The government says its changes will strip back bureaucracy and improve patient safety.
The Lib Dems warned it risks another Stafford Hospital scandal – where years of abuse and neglect led to hundreds of unnecessary patient deaths.
A Healthcare Commission report found the scandal – one of the biggest in NHS history – involved at least 400 more deaths than expected between 2005 and 2008.
Under the government proposals, Healthwatch's responsibilities will be transferred to integrated care boards (ICBs) and local authorities, meaning they would have to respond to feedback about their own services, rather than being challenged by an independent body.
Separately, HSSIB's functions will be transferred to the government-run Care Quality Commission (CQC), which the Lib Dems argue raises concerns there is no guarantee that staff who raise safety concerns are given anonymity.
Other measures include the abolition of NHS England in a bid to centralise the running of health and social care services under the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC).
The government says this will reduce bureaucracy and allow more resources to be delivered to frontline healthcare services.
- NHS England to be axed as role returns to government control 
  - Published13 March 2025
The NHS Modernisation Bill is currently at the report stage and due for a third reading on 7 September.
Liberal Democrat health spokesperson Helen Morgan said this was "a catastrophic step backwards" and described it as the "greatest backward step in patient safety in a generation".
"Andy Burnham must urgently put an end to this, and fix the Health Bill so that modernising the NHS doesn't come at the expense of accountability, transparency or patient safety," Morgan added.
In a speech on NHS reform in January, then-Health Secretary Wes Streeting said "there are many decent people working at Healthwatch who care, but the job of listening to patients can't be farmed out to an arm's length body".
"It must be core business for the NHS. That is why we're taking it back in-house and I won't back down on that either."
The Lib Dems also said the current bill removes the duty for the NHS to cooperate with the Care Quality Commission in providing key safety data and removes automatic "safe space" protections for whistleblowers.
Amendments tabled by the Liberal Democrats would cancel the changes and the party is "urging the new Burnham administration to adopt them".
The party vowed to robustly fight the government in the House of Lords, where Labour doesn't have a majority.
A DHSC spokesperson said NHS Modernisation Bill "explicitly preserves safe space provisions and staff will continue to be protected".
"The reforms we are introducing will give patients a stronger, clearer voice at the heart of health and social care."
Burnham was health secretary in 2009, when the Healthcare Commission's report was released on the Stafford Hospital scandal. Burnham then launched an independent inquiry in 2010.
In May, the Local Government Association (LGA) told the BBC disbanding Healthwatch would be a "significant step back" in accountability.
"Without an independent, locally rooted voice to challenge and represent communities, there is a risk of duplication and gaps in accountability," the LGA said.
There are currently more than 150 local Healthwatch organisations in England.
  - Published16 March 2025
  - Published19 December 2019

title: Thai school shooter learnt how to use guns via social media
summary: Police say they are still investigating the 14-year-old shooter's motive.
full_text:
Thai school shooter learnt how to use guns via social media
- Published
A teenager who opened fire at his home and school in Thailand, killing eight people and himself, had taught himself how to use a gun via social media, police have said.
The boy's consumption of violent social media content, anxiety over his studies and family issues, and conflict with friends might have also fuelled his actions, authorities said.
Senior police official Atthapol Anusit told reporters on Sunday that they have questioned 17 witnesses so far while investigating the 14-year-old's motive.
Thailand's leader has vowed to introduce new gun laws as the country reels from its deadliest shooting in years.
Eight people have died after the shooting in Thailand's Nonthaburi province, which borders Bangkok.
Authorities say the student at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School - a local branch of a prestigious secondary school - had shot dead his grandparents at home using a handgun owned by his grandfather, before heading to school where he opened fire at teachers and students.
When asked by reporters if the act was premeditated, Atthapol said that was "probably" the case.
Evidence that police have gathered include the firearm used by the teen in the shooting, cartridge cases, his mobile phone and a knife found in the bag he had carried to school.
His computer at home indicates that he had accessed violent content on social media, police say.
Forensic officers previously said that the gunshots were "quite accurate", with several hitting "vital spots" on victims' bodies.
Atthapol said on Sunday that the police investigation did not find evidence that the teen had practised shooting or trained at a firearms range.
However, the teen's teacher had previously confiscated a BB gun that he had ordered online and brought to school, Atthapol said.
The teen had lived with his grandparents since he was two years old, as his parents had separated, authorities say.
The boy's mother, who is not named, told Reuters that the teen was a "bright, cheerful person" and "behaved normally".
His mother told Reuters that she had last seen the boy during a recent school holiday.
"We are truly devastated, because no one thought this would happen," she said.
The teen's father apologised for his actions, local media reported.
One of the school's teachers described the boy as a good student with good grades, while education authorities described him as an avid gamer.
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said previously that his grandmother was a teacher who "might have been strict" with the teenager.
As investigations continue into the deadly shooting, many are mourning the victims with some laying flowers in front of the school.
On Sunday, dozens dressed in black gathered at a Buddhist temple in Nonthaburi province for the funeral of a 12-year-old girl, who was injured during the shooting and died two days later.
"She was a good kid. A kid who loved to do every activity," the girl's music teacher told AFP. "She loved to dance."

title: Tech leaders say AI means less work - their staff say they work up to 90 hours a week
summary: Tech companies are not modelling their own claims of the technology giving people more free time.
full_text:
Tech leaders say AI means less work - their staff say they work up to 90 hours a week
- Published
For years now, executives at companies that are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars a year into developing various artificial intelligence tools have insisted that the technology will ultimately mean people will spend less of their time working.
An engineering director at Google said four years ago that AI would deliver a four-day work week by 2025, external.
Earlier this year, and just one year after that engineering director's prediction, OpenAI took up the challenge, in a manner of speaking. It formally urged companies to start testing out a four-day work week (with no change in pay), claiming that AI will soon be able to speed up so much human labour that the corporate world should prepare itself.
However, a former OpenAI technical employee who left the company last year told the BBC the firm never actually trialled the four-day work week it suggested others should try while they were there.
Instead, the person described what was often a gruelling work culture marked by frequent "crisis meetings", working on weekends, and "super cut-throat" performance reviews that would see colleagues suddenly let go.
"You go in on Saturday or Sunday just to catch up or make sure things aren't broken," the person said.
Other companies have also pushed the idea that AI will effectively reduce the number of hours people need to work, for better or worse.
Anthropic has boasted that its popular coding tool and chatbot Claude is capable of working on its own for seven hours without a break, external, essentially a full corporate workday. Meta's Mark Zuckerberg has said his company is in the middle of the year when "AI starts to dramatically change the way that we work" and that such tools let far fewer employees do more than they ever could have before.
While Meta has since laid off 1 in 10 of its employees, Anthropic's chief executive Dario Amodei has warned that as AI tools inevitably become more productive, it could mean, external even broader job losses.
Despite these claims, workers inside these same tech companies, who are not only developing but using the very AI tools that will purportedly perform at least some of people's work, say they are clocking in far more than the typical five-day, 40-hour work week.
'Sprints'
US tech workers are typically well-compensated, external, and while other industries such as investment banking, law and medicine also often see people work long hours, a 14-hour workday was not always the norm in tech. For years, it was a more typical 9-5 office job.
But the former OpenAI employee said they would put in at least 70 hours a week, much more than they did in previous tech jobs. The person now works at a start-up also focused on AI, and said their work-life balance has improved, working closer to 50-60 hours a week, "outside of sprints".
A "sprint" is term for a common period in technology companies in which people work long hours in the weeks leading up to a release of a new feature or product.
Inside AI companies and larger tech companies working furiously on AI projects, however, such sprints can be extreme.
At OpenAI and Anthropic, for instance, sprints can stretch on for many weeks and top 90 hours of work in a seven-day period, tech workers that the BBC spoke to for this story said.
Neither company responded to BBC requests for comment.
Being 'drafted'
At Meta, workers said they have been abruptly pushed onto teams this year doing AI work being treated as urgent. They called it being "drafted", according to one current and one former employee, because people were not given a choice.
"They just move you over," the former employee said. "You can't say no – or if you do, you have to quit."
They said although Meta recently began to walk back, external that strict take it or leave us approach, by then many workers had already been forced onto such work.
The hours on such teams at Meta are often long, with staff working into the night, on weekends, and feeling they are "on call" during the hours they are not working, according to descriptions of the work from the current and former employees.
There are no limits, external in the US on how many hours a person over the age of 16 can work. In the UK and Europe, for instance, laws limit a working week to 48 hours, including overtime.
Meta's current AI projects include the creation of an AI tool that can be used for software engineering and other kinds of work, and building AI model infrastructure that can measure an AI model's success in replicating various tasks, the employees added.
"You're literally working in teams of people trying to replicate humans doing jobs," the former employee said.
That work, the person added, seems "endless".
A Meta spokesperson declined to comment.
Even tech workers who are not directly involved in the development of AI tools are facing longer hours due to the technology.
A former Google employee, Amin Shali, left the company in May due to the ways in which he claimed AI was negatively impacting his job, like having to often work all hours of the night because internal engineering functions had failed. This was happening more frequently as Google moved crucial resources like processing units and memory storage over to AI projects.
A Google spokesperson declined to comment.
Since leaving Google, Shali told the BBC that his sleep and overall health had improved. He said he's realised that heavy reliance on AI tools in large tech companies "creates a bad culture with excess pressure on engineers".
Time savings 'sucked up'
Some new research suggests that AI tools are making people's workloads even more burdensome.
A study, external out of UC Berkeley followed hundreds of workers at a US tech company for eight months as they used AI. It found the employees "worked at a faster pace, took on a broader scope of tasks, and extended work into more hours of the day".
Neil Thompson, an innovation scholar at MIT, said that even at tech companies leading on AI development, it is unlikely that workers are being told to simply deploy the tools that are supposed to do some of their work and move on.
"It leads to a situation where even if there were real time savings, it would be sucked up by the changes, and implementing them, and making sure they worked," Thompson said.
The UC Berkeley research found that the workload of tech employees was expanded in part because of the need to constantly check the output of AI tools.
In a situation where an employee had smoothed out processes for AI tools, people also tend to fill any time saved with more work, Thompson added, either because they want to or they feel they should do in order to prove their value to an employer.
"People assume that 20% less work means four-day weeks," Thompson said. "But new work emerges."
As Shali observed: "AI is supposed to be doing so much for us now, so many more people should at least have better health and better sleep."
Instead, it seems to be the opposite.
Related topics

title: 'Not afraid to stay': The Canadians taking fighting wildfires into their own hands
summary: With wildfires now widespread and frequent, some rural residents in Canada are learning how to fight the flames themselves and protect their own homes.
full_text:
'Not afraid to stay': The Canadians taking fighting wildfires into their own hands
- Published
When a wildfire broke out near his First Nation community in northern Ontario, Hubert Wigwas decided to stay put.
He put sprinklers on his roof to extinguish falling embers. He checked on elders in his community who also stayed behind, and he fuelled up four boats down on the lake in case they needed a quick escape.
"This is everything I've built in my 58 years," Wigwas, a councillor from Gull Bay First Nation, told the BBC. "I'm just not going to run away and let it burn."
Canada has seen some of its worst fire seasons in recent years, and experienced its most destructive on record in 2023, when blazes tore through forest land roughly the size of Syria. As of this August, more than 750 wildfires are actively burning across the country.
The impact has been felt as far as the US Midwest, where smoke had choked the air in cities. Even President Donald Trump has taken note, threatening to further tariff Canada for allowing "filthy, polluted" air to waft south of the border.
The intensifying wildfires have sparked a national conversation: Are there enough firefighters to battle these more challenging fire seasons? What happens when resources are stretched too thin? And how can remote communities, often closest to danger because of their proximity to Canada's vast boreal forest, learn to live with this new reality?
Wigwas asked himself these questions when he decided to stay, even as he faces a fine of around C$800 ($570; £425) for defying evacuation orders.
Leaders of Gull Bay First Nation, also known as Kiashke Zaaging Anishinaabek, have been urging residents to stay away since mid-July as more than 150 wildfires burn across Ontario's northwest.
Its chief penned a letter on 29 July pleading with those who have remained to leave immediately, saying that Ontario firefighters cannot do their jobs safely with people still in their homes.
It is the same message officials across the country have been conveying in British Columbia, where around 115 fires are currently burning.
But with a wildfire 24km outside his community, Wigwas, speaking in late July, said he had yet to see fire personnel from out of town there to help fireproof properties or keep an eye out on the elders who remained.
He said it made him realise that his First Nation would benefit from setting up its own wildfire emergency response and teaching residents how to protect their own homes.
"Everybody talks about climate change, but nobody is doing something to unite the (First Nations) reserves and have a system like that set up," Wigwas said.
Dave Bradley, a spokesperson for Ontario's ministry of natural resources, did not address Wigwas' claim directly, but said the province has been in "constant contact" with First Nations leaders.
He added that fire fighting resources are directed based on "fire behaviour, weather conditions and risks to communities."
In the west-coast province of British Columbia - long the front line of Canada's wildfire response - people are doing just what Wigwas is envisioning for his First Nation, with efforts underway to train residents of rural and remote communities how to safely respond to wildfires before out-of-town crews can arrive.
Sonja Leverkus, a wildfire researcher and specialist, said she has helped train more than 400 people in and around her community of Fort Nelson over the last three years through a firefighting group she helped start called the Northeast BC Rural Incident Management Team.
She told the BBC that her efforts are inspired by a realisation that Canada needs to change how it fights wildfires as climate change increases their frequency and intensity.
"There are not enough human beings in Canada," she said, with the appropriate training, "to fight the fires that we have currently, especially over the last five years".
Remote communities, where the nearest town might be hundreds of kilometres away, can sometimes be bumped down the priority list for BC firefighting crews if there are blazes threatening more populated areas, she said.
Her crew, who are primarily indigenous, have carried out prescribed burns, also known as a hazard reduction burns – a practice of setting planned, controlled blazes to remove fuels that could contribute to wildfires.
They have also helped put out smaller fires before they grow out of control using fire wagons that they purchased through fundraising and grants, sometimes arriving ahead of provincial firecrews and then working in tandem with them, Leverkus said.
When a major wildfire tore through Fort Nelson in 2024, she said she and 40 of her team members stayed behind and were hired by the province to clear flammables and support fire suppression activities.
Leverkus also organised a structural protection training course for locals to learn how to shield buildings from embers that can quickly spur fires that engulf entire towns.
"We have mechanics, we have carpenters, we have real good problem solvers," Leverkus said. "We're all not afraid to stay."
Cam Allen, a 70-year-old former helicopter pilot in Fort Nelson who has previously fought fires from the air, said he recently took Leverkus' course to learn about ground fire suppression techniques, and, more broadly, how to help if a blaze reaches his town.
He mentioned John Carr, a California man who went viral last year, external for staying behind and warding off flames with a garden hose during the Palisades fire, ultimately saving his home even when others around it burned down.
"It makes you wonder, if 100 people had stayed or 1,000 people had stayed behind and actually did what he did, how much more could have been saved?" Allen asked.
But not all were as fortunate as Carr during the Los Angeles fires, which killed a total of 29 people – a few of whom had, too, defied evacuation orders in order to protect their homes, even as officials urged thousands in the area to leave.
Leverkus' group is not officially recognised by BC's government, and what it is trying to achieve highlights simmering tensions in fire-prone regions between those who enforce evacuation orders and those who defy them.
Last week, wildfire crews in BC were forced to rescue a man when his home in the Village of Clinton was surrounded by flames, after he had refused to evacuate.
In a wildfire update on Tuesday, BC's minister responsible for emergency management reiterated that all those who are under evacuation orders should leave.
"We may not be able to get back to you if an emergency happens," warned Minister Kelly Greene, adding that evacuation orders are made as "a last resort to keep people and communities safe".
Paul Kovacs, a researcher at the University of Western Ontario and director of its Catastrophic Loss Reduction Institute, said that Canada has had a lower fatality rate from wildfires despite their frequency in part because of its evacuation approach.
The stay and defend mindset, he said, "is aggressively opposed" by the academic community in Canada, as opposed to other fire-prone countries like Australia.
"In the hierarchy of what is it that you do to manage a wildfire, preservation of life is first," Kovacs said.
Rural and remote communities can and should play an outsized role in informing officials of how best to protect their town, he said, and can do a lot of work to fire proof homes and structures. But that work, he argued, should not be done "while the fire is burning."
A spokesperson for BC's Ministry of Forests told the BBC that self-organised groups in rural areas can be hired temporarily by the province during an active wildfire, but only when there are no more available provincial firefighters in the area.
The ministry added that BC Wildfire's full-time staff has increased by 56% in recent years to respond to the growing frequency of fires, in addition to seasonal staff.

title: 'Roll on 2027' as Fleadh 2026 in Belfast comes to an end
summary: The 2026 festival was being hosted in the city for the first time and ended on Sunday.
full_text:
'Roll on 2027' as Fleadh 2026 comes to an end
- Published
The first All Ireland Fleadh in Belfast ended in the early hours of Monday morning with organisers saying they were overwhelmed by the positive response they received from all communities.
It is estimated that there were more than a million people in the city centre during the eight days of the fleadh.
At least 4,000 were still in the grounds of Belfast City Hall at 01:00 BST to hear the closing speeches and final tunes.
Niall McClean, co-chair of the organising committee, told the crowd they were all part of an historic event.
He said: "We've done something that has never, ever happened in this city before. We've brought every single community together – and everybody has absolutely loved it."
McClean added that it has "put a permanent smile on my face. I'm the happiest man in Belfast. Roll on 2027".
"What an incredible week. Everyone I have spoken to has had an amazing time here in Belfast, thousands of people all on a high.
"Belfast has shone, the world has come to our doorstep, bringing the biggest numbers ever seen for a Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann.
"I'm so proud of our branch and all our members, and what we have achieved together. We dared to dream and those dreams have come true."
To loud applause, he ended by saying: "Well done Belfast, we'll see you next year."
The All Ireland Fleadh returns to the city from 1 to 8 August 2027.
Dr Labhrás Ó Murchú, director general of Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann (society of the musicians of Ireland) which runs the annual All Ireland Fleadh, described this year's festival as a "miracle."
He told the crowd: "I hope that when you go back (home), you'll bring with you not just the memories but you'll tell people that you were part of - and you witnessed and you experienced - a miracle here in Belfast this week.
"Because it was a miracle, a miracle of music, a miracle of friendship, a miracle of creativity."
The final performance of the night came from Lissadell Céilí Band, winners of the senior Céilí band competition.
Earlier performances included Belfast-based Campbell College Bugles, Pipes and Drums and Bangor singer Foy Vance.
Lord Mayor of Belfast councillor Róis-Máire Donnelly officially brought the fleadh to a close.
The eight-day event was jointly hosted by Belfast City Council, Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann (CCE) and Ards CCÉ.
Donnelly, said: "Words cannot do justice to how proud I am of this city and the magic that it has produced over the last eight days.
"Our spirit, our craic and our shared love of music, from all our different communities, have all been embraced and displayed for everyone to enjoy."
She described the event as a "watershed moment" adding: "A sign of our city's strength, ambition and future potential. Fleadh 2026 has surpassed all of our expectations."
John Walsh, Chief Executive of Belfast City Council, said bringing the Fleadh to the city "has been a long time in the making".
"Seeing it come to life on our streets this past week will live long in the memory.
"Whether you volunteered, performed or became a proud tourist in your hometown, your support, co-operation and positivity have all been essential in making the event such a huge success – I hope to see you all at the Fleadh again, 1-8 August 2027."
Dr Labhrás O Murchú from CCÉ said the event was "unprecedented".
"Belfast opened its doors and hearts to the multitudes who came from far and near for this amazing celebration, which will have an encore in 2027.
"One million fans can say to Belfast 'you are the envy of the world', with perhaps billions worldwide aware of the cultural history made in August 2026."
Calls for city centre to be pedestrianised
The success of the Fleadh has prompted calls for Belfast city centre to be pedestrianised permanently.
A large zone in the city centre was created over the course of the festival.
Representatives from the Alliance Party from across Belfast have now written to the council and other bodies calling for a "comprehensive review of pedestrianisation" in the city centre.
South Belfast MLA Kate Nicholl said the Fleadh showed "Belfast at its best, open, welcoming and full of life".
"When we design our streets around people instead of traffic, our city centre becomes somewhere people actually want to spend time, and that's good for our shops, our hospitality sector and as we've seen so clearly this week, our sense of civic pride".
She said accessibility had to be taken seriously, however.
"Any expansion has to be designed with disabled people and accessibility organisations from the start, not bolted on afterwards. That means looking properly at disabled parking, accessible drop-off points, public transport connectivity and wayfinding," she said.
Green Party councillor Brian Smyth said the "bottom line" is that the Fleadh "would not have worked without pedestrianisation in the city centre".
"I think it is starting a conversation with people," he said.
"This isn't some new, radical idea."
However disability campaign groups, such as Disabled People Against Cuts Northern Ireland (DPAC NI), have voiced concern.
On social media they said: "We've seen this played out elsewhere and it's disabled people who pay a price for 'progress'."
DPAC NI spokesperson Dermot Devlin said that "many disabled people can only walk or wheel short distances".
"We need to park or get off public transport close to our destinations."
He added that "further pedestrianisation" of the city centre "without significant mitigation will exclude many of us from our city".
"We have a right to access the city on an equal basis to everyone else. Like everyone else we use the city centre as a place to shop, a place to work and place to go out in.
"Agencies involved in making permanent or temporary changes to the city centre must uphold our rights, not ignore them."

title: 'Body in suitcase' found in Australia turns out to be lifelike doll
summary: Forensics revealed that the 'realistic' looking body was in fact not human.
full_text:
'Body in suitcase' found in Australia turns out to be lifelike doll
- Published
Australian police called in to investigate a body found in a suitcase have concluded that the "victim" was in fact a lifelike doll.
The suitcase was discovered by two men on the side of a road near the small village of Oallen, about 230km (143 miles) south-west of Sydney.
On Monday, police announced a murder investigation, sparking intense interest in the case but backtracked hours later, saying forensic testing had proved the contents were not human.
The contents in the suitcase were "mistaken for a human originally, so they are very realistic in terms of looking like human remains," said Supt Linda Bradbury from the Hume Police District.
"But we've confirmed by other means that they are not."
The doll was wearing clothing, had hair and a nose piercing," police said, adding that "the item also had markings that resembled bruises and grazes".
Supt Bradbury said forensic teams and investigators had attended the scene on Sunday and that all processes had been followed.
"The idea is to not disturb crime scenes as much as possible, to maintain the integrity of our investigation," Bradbury said, adding she had "no regrets" about how the case was handled.
Hours earlier, Bradbury had told media that it has been "quite a shocking discovery" for the two men who found the suitcase.
"Unfortunately, they were on a weekend drive as a lot of people do over the weekend and stopped for a break," she said.
She said the pair had made the "right decision" to report the find.
"They were affected yesterday and we will be in touch to let them know that it was not human remains," Bradbury said.
Police have now closed their investigations.

full_text:
Chinese researchers use microbubbles to shrink aggressive liver tumours: paper
Cancer patients who received the experimental treatment in combination with standard therapies saw improvement, study finds
Chinese researchers have found a safe way to shrink advanced tumours from an aggressive form of liver cancer, an advance that could see microbubbles used to enhance current treatments.
The tiny gas-filled bubbles, typically a few micrometres in diameter, were originally designed as contrast agents in ultrasound imaging, but scientists have recently been exploring their therapeutic potential.
According to a paper published by the peer-reviewed Scientific Reports on July 19, the study compared cancer patients who received the standard therapy with a group that also received the experimental ultrasound and microbubble treatment.
The researchers, from the Affiliated Hospital of Guangdong Medical University and Huzhou Central Hospital, found that tumours in the second group of patients grew smaller than in those who only received the standard therapy.
“This technology shows [promise] for enhancing localised treatment approaches in cancer patients,” they wrote in the reviewed but unedited manuscript, which was provided with legal disclaimers to give early access to the findings, according to the journal.
Microbubbles are used in various fields, including engineering, environmental clean-up, and medicine. When injected into the bloodstream and hit by ultrasound waves, these bubbles can expand or contract.

full_text:
A “preconceived plan” to do harm at a party has resulted in a young man’s death and murder charges for eight teenagers, police say.
The group of teens allegedly attended an Airbnb gathering south of Brisbane armed with various weapons before it erupted into violence and left the 21-year-old man with catastrophic head injuries.
He was gravely injured after the party at the rented home in Bahrs Scrub, a suburb of Logan, on 26 July, Det Insp Ian Galpin told reporters on Monday.
‘‘A 21-year-old Redbank Plains man was located in an unconscious state, suffering head injuries,’’ he said.
He was transported to hospital in a critical condition and died six days later.
A group of young men have been accused of arming themselves before they arrived at the party which left several vehicles destroyed, a home extensively damaged and a street shut down, police said.
‘‘The police will allege that this group had a preconceived plan, which included arming themselves with various weapons before attending Bahrs Scrub with the common purpose of inflicting harm on persons at that address,’’ Galpin said.
The fatal attack triggered a major homicide investigation.
‘‘More than 80 police were involved in the execution of 14 search warrants across three police districts,’’ Galpin said.
Four teens were initially charged with murder on 6 August – two 18-year-olds and two 19-year-olds.
Another four were located and charged on Sunday – a 17-year-old and three 18-year-olds.
“Our investigations have continued, and [on Sunday] … we located an additional four persons at short-term accommodation in Morayfield, and those persons were also arrested and charged with murder,” Galpin said.
Police have warned more arrests are possible.
‘‘It is an ongoing investigation, so that is a possibility. If we identify more persons involved in this offence, then they will be charged.’’
Police liaison officers and community leaders have been working to prevent any retaliation.
‘‘Everyone that we have spoken to, they want nothing but peace within their community, and that’s why I’m confident there won’t be any further retaliation,’’ Galpin said.
‘‘We’ll continue to support the community, and we’ll also continue to deliver our message that any form of violence will not be tolerated.’’
Galpin praised the response from local residents, saying community cooperation had been “nothing short of amazing”.
‘‘If not for this cooperation, I don’t think we’d be in the position that we’re here in today and I think it highlights the importance of police working with the community and vice versa to solve these serious crimes.’’

Good morning. In late July, Itamar Ben-Gvir, West Bank settler and far-right extremist minister of security in Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, joined a group of more than 2,000 Jewish extremists to storm al-Aqsa mosque compound, Jerusalem’s most sensitive holy site. The far-right group has been doing this for years. Ben-Gvir has made series of visits to the site over the last three years, eroding norms and inflaming tensions. Jordanian officials have recently warned that it could be at risk of an “imminent” Israeli takeover.
With national elections scheduled in October, and many eyes still firmly on Gaza (this weekend, Netanyahu rejected a US-backed 15 point plan for peace), the Israeli government appears to be racing to expand Israeli settlements and accelerate ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem before its mandate expires.
For this morning’s First Edition, I spoke to our senior international correspondent, Julian Borger, about the latest incursions, and how Israeli extremists are trying to create a new reality in Jerusalem. That’s after the weekend roundup.
Weekend roundup
- 
  UK politics | Sadiq Khan has called on the government to commit to revamped climate action and to reduce the UK’s reliance on oil and gas, as the UK endures a summer of drought, wildfires and heatwaves.
- 
  US politics | The US Senate voted to confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general in a win for Donald Trump, who will now have his one-time personal attorney sitting atop the nation’s law enforcement apparatus.
- 
  US-Israel war on Iran | Iran has issued tough new demands for reopening the strait of Hormuz, as a deal to open the strategic waterway remained out of reach on Saturday.
- 
  Russia-Ukraine | Up to 50,000 North Korean soldiers will be deployed in Russia, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said. On Saturday, Turkey called for a “moratorium” on attacks by Russia and Ukraine in the Black Sea after a series of strikes on civilian ships there
- 
  World news | The alleged leader of the Kinahan organised crime group was extradited from Dubai on Sunday and met by a huge security operation in Dublin, marking the end of a global game of cat and mouse with European, US and Gulf authorities.
In depth: ‘To erect structures, even if they’re temporary, is a red rag to a bull’
The al-Haram al-Sharif site in Jerusalem’s old city, known to Jews as the Temple Mount, is one of the most contentious places on earth. It’s governed by a fragile agreement that gives Muslims exclusive rights to pray and worship there, while Jews pray at the Western Wall below. But Israel’s messianic right, which has gained a powerful foothold in Netanyahu’s coalition government, is fixated on the site as a symbol of its political project. Their vision of building a new Jewish temple on one of Islam’s holiest sites – once a fringe idea – has become increasingly widespread.
Since 2023, Jewish religious extremists have made numerous visits to the 35-acre compound which is home to both al-Aqsa mosque and Dome of the Rock, the holiest sites for Muslims in Jerusalem and one of holiest sites for Muslims in the world. “At first, you had groups of perhaps 20 Jews, mostly settlers, who were escorted by the police to the far wall of the compound to pray discreetly,” Julian tells me. “If you were just a casual visitor, you wouldn’t necessarily see them”. Over the last two years, however, the groups have grown bigger and more audacious. On 23 July, they sang the national anthem, and prayed and performed rituals in the centre of the compound, while Israeli police – who report to Ben-Gvir, who was in attendance – set up tents to provide shade to the worshippers.
“To erect structures, even if they’re temporary, is a red rag to a bull,” Julian says. “The longstanding fear is that Israelis would knock down the Dome of the Rock or the mosque, or rebuild a [Jewish] temple on the site. And these tents were part of a gradual attempt to push the boundaries.” Eight Arab nations swiftly issued a joint statement condemning “mass incursions by settlers led by extremist Israeli ministers”. Last Wednesday, the Jordanian authorities, who administer the site, held an emergency meeting of Arab and Islamic nations to discuss these risks, and afterwards, the Jordanian authorities condemned Israeli violations and warned that they constituted a “blatant provocation” to Muslims worldwide.
“All they can do is issue strong statements, saying, ‘don’t do this’,” says Julian. The Waqf, the Jordanian-appointed foundation that manages the site, is “defenceless”, he explains. In the run-up to Ramadan this year, Waqf sources told the Guardian that five of its staff had been detained by the Shin Bet, Israel’s counterintelligence service. Meanwhile, Israeli police have begun actively recruiting extremist activists to serve in the Temple Mount Unit, the force responsible for policing the compound. According to Haaretz, the deputy commander of the police’s Temple Mount Unit published a callout to officers on social media and in WhatsApp groups associated with West Bank settlers. “Anyone who wants to take part in implementing sovereignty is welcome to contact me,” he wrote.
Why is the site so significant?
The site’s history is constantly enlisted in attempts to justify the present. Muslims know the raised compound in the south-east of Jerusalem as al-Haram al-Sharif (the Noble Sanctuary), or simply al-Aqsa, after the mosque located at its southern edge. Next to the mosque, at the centre of the compound, is the Dome of the Rock, one of the oldest surviving Islamic places of worship. It’s on this site the prophet Muhammad is said to have ascended to heaven.
At the base of the compound is the Western Wall, a section of retaining wall that survived the destruction of the second Jewish temple in 70CE. The Temple Mount is also the holiest site in Judaism, the site of two temples which were built and then destroyed by invaders in ancient times.
Access to the site has been delicately managed for centuries. After the six-day war in 1967, when Israel captured East Jerusalem from Jordan, the Israeli government agreed that Jordan would continue to be the site’s custodian. Since then, the “status quo”, as it is known, has sought to prevent violent conflict by circumscribing the rights of Muslims and Jews to access the compound. While Jews are permitted to visit the site at specific times, they cannot pray there. Many Jews opt not to visit the site, out of fear of treading on holy ground while ritually impure.
“The status quo represented a historic compromise. Jews got the Western Wall. Muslims got Haram al-Sharif,” Julian says. “But the site has always been a detonator, sitting right there in the centre of the old city, with strong religious beliefs crammed together in a small area.”
How has this erupted in the past?
It’s not uncommon in the region for holy sites to be carefully managed with intricate arrangements. Elsewhere in the Old City, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre is divided up between six Christian denominations, with its keys held by two Muslim families. At the Cave of the Patriarchs in the occupied city of Hebron, a mosque and synagogue share one building.
Past Israeli moves to challenge the status quo at al-Haram al-Sharif have been incendiary, sparking deadly violence. In 2000, then Israeli opposition leader and future prime minister Ariel Sharon made a visit to the site in an attempt to demonstrate Israeli sovereignty, sparking a chain of events that helped ignite the second intifada. More recently, Hamas gave the name “al-Aqsa flood” to its attack on Israel in October 2023 that killed 1,200 Israelis and triggered the war on Gaza, claiming it was provoked by Israeli violations at the Jerusalem mosque.

title: Inside stablecoin firm BVNK’s journey to a $1.8B acquisition by Mastercard
full_text:
Inside stablecoin firm BVNK’s journey to a $1.8B acquisition by Mastercard
Early BVNK investor Concentric shares a fascinating inside view on the stablecoin startup’s journey and the eventual Mastercard deal.
- Mastercard recently closed its acquisition of stablecoin infrastructure firm BVNK for $1.8 billion.
- The deal followed intense competition from Coinbase and Visa, with BVNK ultimately favoring Mastercard over a reportedly higher Coinbase offer because of better cultural fit and strategic alignment.
- The acquisition underscores how major payments players, including Stripe, Visa, Mastercard and Coinbase, are racing to secure positions in the roughly $300 billion stablecoin market..
Long before big-ticket crypto deals and billion-dollar acquisitions make headlines, there’s a long and hard-fought journey, often culminating in a secretive contest where jockeying suitors bid, bluff or walk, until eventually the best match makes it down the aisle. Mastercard’s recent $1.8 billion acquisition of stablecoin infrastructure firm BVNK was no exception.
It’s a process that takes place out of view, under iron-clad non-disclosure agreements, but venture capital firm Concentric — an early investor in BVNK — gave CoinDesk a rare peek behind the curtain, beginning with the startup’s rise and ending with the completion of the deal earlier this week.
The venture capital business is a numbers game. In the case of BVNK, Concentric’s bet paid off: the VC firm backed the stablecoin startup in 2019 at a valuation of just $4 million. Founding partner of Concentric, Kjartan Rist, recalled being introduced to BVNK in 2018.
“They came to us highly recommended by an alumni CEO that we had already backed,” Rist told CoinDesk in an interview. “So, there was a lot of trust there, and this CEO said, ‘You got to meet these guys’. They were serial entrepreneurs coming out of South Africa. They’d never built businesses outside of South Africa, but they were hungry. They were relentless.”
Despite enjoying a sturdy exit, Rist said he feels mixed emotions toward the Mastercard acquisition, having been part of the whole BVNK journey. “It’s actually sad to sign the papers, almost like sending your son off to boarding school,” he said.
Chris Harmse, co-founder and chief business officer at BVNK echoed this: “It's been an incredible journey,” he said in an email. “Concentric has been a valued partner throughout that journey.”
Stablecoins, one of the busiest areas of crypto, have become a focal point for the large card networks and payments players. The total stablecoin market cap is about $300 billion, according to CoinGecko data.
The proverbial cat was set loose among the pigeons when Stripe acquired stablecoin infrastructure firm Bridge in late 2024 for $1.1 billion. This probably put pressure on the likes of Visa and Mastercard to start kicking the tires of other stablecoin shops so as not to be outflanked by Stripe’s aggressive approach.
Mastercard has the deepest respect for Stripe, Rist of Concentric said. “I think that's another way of saying that they're looking over their shoulder. So they are aware of the competitive threat that is coming from Stripe because of the way they execute, the simplicity in their offering and the lack of legacy they have,” he said.
During the cut and thrust of the deal formation, U.S.-listed crypto exchange Coinbase was reported to have had the upper hand at one point, potentially offering as much as $2.5 billion for BVNK. But something changed, which was to do with chemistry, according to Rist.
“The founders, when choosing a partner or choosing someone to buy them, emphasize a lot on the culture and the chemistry,” Rist said. “And the chemistry with Coinbase — although they probably put a bigger number on the table — it didn't work.”
This came down to the fact that Coinbase is an exchange, while Mastercard is a financial services company, Rist added.
“Mastercard was part of the first discussions and BVNK were quite clear when they got into discussions with Mastercard that there was a meeting of minds,” Rist said. “But they decided to try it out with Coinbase. Mastercard stood outside on the porch waiting for them when that didn't work out. So it's been a painless process, to be honest.”
But it wasn’t just Coinbase who muscled in, Rist said. Visa also took a shine to BVNK.
“All the usual suspects were involved, and Visa had an advantage because they were an investor. They made some money out of BVNK…and they actually had an observer position on the board,” Rist said.
In the end, however, Rist said Visa decided not to pursue a potential acquisition. “I think they are adopting a slightly different strategy when it comes to to stablecoins. Rather than owning an operator, they will partner with multiple operators and partner also with Stripe, etcetera,” he said.
CoinDesk recently broke the news that all four firms — Stripe, Visa, Mastercard and Coinbase — were involved in backing a new stablecoin platform, which has since gone live. This only underlines the fact that stablecoins continue to be an area of importance for TradFi institutions despite an ongoing bear market in the crypto industry more broadly.
Looking at specific use cases keeping BVNK busy, Rist pointed to various treasury functions that are streamlined by the use of stablecoins.
“One large payments company working with BVNK rolls its treasury every 24 hours, and now they're using stablecoins to roll it,” he said.
Another benefit comes from the way BVNK and others are servicing companies that have a huge distributed workforce with a number of these workers or freelancers in countries that have very high levels of inflation.
“These firms are using dollar-nominated stablecoins so workers can choose to keep them in their wallets and don’t have to receive pesos or naira, for example,” Rist said.
After backing a winner in the form of BVNK, Concentric is looking for its next stablecoin company to invest in.
“There are hundreds of companies out there now claiming to be the next [big] stablecoin company. In my opinion, only about 10% of these guys are full stack, institutionally verified, and can actually become a winner of some sort,” Rist said. “The other 90% of them are just a front end and some APIs, so it’s our job to figure out who the real guys are.”
