title: Asylum seeker who groomed and raped girl, 13, jailed
summary: Abdul Khan attacked the girl at a nature reserve after pretending to be 14 on Snapchat.
full_text:
Asylum seeker who groomed and raped girl, 13, jailed
- Published
An asylum seeker who raped a 13-year-old girl after pretending to be a teenager on Snapchat has been jailed.
Abdul Khan attacked the girl in a nature reserve in Clifton, Nottingham, on 14 May last year.
Khan arrived in the UK in the back of a lorry in 2015, Nottingham Crown Court heard, and faces automatic deportation to Afghanistan after he has served two thirds of his sentence.
He was jailed for nine and a half years on Monday after he was convicted of two counts of rape, one count of sexual activity with a child, sexual communication with a child, meeting a child following grooming and perverting the course of justice.
A four-day trial was told Khan, who is believed to be 28 and already serving a 23-month sentence for sexual communication with a different child in Derbyshire, arranged to meet his victim in woodland after telling her on the Snapchat messaging app he was a 14-year-old boy.
When they met in person and it was clear he was not 14, he tried to appease her by claiming to be 16, the court heard.
After activity that jurors found had been consensual, Khan, of HMP Nottingham, twice raped the girl.
Judge Mark Watson said the victim told her father what had happened and he contacted police.
Khan was then linked to the rapes by a mobile phone seized during his arrest over his contact with the child in Derbyshire.
Yet despite DNA evidence subsequently linking him to the attack, Nottinghamshire Police said he continued to deny having met the victim.
Addressing Khan, the judge said: "You deliberately concealed your true identity. She thought she was communicating with a child of her own age.
"It was a lie you have persisted with throughout these proceedings."
'Predatory offender'
Prosecutor Dawn Pritchard read out a victim personal statement telling the judge the victim "feels numb when she thinks back to how she felt at the time".
Summarising the statement, Pritchard added: "She felt scared of the world after it happened and felt overwhelmed.
"When she has flashbacks, she sees his face and what happened. She feels like she can't trust anyone."
Defence barrister Andrew Wesley said he was unable to offer any personal mitigation on behalf of Khan, as he still disputed the identity and age under which he was prosecuted.
The judge, describing the defendant's claims over his age and identity as "nonsensical" and bound to fail, added: "The police were called by her father, he learning from her that she had been raped.
"She has on any view been profoundly affected, as her parents must also have been.
"Your sentence will mean automatic deportation."
The defendant, who covered his face with his hands as he walked out of the dock, was also ordered to register as a sex offender indefinitely.
Det Con Madeleine Johnson, from Nottinghamshire Police, said: "Khan is an opportunistic and predatory offender who poses a clear risk to teenage girls and other young women.
"As his previous grooming conviction demonstrates, he was absolutely determined in his ambition to strike up sexual relationships with young girls.
"The victim in this case was particularly vulnerable at the time of this offence and has unsurprisingly suffered a great deal as a result of what Khan did to her."

title: Nigel Farage says incident at his home 'directly linked' to Ann Widdecombe murder
summary: Counter-terrorism police have reopened an inquiry into an incident at the Reform UK's leader's house.
full_text:
Nigel Farage says incident at his home 'directly linked' to Ann Widdecombe murder
- Published
Nigel Farage said an incident at his London home last year was "directly linked" to the murder of Ann Widdecombe, after counter-terror police reopened an inquiry into it last week.
It relates to what Farage described as a "lit incendiary device" being pushed through his letterbox in April 2025, the BBC understands.
Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London has also referred itself to the police watchdog over how the initial investigation was handled.
At a Monday press conference, the Reform UK leader said: "I understand this is a completely unprecedented move, and yes, this is directly linked to the murder of Ann Widdecombe, and I'm afraid I just can't tell you any more than that at this stage."
Asked about the investigation, he said: "Clearly, counter-terrorism made some mistakes, which is why they referred themselves to the Independent Office of Police (Conduct)."
It is not yet clear how the incident at Farage's house is linked to Widdecombe's murder.
Police said at the time that "damage was caused to a door but nothing was stolen".
Both CTP London and the Metropolitan Police were involved in enquiries. No arrests were made and the investigation was closed.
But on Friday, CTP London said a new line of inquiry had been identified that was not "pursued by them at the time".
The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had "decided to independently investigate the conduct of a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member following a referral received earlier [on Friday]".
A statement continued: "The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of enquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025."
CTP London said it would fully engage with the watchdog's investigation, and that the "victims and families in both investigations have been updated".
Ann Widdecombe, the 78-year-old former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman, was found dead at her home in Devon last month with serious injuries.
Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was later charged with her murder.
Kerry was initially arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July, before being additionally arrested on 13 July on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.
Widdecombe had served as Tory MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

title: Rising singer Kamal on 'scary' moment he hit up Dave for debut album
summary: The London-based musician reflects on aiming for "honesty" within his debut album and TikTok content.
full_text:
Rising singer Kamal on 'scary' moment he hit up Dave for debut album
- Published
He's been backed by British rappers Dave and Central Cee, but rising singer-songwriter Kamal says he'll always focus on making music for the "real ones".
The 24-year-old musician from north-west London has just released his debut album after years of navigating the music industry, having signed to independent label Neighbourhood Recordings as a teenager.
Along the way, his 2020 breakout single Homebody became a lockdown hit and the R&B-tinged track Blue gained him further recognition, including reportedly from US superstar Billie Eilish.
"Apparently she [Billie] put me on a playlist that she'd curated for Spotify, so I mean I was gassed to be part of that sort of taste profile," Kamal tells BBC Newsbeat from his home garden studio in London.
He aims for "honesty" within his music, which also means admitting it was "scary" to ask Brit-award winner Dave to feature on his new album.
"Dave is such a humble guy and he doesn't feel too inaccessible because I feel like he really leads from a love of music, first and foremost," says Kamal.
"Which is the exact same way that I feel."
Dave featuring on his album is a full circle moment as Kamal previously featured on the rapper's 2021 track Mercury.
"I feel like the connection was already established for the most part," Kamal says of their relationship.
"But yeah, it still feels scary when you hit him up because you're like, obviously it is Dave, I grew up listening to him so it feels like a massive moment."
Rapper Dave, who has numerous Brit Awards, Ivor Novellos and a Mercury Prize to his name, opens up Kamal's track, The People That Saved Me, with poignant lyrics about love and memories.
Kamal says the verse was "perfect for the album" and "the kind of message" he wanted to send.
He has also featured on Mobo award-winning rapper Central Cee's 2025 track Now We're Strangers, and joined him on stage at London's The O2 to perform it.
"I feel like the O2 is a dream venue for so many of us musicians so to be up there was proper surreal," he says of that moment.
Amidst the major collaborations, Kamal wants to create music that is meaningful - something which comes across in his work.
"The music is always going to be the leading factor and you don't even get the co-signs unless there's a little something there in the first place," Kamal says.
And he plans to keep his day one fans at the forefront of it all.
"For the people that really love my music, they see the common thread, separately of those external things, of really vulnerable writing, which is what I always try and lead with," he explains.
"I always say I try and lead with honesty in the music, and I feel like that's the best way I can express myself.
"The people that latch onto that are always the real ones at the core of the fan base."
The singer's 13-track album also includes songs like Suffer, which explores topics around love and heartbreak, and All My Favourite People Are Sad, which talks of depression and friendship.
It's a lot of reflection for someone so young, and includes experimental tones which add a different layer to his usual soft singing voice.
Kamal describes his background as a mix of Trinidad, Belize, English and Palestinian and his childhood was filled with music.
But his relationship with music came before any hopes he might have had about making it big - and he says he still has much to learn.
"I feel like there's still a long way to go when I look at my music career, but I'm also very grateful for everything that's happened so far," he says.
And when it comes to the "doomscrolling" generation, Kamal has thoughts.
While he accepts that platforms like TikTok help artists who might not have a "fighting chance in the industry", he says the constant stream of content can sometimes feel like "fast food" music.
"I feel like lots of art forms are a bit more oversaturated now and they feel like they're more content pieces rather than pieces of art," he says.
He feels you have to "weed through" this to try and "maintain some sort of sense of taste".
As he's still in the early stages of his career, Kamal is taking it "day-by-day".
"I'm more just trying to figure out what's the best vibe of music and what's the best sonic and lyric that I can lead with next," he says.
"So I really take it day-by-day, studio session by studio session.
"It feels great, but there's a long way to go still."

title: Mars Bar from 1991 found - and it's 20g bigger than one from today
summary: The woman who found the chocolate bar during a house clearance compares it with today's Mars Bars.
full_text:
Honey, they've shrunk our Mars Bars
- Published
A 35-year-old Mars Bar has been found during a house clearance – and the discovery has gone viral amid claims it highlights the effect of "shrinkflation".
The chocolate bar with a best-before date of 1991 was found during a clear-out of a house in Scunthorpe.
Victoria Gordon, who runs the cleaning service, posted a photo on social media of the 62.5g bar alongside one of today's Mars Bars, which is 40g.
"It was nearly as big as my hand, which was kind of why I noticed it," she said.
Speaking on BBC Radio Lincolnshire, Gordon said: "We were clearing out a hoarder's house and everything we were rooting through was decades old.
"This Mars Bar stood out to me because as I picked it up it was nearly the whole length of my hand.
"I was like, 'Wow, look at the size of that!'"
A Mars spokesperson said: "Over the last 35 years, we have made a number of updates to our bar sizes and pack formats to reflect consumer demand, alongside considering wider external factors such as manufacturing costs and the price of cocoa."
Gordon, who runs Pocket Rockets, is not sure what she will do with the bar, but she said she might be sitting on a "gold mine".
"I do post some hoarding videos but I've never had anything go this viral," she said.
"It's so fascinating what people find so interesting. I almost put it in the skip [but] I might do a UK tour with it."

title: Send foreign prisoners abroad to end early releases, says Reform
summary: The party also plans to create additional capacity in the system by building 'Nightingale' prisons.
full_text:
Send foreign prisoners abroad to end early releases, says Reform
- Published
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has proposed that all foreign prisoners are sent to serve their sentences abroad in order to scrap Labour's early release scheme.
Farage said his party was exploring options with third countries over renting prison spaces, including El Salvador, which he said Reform chairman Lee Anderson would visit soon for initial talks.
Reform said removing foreign nationals from the prison estate, as well as building emergency "Nightingale" prisons, would enable changes to be made to sentencing laws so that serious criminals serve out their full terms.
Labour said the plan "does nothing" for the current situation as it would take years to arrange renting prison places overseas.
Under Reform's plans, foreign criminals handed non-custodial sentences would be deported to their country of origin.
Those with custodial sentences would serve all of it out in their home country, or a third country offering rented prison spaces if they refuse to take them.
The party has previously suggested Kosovo and El Salvador as possible options, with Farage suggesting on Monday that Estonia and Lithuania presented "Baltic state options as well".
There were 10,134 foreign nationals held in custody in England and Wales at the end of June, representing 12% of the total population.
Reform claims its proposals for foreign prisoners would free up more than 10,000 prison spaces, but its policy document does not explain whether it would apply to remand prisoners awaiting trial, which make up around a third of that number.
Both Farage and home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf did not address this point when asked to do so at a press conference to unveil the plans on Monday.
'Half the cost'
When proposing similar measures last year, Farage said El Salvador was an "extreme example" of a country where the party could send foreign prisoners.
On Monday, he played down accusations of human rights abuses in the Central American country, saying: "Not all of the prisons are cages."
El Salvador has the highest incarceration rate in the world, following a government crackdown on gang-related crime, and is home to the notorious mega-jail, the Center for the Confinement of Terrorism (Cecot).
Farage added: "To house a foreign national offender in El Salvador will be half the cost of housing a foreign national offender in this country, and will give us more prison spaces."
Reform says on completion of their sentence, foreign national offenders would return to their home country and be barred from re-entering the UK.
The idea of renting prison places from third countries has reportedly been looked at by successive UK governments.
Other countries have pursued similar arrangements - in 2021, Denmark agreed to pay Kosovo an annual fee of £12.8m for an initial five-year period to rent 300 of their prison spaces.
- Prisoner release row proving to be Burnham's first big test as PM 
  - Published2 days ago
It comes as the government comes under increasing pressure over its early release scheme, which is now due to start in October in England and Wales when the first batch of a total 5,000 prisoners are due to be released.
Last week, Andy Burnham announced that prisoners convicted of rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences would be excluded from the scheme, adding that he wanted to exclude more but prison overcrowding prevented this.
Under the plans, two of PC Andrew Harper's killers remain eligible to be freed halfway through their 13-year sentences after they were convicted of manslaughter in 2020.
More than 850,000 people have signed a petition calling for Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers to remain in prison.
On Monday, Downing Street said it was "not possible" to exempt "one or two offenders" convicted of manslaughter from early release.
Farage said that "Labour have inherited a very, very difficult situation" from the Conservatives, but added: "They don't appear to have the imagination or the will to solve it."
Deportation automatically applies to foreign nationals who are sentenced to at least 12 months in prison, though there is an appeals process.
The UK returned 5,858 foreign national offenders in the year ending March 2026, up 13% on the previous year and the highest observed since 2017, according to the latest Home Office figures., external
A further 15 countries were added to the Home Office's "deport now, appeal later" scheme last year, allowing the government to send foreigners who commit crimes in the UK back to their home countries before they can appeal the decision.
'Free for all'
As well as freeing up places, Reform's home affairs spokesman said: "There will be a lot more people in prison under a Reform government."
He said that "killers, rapists and thugs will never be released a day early".
The party's proposals include reinstating short sentences for shoplifters and ensuring serious offenders serve their full sentences.
The party claims its proposed sentencing changes would increase the prison population by 18,000, which would be covered by the 22,000 places made available under its deportation and Nightingale plans.
The Nightingale label is a reference to the network of emergency temporary hospitals set up during the Covid pandemic.
The prison population in England and Wales on 3 August was 86,495, which was 97% of useable capacity.
The Ministry of Justice has warned the prison population will overtake capacity as soon as this November.
A Labour Party spokesperson said of Reform's proposals: "This isn't a serious prison plan.
"Nigel Farage knows full well that renting prison places overseas would take years to arrange and does nothing to tackle the pressures we face now.
"While Reform chase headlines, this Labour government is getting on with the job - building 14,000 additional prison places and removing foreign criminals at pace.
"Almost 10,000 foreign criminals have been removed since the election, up 36% on the previous 21 months."

title: Radio Caroline breached Ofcom rules after mistakenly announcing King's death
summary: A correction and apology wasn't aired until 30 minutes after the incident occurred.
full_text:
Radio Caroline breached Ofcom rules after mistakenly announcing King's death
- Published
Radio Caroline has been found in breach of broadcasting rules after it mistakenly announced the death of King Charles III.
The station aired three pre-recorded announcements falsely stating the King had died during the Barry Marsh Show on 19 May.
The messages claimed the "news media" had "confirmed" the death, and were followed by the national anthem and 16 minutes of silence on DAB+, while AM listeners heard back-up music. A correction and apology was broadcast 30 minutes later.
The ruling by media watchdog Ofcom stated that once the staff member who accidentally played the files realised what they had done, they stopped playing them, "panicked and left the premises".
Ofcom said the incident breached Rule 5.1, which requires news to be reported with due accuracy, and Rule 5.2, which says significant mistakes must be corrected quickly.
It described the false announcement as a "very significant inaccuracy" on a matter of "very high public interest".
The mistake happened after a staff member carrying out maintenance accessed pre‑recorded obituary files intended for use in the event of the King's death.
Ofcom said the files were played "out of curiosity", cutting off the presenter's remote stream and putting the announcements on air.
Two complaints
Radio Caroline said the presenter did not realise they were off air because, as is common practice, they were streaming the programme remotely.
The station said its presenter "would not realise that they had gone 'off air' unless they were monitoring their output via an internet monitor."
It added that the station director was across the station's AM output but was on a call when the inaccurate announcement was broadcast.
The station director noticed the issue only when he heard continuous music instead of the scheduled programme and contacted the engineer, who was aware of the issue and was already investigating.
A brief apology was then made, with the presenter saying the earlier information had been "incorrect" and that it was due to "a technical issue."
The station said it "took the matter very seriously" and acted "as soon as possible".
The staff member involved has been reprimanded, and the obituary files have been moved off the studio desktop to prevent a repeat incident.
Radio Caroline noted Ofcom received only two complaints about the incident and said the station is "100% volunteer-led" without the resources of larger broadcasters.
Founded in 1964 as an offshore pirate station, Radio Caroline broadcast from a ship until 1991, when it was shipwrecked off the Kent coast.
The station is still based off the north-east Essex coast, although many presenters broadcast their shows remotely.

title: Championship all-stars to global gamble - will Ipswich's approach work?
summary: As Ipswich prepare for their return to the Premier League, BBC Sport look at how they are approaching the transfer market differently.
full_text:
Championship all-stars to global gamble - will Ipswich's approach work?
- Published
Newly promoted Ipswich Town have quietly been the Premier League's fourth-biggest net spenders so far this summer, behind only Chelsea, Tottenham and Arsenal.
Ten players have joined for a combined £106.6m, but what is most notable about the Tractor Boys' approach under new manager Gary O'Neil is the sea change in recruitment strategy, shaped by lessons learned from their chastening single season in the top flight in 2024-25.
Under O'Neil's popular predecessor Kieran McKenna, who stepped down on 10 June after overseeing three promotions in four full seasons, the Blues targeted players familiar with English football.
McKenna's success was built mainly on players from the UK and Republic of Ireland, supplemented by a handful of overseas additions already accustomed to the language and culture through spells at other English clubs.
Ipswich made 39 permanent first-team signings during McKenna's four-and-a-half-year reign, 32 of them either born or raised in Britain or Ireland, with just two joining directly from European clubs.
But the premium on domestic talent makes it difficult, if not impossible, to bridge the gulf between the Championship and Premier League. The success of Sunderland and Leeds last season demonstrated that for promoted teams to thrive, finding value in the transfer market is essential.
When Ipswich last went up in 2024, 10 of their 12 summer signings were British or Irish players acquired from other English sides.
This time, the Blues have cast their net far wider, with Emersonn and Florentino Luis set to be the first Brazilians to represent the club, Sasa Lukic the first Serbian and Daizen Maeda the first Japanese player.
Of the 10 players purchased, the only Briton is Chuba Akpom from Ajax. Even his arrival is an anomaly, given Ipswich were obliged to buy him following promotion despite an underwhelming loan spell.
The blueprint behind Ipswich's rise
Ipswich's previous recruitment model can be traced back to their four seasons in League One.
After guiding Town back to the Championship in 2023, McKenna admitted the club had made a "conscious decision" not to target overseas players because of the fast and frantic nature of England's third tier.
A largely unchanged – but tightly knit – squad then exceeded expectations by finishing second in the Championship in 2023-24, making Ipswich the first side in 12 years to reach the Premier League through back-to-back promotions.
At that point, the Blues' hierarchy could have ripped up the modus operandi that had served them so well and pivoted towards more extensive overseas recruitment. Instead, they doubled down on the approach, focusing mainly on emerging domestic talent largely unproven beyond the Championship.
A £100m summer spending spree brought Omari Hutchinson, Jack Clarke, Liam Delap, Dara O'Shea and Jacob Greaves to Portman Road – players who had primarily shone in the second tier but were identified as having the potential to develop into established Premier League performers.
Mindful that the odds were against survival, Ipswich also targeted players thought unlikely to baulk at remaining part of the project in the event of relegation.
McKenna's 'Championship all-stars' fell well short of safety, finishing second bottom with just 22 points, 16 adrift of 17th-placed Tottenham Hotspur.
But once relegation had been confirmed, the Northern Irishman maintained that recruitment had been in the club's "best long-term interests", a view that has arguably since been vindicated.
Despite spending heavily on transfer fees, Ipswich's £77m wage bill was comfortably the Premier League's lowest in 2024-25. That restraint, coupled with a massive boost to TV income and the quick gain made on Delap's move to Chelsea, enabled the club to post a £4m pre-tax profit for the financial year ending in June 2025.
Hutchinson's sale to Nottingham Forest later that summer provided another windfall but O'Shea, Clarke, Greaves and January 2025 arrival Jaden Philogene stuck around to play crucial roles as Town secured an immediate return to the top flight.
Time to be 'braver'
This time around, chairman Mark Ashton says Ipswich have to be "a bit braver" in their approach to the Premier League, and the type of players the club are pursuing reflects that increased ambition.
Japanese attacker Maeda and Morocco centre-back Issa Diop were both on target at the World Cup this summer, and a third goalscorer from that tournament could follow.
The Tractor Boys have been linked with a move for Paraguayan forward Julio Enciso, who played under O'Neil at Strasbourg last season and had an injury-blighted loan spell at Portman Road during the second half of 2024-25.
While McKenna had enough credit in the bank to play the long game, O'Neil knows he needs to forge a competitive side quickly.
"Two seasons ago, the club didn't get anywhere near staying in the division and this time we need to do better," he said last month. "That's why we're trying to add quality to the squad from different parts of the world and we're trying to add some different attributes."
The former Bournemouth and Wolves boss indicated after Saturday's 3-0 win against Rayo Vallecano that more incomings are likely, saying the "plan is to do quite a bit more".
Will the new recruits deliver?
Ashton acknowledges that one of the key lessons from their previous Premier League campaign was the need to bring in more athletic players "with a different set of physical attributes".
The midfield lacked power and ball-winning ability in 2024-25, and it is imperative that new arrivals Florentino Luis and Sasa Lukic – both experienced at the highest level – hit the ground running. That will be especially important with last season's mainstays Azor Matusiwa and Jack Taylor doubtful for the opening game following operations over the summer.
It is no surprise that O'Neil is also seeking greater cutting edge given that no Ipswich player scored more than 10 non-penalty goals in the Championship last season.
The Blues broke their transfer record to sign Brazilian striker Emersonn, 22, for an initial £24m. He certainly fits the desired physical profile but is relatively raw, having only established himself as a regular last season at Toulouse, where he scored seven goals in 31 appearances, 22 of them starts.
Maeda, a hardworking forward or winger, had an excellent record at Celtic, netting 79 times in 212 games, but won't get the same volume of chances in a team battling to stay up.
The Suffolk side have also recruited two Dutch goalkeepers, including Kjell Scherpen, whose imposing 6ft 9in (2.06m) frame means he is set to become the tallest player to appear in the Premier League.
With a new manager in place and a £30m training ground redevelopment close to completion, this could be a defining summer for Ipswich. But will their transfer business be enough to secure successive top-flight campaigns for the first time in a quarter of a century?
Only three promoted clubs have splashed out more in a summer window – Sunderland in 2025, Nottingham Forest in 2022 and Aston Villa in 2019 – and all survived.
Yet Fulham, Southampton, Burnley and Ipswich themselves have spent comparable figures in recent years only to swiftly return to the Championship - with that level of investment increasingly the bare minimum needed to be competitive rather than a guarantee of safety.

title: Has the army turned the page on control of western Sudan?
summary: Sudan's military repels a series of offensives by the RSF paramilitary in a strategically significant region.
full_text:
Has the army turned the page on control of western Sudan?
Sudan’s military repels a series of offensives by the RSF paramilitary in a strategically significant region.
Khartoum, Sudan – A Sudanese army-led counteroffensive in the western region of Darfur has led to a series of gains for government-aligned forces over the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group in recent days.
In early August, Sudan’s military and allied groups repelled two successive attacks by the RSF in the strategically important Bir Saliba region. It lies about 30km (nearly 20 miles) north of el-Geneina, the capital of West Darfur state and the RSF’s last stronghold in the region.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Sudan army drone attack on Darfur kills 35, rights group says
- list 2 of 4Women expose rape as a weapon of war in Sudan
- list 3 of 4Sudan war threatens ancient Meroe pyramids
- list 4 of 4Sudan’s war threatens an ‘entire generation’s’ future, UN warns
Government-backed forces have tried to put pressure on RSF supply lines by seizing control of crossings and desert routes along the border with Chad. The strategy could signal a shift in fighting towards el-Geneina.
Leading to el-Geneina, the Bir Saliba region is of strategic importance. It has a network of roads that link the state capital with areas in the northwest of the region, particularly Jebel Moon and Kulbus, according to General Bahr al-Din Adam Karama, the governor of West Darfur state.
Attempt to encircle Bir Saliba
Darfur Regional Governor Minni Arko Minnawi announced that Major General Mahdi Adam, known as “Jebel Moon” and one of the RSF’s most prominent field commanders, was killed in fighting in western Sudan. The RSF has not officially confirmed his death, but if true it would represent a significant loss for the paramilitary group and leave a leadership gap along this key western front.
Minnawi said the Joint Force of the Armed Struggle Movements, a coalition of former Darfur rebel groups that signed the 2020 Juba Peace Agreement and now fights alongside the Sudanese army against the RSF, also thwarted an attempt by the RSF to encircle Bir Saliba. One RSF force advanced from north of Kulbus while another moved from the direction of Sileia in the Jebel Moon area before launching a large-scale attack on the Joint Force.
“[The RSF] bet on the element of surprise to break through the Joint Force’s defences, but they received another lesson,” Minnawi said.
Battlefield gains
Major Mutawakkil Ali Wakil Abu-Ja, the Joint Force’s spokesman, told Al Jazeera that the Joint Force destroyed more than 38 combat vehicles and seized 27 others in the campaign.
The commander of the attacking RSF force was also killed, he said, with fighters fleeing the battlefield and leaving their dead comrades behind.
Abu-Ja said efforts were under way to secure the western axis and increase pressure on the RSF before what he described as a decisive battle for el-Geneina.
Air strikes on a convoy travelling near the border with Chad have further isolated the RSF and struck a key supply route for the paramilitary group, Major General Othman Siraj said.
Pressure on multiple fronts by the army was preventing the RSF from regrouping its forces and paving the way for what he believes will be the final battle for el-Geneina.
Fadel Kaya, a leader and adviser with the Sudan Liberation Movement/Army – Transitional Council (SLM/TC), a Darfur rebel faction that split from the original Sudan Liberation Movement and signed the 2020 Juba Peace Agreement, told Al Jazeera that the Joint Force’s victories in West Darfur indicated that the RSF had shifted away from trying to gain territory to retreating from key positions.
Drone warfare
In North Kordofan state in central Sudan, the RSF had turned to drones to compensate for the loss of the strategic route linking Omdurman and el-Obeid. This had served as a major supply artery for the RSF before the army recaptured it on July 27.
Amin Ishaq Zakaria, a SLM/TC spokesman, told Al Jazeera that the RSF’s increased use of drones reflected “a predicament on the ground and an inability to engage in direct confrontations after losing vital positions”.
Sudanese armed forces had seized a number of attack drones along the Jabra al-Sheikh axis during the counteroffensive, he added.
The International Organization for Migration reported on Saturday that the recent escalation in fighting has seen more than 6,650 people from 11 villages in the Sirba region displaced.
More than 13 million people had already been displaced since the war between the military and RSF began in April 2023, according to United Nations estimates.
The RSF and its allies have also established a rival administration, known as the Tasis government, in opposition to the Sudanese government based in Port Sudan.
Al Jazeera reached out to the RSF and Tasis government about the fighting in the Bir Saliba area but received no response by the time the report was published.

title: Jeff Bezos consortium nears deal to buy stake in Liverpool FC: Reports

full_text:
Jeff Bezos consortium nears deal to buy stake in Liverpool FC: Reports
Investment reportedly values the club at about $5.9bn, making it one of the largest ever football club valuations.
A consortium that includes Amazon founder Jeff Bezos is close to a deal to acquire a stake of about one-third in Premier League club Liverpool, multiple media outlets have reported.
The investor group also includes Facebook cofounder Eduardo Saverin, the reports said on Monday.

title: ‘Long-range sanctions’: Ukraine hopes strikes cause Russia fear and losses
summary: Al Jazeera is given rare access to one of Ukraine's long-range drone units tasked with targeting Russia.
full_text:
‘Long-range sanctions’: Ukraine hopes strikes cause Russia fear and losses
Al Jazeera is given rare access to one of Ukraine’s long-range drone units tasked with targeting Russia.
Eastern Ukraine – In a farm field in eastern Ukraine, a choking engine interrupts the sound of crickets and nightingales.
Then come indistinguishable shouts of male voices, followed by a crescendo – a loud sound like scissors tearing through wrapping paper.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Woman screams in fear as Ukraine war recruiters pounce on man
- list 2 of 4Russian forces kill several in Ukraine, launch ‘brutal’ attack in Odesa
- list 3 of 4Germany warns of ‘daily hybrid warfare’ after explosive-laden drone found
- list 4 of 4‘Like the movies’: How Ukraine’s ground robots are changing rules of war
It pierces the night as a brief flare of flame illuminates the sunflower field below.
“Like an orchestra, every part has to work together in order for us to achieve effective strikes,” says Colonel Ray, commander of the Kairos Battalion of the Magyars Birds Brigade.
The drone, roughly the length of a compact SUV with a wingspan of nearly 6 metres (19.7 feet), climbs into the night. Where exactly it is headed is known only to him.
Before reaching its target, the drone will travel at about 160km/h (100mph), thousands of metres above the ground, passing over the bombarded cities and battlefields along Ukraine’s front line.
Once it reaches cruising altitude, control is handed over to a command centre elsewhere in Ukraine.
“You could pilot it from Pennsylvania once it’s up there,” the brigade’s spokesperson says, explaining how the drones navigate using satellite systems.
Scaling up
Along its journey, the drone is careful to avoid towns and cities where it risks being intercepted.
Data on Russian air defences is fed back to planners, helping give the hundreds of drones Ukraine now launches on some nights the best possible chance of making it through.
Lately, Ukraine’s long-range drones are striking targets sometimes more than 2,500km (1,553 miles) inside Russia, reaching cities like Moscow and St Petersburg, across the Ural Mountains and even into Siberia.
Their targets include oil refineries, factories and warehouses.
While long-range drones are not new to the war, the scale of their use has changed.
Ukraine now produces its own one-way attack drones by the hundreds, allowing it to cut through red tape from Western partners that once prevented it from striking deep into Russia.
When it began ramping up such attacks in March, some Western allies urged restraint.
The US-Israel war on Iran had already disrupted global energy markets, and Ukraine’s increasing attacks on Russian energy infrastructure have threatened to add further pressure.
But Kyiv kept going.
Ukrainian officials began calling the strikes “long-range sanctions”, a tongue-in-cheek way of arguing that Kyiv was enforcing, through drones, the economic pressure Western sanctions had failed to deliver.
The logic behind this is that Russia’s oil and gas industry remains a critical source of money for the state, accounting for roughly one-fifth of federal budget revenues.
More recently, however, Ukraine’s long-range campaign has expanded beyond oil and gas.
Among its targets is Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer. Ukraine says the company’s marketplace is used to sell dual-use goods, pointing to listings for items including body armour, military helmets, drone components and fibre optic cables used in drones that kill Ukrainian soldiers and civilians alike.
“Thirty percent of all dual-use or military goods are bought and sold by [Russia’s] Ministry of Defence through Wildberries marketplace,” Mykhailo Podolyak, an adviser to Ukraine’s president, tells Al Jazeera.
He says the strikes have three objectives.
“First, fear. Second, losses – business losses, lost revenue, lost goods, whatever it may be. And third, making [Russians] feel the reality of war.”
‘It’s like a boxing match’
Back at the launch site, the soldiers pack up quickly.
Six drones have been propelled in about five minutes. Each flash carries the risk of exposing the position to Russian reconnaissance drones. For the crews responsible for a campaign reaching deeper and deeper into Russia, remaining hidden is crucial.
These are just six of hundreds of drones that will be launched that night, Colonel Ray tells Al Jazeera. The next night, his team will likely do it all again.
“It’s like a boxing match,” he says, describing the war. “In the first 10 rounds, professionalism is what matters. But in the final two championship rounds, it’s also about morale.”
Ray says Ukraine’s success with its deep strikes has greatly improved the outlook of many in the army. As the war grinds on, the fight is increasingly one of endurance.
“It comes down to one question: why are we doing this? I think the Russians still don’t know why they are doing this. But our guys have a clear understanding of what it is all for – because we are defending our people and our land.”

title: Flood death toll in India's Assam reaches 100 as thousands lose their homes
summary: Days of heavy monsoon rain has caused rivers, including the Brahmaputra, to overflow, inundating communities, disrupting livelihoods and damaging infrastructure.
full_text:
Flood death toll in India's Assam reaches 100 as thousands lose their homes
GUWAHATI, India — The flood crisis in India's northeastern Assam state remained critical on Monday, with the death toll reaching 100 after two more people died overnight, officials said.
Several rivers remain above danger levels, raising the risk of fresh flooding in vulnerable areas, the Assam State Disaster Management Authority said. Days of heavy monsoon rain has caused rivers, including the Brahmaputra, to overflow that inundated communities while disrupting livelihoods and damaging infrastructure.
The river, one of Asia's largest that originates in China's Tibet region and flows about 900 kilometers (560 miles) through Assam, flooded villages, swept away homes and forced nearly 300,000 people into government-run relief camps, officials said.
The floods that began last month displaced more than 700,000 people and submerged vast stretches of farmland and damaged roads and other local infrastructure. Although many residents have begun returning to their homes as floodwaters recede, at least 49,000 flood-affected residents remain housed in 125 relief camps and relief distribution centers, officials said.
Authorities remained engaged in relief and monitoring efforts as they assessed the extent of the damage and the needs of affected populations.
The floods also devastated livestock, with large numbers of cattle lost, dealing a blow to rural communities and raising concerns about disease outbreaks. As the waters receded in some areas, many families returned to homes buried under thick layers of silt, adding to the challenges of recovery.
Farukuddin Ahmed, a 47-year-old trader from Nazira town in Assam's worst-hit Sivasagar district, said displaced families were slowly returning home, many to rebuild on ground still buried under two to three feet (up to a meter) of silt.
A nearby village, Nepali Khuti, had about 100 households before the floods. "Only a few houses are left and the rest washed away by the surging flood waters," Ahmed said.
"The residents, mainly dairy farmers, have to rebuild their lives from scratch having lost all their cattle."
Aid in the form of roofing sheets and other building materials was beginning to arrive, he added.
"We have directed officials to complete damage assessment as soon as possible so the government could provide financial assistance for their rehabilitation," Assam Agriculture and Irrigation Minister Pijush Hazarika said after a review meeting. He said some 50,000 affected people were already paid interim monetary compensation.
The annual monsoon season frequently triggers flooding in Assam, where swollen rivers inundate large areas and displace thousands of residents each year.
Experts say human-caused climate change is intensifying South Asia's monsoons, which traditionally run from June to September and again from October to December. The rains, once predictable, now arrive in erratic bursts that dump extreme amounts of water in short periods, followed by dry spells.

China challenges Western ‘tribute system’ theory in push to control its narrative power

Beijing is stepping up efforts to challenge the Western concept of the “tribute system”, arguing that foreign frameworks distort ancient Chinese diplomacy and misrepresent the country’s contemporary global rise.
China is redoubling efforts to define its own practices, experiences and ideas through original, home-grown social science language rather than through what it says are Western conceptual lenses.
The theory was forged and made popular in the US decades ago as a means to interpret both ancient and contemporary Chinese diplomacy. China’s push for narrative power to win over a broader overseas audience continues to be tested, including among foreign perceptions of Chinese history and practices.
In a recent example, American billionaire investor Ray Dalio wrote in an article published on his Substack on June 19 that “we are in the very early stage of a shift to a tribute system-type order in the Asia region and even beyond”.
He argued in the article “The Tribute System: The New World Order” that while China’s economic and financial powers were growing rapidly, the US handling of Iran’s seizure of the Strait of Hormuz had convinced others that Washington “doesn’t have what it takes to fight to maintain its empire”, prompting a change in thinking by global leaders.
The founder of Bridgewater Associates, one of the world’s biggest hedge funds, said the dynamic was reflected in the many visits by foreign heads of state and their delegations to Beijing since late last year, which Dalio characterised as efforts “to build tribute-type relationships” with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

title: US does its robotics industry no favours by fencing it off from China
summary:
Concession speeches follow a formula: the vocabulary of defiance, thanks to the faithful, a promise that the fight goes on. Last month, Brendan Carr, chairman of the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC), essentially delivered one on behalf of American robotics.
Acting on findings from a White House task force, Carr added new foreign-made humanoid robots, quadrupeds and power inverters to the agency’s Covered List, denying them the authorisation nearly every electronic device requires to be...
full_text:
US does its robotics industry no favours by fencing it off from China
By banning Chinese humanoid robots, Washington is trying to buy its industry time, but the lack of competition is not a strength
Concession speeches follow a formula: the vocabulary of defiance, thanks to the faithful, a promise that the fight goes on. Last month, Brendan Carr, chairman of the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC), essentially delivered one on behalf of American robotics.
The unstated ground is arithmetic. Chinese manufacturers account for roughly 85 per cent of the global humanoid market. There is no established American industry to protect, only an infant to be raised behind a wall.
That’s the message the industry received. Evan Beard, CEO of Standard Bots, hailed the order as among the strongest technology-security actions in modern American history, vowing that foreign-subsidised machines would not “dominate US robotics as they did solar”.
The security case deserves a fair hearing. A networked machine with cameras, microphones and limbs, stationed in a factory or a care home, is a plausible platform for espionage and sabotage. But the order makes clear how seriously Washington takes its own warning: it exempts the federal government, which may keep buying the machines deemed too dangerous for ordinary citizens. A menace to every American except the American government is less a threat assessment than a tariff in uniform.
Which returns us to Beard and solar. Although Washington began walling out Chinese panels with anti-dumping duties under the Obama administration in 2012, China now controls over 80 per cent of every stage of global solar panel manufacturing. The wall decided who could sell to Americans but not who won the industry.

title: Breaking Down the Euphoric Ending of Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma
summary: Jane Schoenbrun on the layers of meaning beneath their new queer slasher film.
full_text:
Warning: This post contains spoilers for Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.
The last thing Kris Williams (Hannah Einbinder) does before she dies is watch herself do it. She lies on a twin bed in Camp Tivoli’s Bunk 5, candles burning around her, rose petals scattered across the sheets, while Billy Presley (Gillian Anderson) stretches out on top of her and coaches her toward the end. “You’re almost there now,” she says. “You’re almost dead.” Billy tells Kris to watch herself through the killer’s eyes, and the film obliges: The camera slips out of the cabin and into Little Death’s helmet as he climbs the steps, breath ragged, spear in hand.
What follows is impalement and orgasm in the same instant—one spear through both women, blood passing from Billy’s mouth onto Kris’s upturned face—and when their breathing stops, the hole at the bottom of the lake pushes out a fresh videotape.
That tape, and the women’s smiles in the film’s final moments, hold the keys to Jane Schoenbrun’s latest feature Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma: a horror comedy, a love story, and the most sexually direct film of their career. It follows Kris, a young queer director hired to reboot the moldering Camp Miasma slasher franchise, as she tracks down its original final girl, Billy, who now resides at the abandoned camp where the movies were shot. Kris’ trip turns into a courtship, and the courtship into something the film doesn’t quite spell out, though Schoenbrun will name what it’s chasing. “It’s a movie about getting out of your head and getting into your body,” they tell TIME.
Schoenbrun realized they were trans while writing the 2021 release We’re All Going to the World’s Fair, and began physically transitioning after finishing it. Where that film and its 2024 follow-up, I Saw the TV Glow, grew out of the frightening early days of coming out and transitioning, this one, Schoenbrun says, “came from the fun parts” of their transition—a period when, “for the first time, I think, since childhood, it felt like the world around me was real.”
Kris begins the film investigating desire the only way she knows how: academically, through film theory, a method that has not met with much success thus far in her personal life. “By the end of the movie, the only way she’s able to actually do that is with her whole body, by embracing the flesh and fluids of it all,” Schoenbrun says. The surest way to understand the film’s transcendent final moments is to approach it the way Kris does: from the beginning.
Who gets to watch whom
The film settles in early on with Kris alone in a hotel bed, a bucket of popcorn and Raisinets in hand, watching Camp Miasma Part VI: A New Beginning and writing the word “Desire” in her notebook, underlined twice. “People giggle at it,” Schoenbrun says. “What a pretentious, film-school-y thing to do.” The character, they add, is “a bit of a funhouse mirror” of them. The sequel Kris falls asleep to ends with a bloodied final girl refusing a cop’s reassurance that the killer is gone. It’s never over, she says, warning that “he’s still down there at the bottom of the lake” and “still hungry.”
Kris continues driving to Camp Tivoli to court Billy for an appearance in her film. Billy, for her part, vanished from acting directly following the first Miasma movie and now lives on the property: crafting, sketching, and painting. Their first encounter sets the terms for everything to follow. In the camp’s Cinema building, an old projector flickers to life on the scene where young Billy (Amanda Fix) loses her virginity, and the real Billy materializes behind Kris, hoping for a jump. “It’s only fair, right?” she says. “You’ve already seen me.” Kris has spent a lifetime studying this woman’s most exposed moment on a screen; Billy answers by watching her back.
That exchange starts an open question of power between the two, and their sensual fried-chicken dinner is the first round of the negotiation. Kris arrives with what Schoenbrun calls her “whole spiel down pat.” Billy “sees right through it” and needles her “in a way that gives her power in that dynamic.” “Well, you remade Psycho from the perspective of the shower curtain,” she says of Kris’s feature debut film. Eventually, Billy correctsKris’s theories with just three words: The original Camp Miasma was never about monstrosity or gender trouble so much as simply “flesh and fluids.”
On the cabin wall behind them hangs a vintage poster bearing the franchise’s old tagline: “If it gets too real, you can always turn it off.” A leftover Billy says she’s kept from the home-video campaign. From there, Schoenbrun says, the two spend the movie “yes, and-ing” each other—the comedy improvisation principle of accepting a partner’s offer in a scene and building on it—a courtship built on daring one another to admit what they want.
The tagline on the poster
That night, with the fire burning and the snacks close by, the film’s tagline gets put to the test. Smoking a joint in front of the mirror, Kris glimpses the young boy Little Death used to be, the bullied camper who, by franchise lore, was drowned in the lake. She emerges blissfully stoned, flirts with Billy, then confesses an intimate truth she has never told anyone: She can only approach pleasure by leaving herself, imagining her way into an old slasher film, becoming either the bookworm in Camp Miasma: Part II, or the girl in the outhouse in Camp Miasma: Part IV, or even young Billy in bed with that look in her eye.
She calls it dissociation, stupid and misogynistic. It’s all just play, Billy assures her, and if it gets too real, you can always turn it off. Then she urges Kris’s gaze up at the Little Death mannequin looming over the room and tells her to look into his eyes and make them her own. “Let’s make a movie,” Billy says.
For Schoenbrun, the meaning of this line is simple. “It’s about consent,” they say. One way to think about the film is that it is “structured like queer sex”: the long hangout, the shared joint, the rises and rests, the breaks for junk food. Good sex, in their view, involves “stopping and laughing for a while in the middle.”
What the tagline promises is the shared understanding that all of this is performance and play, and that play only works when you are fully inside it and free to step out of it at any moment. The promise, in Schoenbrun’s terms, extends even to “places that feel taboo or embarrassing or traumatic,” the ones people who have experienced sexual trauma often have to revisit to come out the other side: “You can go to those places, and then we’ll eat some candy and have some aftercare.”
The tale of Little Death
The next day, the courtship escalates: Billy screens her personal print of the original Camp Miasma for Kris. The film-within-the-film’s campfire story invents Little Death as a gender-confused child, mocked by campers, drowned in the lake, their death covered up. The killer that legend produced wears a camper’s uniform sheathed in plastic, a drowned thing the lake never quite gave back. “This part’s transphobic,” Kris announces, ever the annotator. Billy tells her to shut up.
As the film approaches young Billy’s sex scene, the older Billy’s pencil digs harder into her sketchbook until the tip snaps, and she murmurs a single word at the screen—“Rise”—and the movie-within-the-movie erupts.
Until this moment, the old film was styled as a half-remembered ’80s slasher, a collage of borrowed images. Then, in one roving, unbroken take set to the Counting Crows’ “A Long December,” the camera becomes Little Death, surfacing from the lake and cutting down counselor after counselor, the fuzzy, faded look of an old print giving way to a sleek, furious sequence that moves like a dance. Here, the movie hands the massacre to the monster the franchise built out of transphobic panic, and lets him move like a star. Schoenbrun grew up on that era’s horror villains imagined as men in dresses and gender-confused boys, from Sleepaway Camp to The Silence o

title: Steam hardware shipper breach leaks customer data, including names and addresses
summary: Valve says a data breach may have exposed the personal information of customers who ordered its Steam hardware in Europe. In an email sent to users, Valve says its European shipping partner, CEVA Logistics, suffered a data breach that may have included customer names, addresses, phone numbers, and email addresses. The breach at CEVA occurred […]
full_text:
Valve says a data breach may have exposed the personal information of customers who ordered its Steam hardware in Europe. In an email sent to users, Valve says its European shipping partner, CEVA Logistics, suffered a data breach that may have included customer names, addresses, phone numbers, and email addresses.
Steam hardware shipper breach leaks customer data, including names and addresses
The incident impacts customers who ordered Steam devices in Europe.
The breach at CEVA occurred between July 29th and August 1st, weeks after Valve began taking reservations for its new Steam Machine and Steam Controller. Valve adds that European customer data “was likely compromised” as part of the breach, as CEVA stores “delivery-related information” for up to 90 days after orders.
As a result of the breach, Valve says to “expect fake messages” over email, text, or on the phone that claim to come from Steam, Valve, or a delivery company. “They may quote your address back to you to prove they’re genuine. They may ask you to confirm a delivery, pay a small customs or redelivery fee, or sign in somewhere to ‘verify’ your order,” Valve says. “Treat all of them as fake.”
The notice says additional data linked to users’ Steam accounts or purchases wasn’t impacted, adding that CEVA “does not have access to your payment information, passwords, Steam Guard codes or other information.” Valve notes that it only deals with account issues from help.steampowered.com, and won’t contact users over email, Steam chat, or Discord.

title: This great retro-inspired keyboard now comes preassembled
summary: You probably know just by looking at it if the Classic-TKL Underscore Edition is for you. Do you want a retro-looking wired keyboard without a number pad? Great. Do you care that it doesn't have wireless? Perfect. Do you want it preassembled? Buddy, you're in the right place. But Nathan, you might say, preassembled is […]
full_text:
You probably know just by looking at it if the Classic-TKL Underscore Edition is for you. Do you want a retro-looking wired keyboard without a number pad? Great. Do you care that it doesn’t have wireless? Perfect. Do you want it preassembled? Buddy, you’re in the right place.
This great retro-inspired keyboard now comes preassembled
The Classic-TKL is one of my favorite keyboard kits, and now you don’t have to build it yourself
If you buy something from a Verge link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
But Nathan, you might say, preassembled is the regular way to buy a keyboard. That is the baseline expectation. Most people buying a cake expect a cake, not a box of cake mix. And that’s true, for most people and most keyboards. But until now, the Classic-TKL has only been available as a bare-bones kit, and now you can buy one ready to go, with quality components, for less than the price of doing a similar build yourself.
If you’re like me, figuring out what keycaps, switches, and stabilizers to use, then putting them all together, is a big part of the fun of mechanical keyboards. But if you just want something to type with that looks retro and sounds and feels nice, without having to build it yourself — or if you were going to use classic beige keycaps anyway — then the Underscore Edition might be up your alley.
The Good
- Great retro beige aesthetic
- Fully remappable
- High-quality components
- Hot-swap sockets
- Great sound and feel
The Bad
- Only one keycap option, only one switch option
- Wired only
- No extra keycaps
The $189 NovelKeys Classic-TKL Underscore Edition is a wired-only, gasket-mounted tenkeyless mechanical keyboard. It has an injection-molded plastic case with a high forehead, reminiscent of the 18-year-old Realforce 86U, and a silicone mat on the base for sound dampening. It also has hot-swap MX switches, full RGB backlighting, and a light bar (both of which can be turned off), and it’s fully programmable using the Via web app.
The Classic-TKL has been around for a couple of years in kit form. I built one and wrote about it in 2024; I also tested the glow-in-the-dark version. I like them a lot! But apparently not everyone who wants a nice retro-looking keyboard also wants a craft project. Michael Sickler, who owns NovelKeys, told me that the Underscore Edition is aimed at giving NovelKeys’ keyboard enthusiast customer base something they can recommend to friends and family. It’s also aimed at professionals who might lurk on the keyboard subreddits and Discords enough to know what they want, but don’t want to build it themselves. (This is basically the same thing Ryan Norbauer told me about his Seneca, except the Seneca is 20 times more expensive.)
The Underscore Edition comes in clay (warm beige), boulder (taupe-ish), and lichen (a dusty green). My review unit is clay, but I’d buy the lichen personally. It ships with NovelKeys’ own Classic Blue switches, GMK CYL Classic Beige keycaps, a USB A-to-C cable, and preinstalled and pretuned TypePlus stabilizers.
These are name-brand parts. GMK CYL keycaps are the benchmark for doubleshot Cherry-profile keycaps. They’re several steps in quality above the keycaps that come with a Keychron, for example. The letters and numbers are crisp and clear and the consistency is unmatched. They’re also expensive; you’d pay at least $120 if you bought them on their own, though you would get more keycaps. The Classic-TKL comes with just the ones you need to cover the board.
The TypePlus stabilizers are also a good choice; I’ve installed and tuned a couple sets myself, but the people who made them do a better job. There’s no rattle or tick on any of the stabilized keys. And the Classic Blue linear switches (also made by TypePlus) are also nice. They’re smooth and stable, with almost no wobble; at 53g actuation force and 63g bottom-out, they’re medium-heavy, like a lighter version of the Cherry MX Blacks in my first-ever mechanical keyboard in 2009. They’re not silent, but they’re also not as loud as you’d expect a keyboard this beige to be. (I still feel like a blue switch should be clicky, though.)
I try to avoid the “fans of the genre” review. You know, “if this is the kind of thing you like, you’re going to like it.” But once you get past the strictly utilitarian, pretty much everything about mechanical keyboards comes down to preference and taste.
The Classic-TKL Underscore Edition is a well-executed version of what it is. If you want an earth-tone retro-looking tenkeyless board — a classic TKL, if you will — with linear switches and beige Cherry-profile keycaps, it’s a great choice.
When you think of it as a high-quality preassembled version of an enthusiast DIY keyboard, with name-brand parts, it’s also a good deal. I built the DIY version of the same board with the same stabilizers and similarly priced keycaps in September 2024. It worked out to $276, and took me an hour to put together (most of which was spent lubing and tuning the stabilizers). The Underscore Edition costs $189, $100 more than the bare-bones kit. You can’t get keycaps, switches, and stabilizers of this quality for $100 combined.
But it’s also true that $189 can get you a lot of keyboard these days, especially if you’re not attached to the Classic-TKL’s particular vibe.
Even within the tenkeyless form factor, the Evoworks Evo80 costs $169 and comes with an aluminum case and both Bluetooth and 2.4GHz wireless. Same for the $179 Wobkey Crush 80. But those are different keyboards, with different aesthetics. The 8BitDo Retro 87 is closer, with several classic-computing-inspired flavors including Commodore 64 and IBM Model M, for around $100. But — no disrespect to the 8BitDo here — those look maybe a smidge more casual than the Classic-TKL.
I prefer the Classic-TKL’s plastic chassis to the aluminum of the Evoworks or Wobkey boards. But I wouldn’t mind if it had wireless. It’d also be nice if it shipped with a few extra keycaps, in case you want Mac legends or Control in its proper place (Caps Lock). While I’m being picky: I also wish it came with the option for MTNU Classic Beige keycaps, rather than just CYL, because I like MTNU better. An electrocapacitive switch option would be nice too, but now I’m just getting greedy. (Actually, now I’m just reinventing the Realforce.)
If you want the Classic-TKL in a different color, or with different switches or keycaps, there’s still the kit version and the Glo version. And if you want a different keyboard entirely, well, those abound. The Classic-TKL Underscore Edition is the thing that it is, and it’s good at that.
I’d still go for the green one, though.

title: Solana lending giant Jupiter now lets the same dollar earn twice
full_text:
Solana lending giant Jupiter now lets the same dollar earn twice
The new Lend v2 product turns deposits and borrowed assets into trading liquidity, tying higher returns to whether Jupiter’s router can send enough swap flow to the new vaults.
- Jupiter’s Lend v2, introduced Monday, allows deposits and borrowed positions to double as trading liquidity so users can earn both lending interest and a share of swap fees from the same capital.
- The product introduces optional Smart Collateral and Smart Debt features that automatically pair assets into correlated liquidity pools, boosting yields for depositors and offsetting borrowing costs when traders route swaps through those pools.
- While borrowers in correlated pools are protected if one stablecoin depegs, collateral providers bear the loss on either asset, a risk Jupiter seeks to limit by confining the design to stablecoin pairs and SOL versus its staked versions.
Solana decentralized-lending giant Jupiter rolls out its new Lend version 2 (v2) product on Monday, allowing deposits and borrowed positions to simultaneously act as trading liquidity so the same dollar earns interest as a loan and a share of swap fees.
Jupiter Lend holds about $1.9 billion in deposits, according to DefiLlama data, and generated $1.6 million in fees over the past 30 days, or roughly 1% a year on the capital sitting there before any split with the protocol.
Active loans stand at $822.7 million and have fluctuated between $600 million and $900 million since September, Token Terminal data show. Deposits and loans have both slipped over the past month.
The new version of Lend introduces two features, both optional.
Smart Collateral lets a deposit of USDC, USDT, SOL or JupSOL be paired automatically into a correlated liquidity pool. That allows the assets to earn yield on any loans while gaining trading fees and, where applicable, staking rewards from one position. Smart Debt does the same for borrowed assets, so fees generated by a debt position offset the cost of the loan. Users who want ordinary lending can ignore both.
The extra yield exists only if traders actually swap through those pools, which means Jupiter not only runs Solana's largest swap router, the software most wallets and apps use to find the best price across venues, but it also owns pools that need that flow to arrive.
The company told CoinDesk the router does not favor its own vaults and sends swaps wherever the price is best.
The risk of pairing assets falls unevenly, however. Jupiter said margin is valued using primary market oracles, or data providers, so a temporary price wobble on an exchange does not trigger anything, and a position liquidates as normal once its loan-to-value ratio passes the threshold.
A genuine depeg is different. On the debt side the borrower is protected — someone borrowing $100 split between USDC and USDT would see the pool rebalance into whichever asset held its value and still owe $100. On the collateral side there is no such protection, and a supplier carries the loss on both assets if either breaks.
That is why the design is confined to correlated pairs, stablecoins against each other and SOL against its staked versions, rather than volatile assets.
"There's been a wall between the two primary ways people earn APY onchain, lending and LPing," said Kash Dhanda, Jupiter's chief operating officer, referring to lending and supplying liquidity to exchanges.
The design lets Jupiter offer higher deposit rates and cheaper borrowing, he said, and terms improve as the vaults attract more trading. "It is not about just serving existing loans, but providing efficiency to grow the entire market."
Jupiter said it expects a mix of new loans and migrated positions, without giving a target or a cap. A protocol whose loan book has not grown in a year now has a product that pays more, and the next 30 days of active loans will show whether yield was the thing holding it back.

title: Bitmine’s ETH buying slows as Tom Lee's firm shifts capital to share buybacks
full_text:
Bitmine’s ETH buying slows as Tom Lee's firm shifts capital to share buybacks
Chairman Tom Lee said easing financial conditions could support crypto, even as the CLARITY Act failed to reach a Senate vote before the August recess.
- Ethereum treasury firm Bitmine (BMNR) bought just 7,391 ether (ETH) last week, its smallest weekly haul in 2026.
- The firm shifted more capital toward its own stock, repurchasing 3 million shares worth an estimated $50 million-$58 million.
- Tom Lee pointed to softer inflation and jobs data as a potential tailwind for crypto, despite the latest delay to the CLARITY Act.
Bitmine Immersion (BMNR), the largest Ethereum treasury firm, bought another 7,391 ether 
The purchase, worth roughly $14.2 million at ether’s price as of writing of $1,915, lifted the company’s holdings to over 5.8 million ETH, or about 4.8% of Ethereum’s total supply.
The latest haul, which extends Bitmine’s ETH buying streak to 58 weeks, was the smallest weekly purchase through the year and remains a fraction of the 100,000-plus weekly acquisitions Bitmine made earlier this year.
Thomas Lee, chairman of Bitmine, noted earlier this year that the firm would slow the pace of crypto accumulation as it gets closer to its goal of owning 5% of ether’s supply.
Instead, the company has shifted towards buying back shares. It repurchased another 3 million shares last week, which would have cost roughly $50 million to $58 million based on the stock’s trading range during the period. Since July, the firm has bought back 19.1 million of its own shares.
Bitmine also holds 209 BTC, $104 million in cash and marketable securities and stakes in Beast Industries and Eightco Holdings.
Bitmine shares traded flat neat $18.80 in pre-market trading.
Clarity delay
Lee focused on the macro backdrop despite another setback for U.S. crypto legislation, with the CLARITY Act failing to secure a Senate vote before the August recess.
"We are disappointed that the CLARITY Act will not see a Senate vote before the August recess, but financial markets seem more focused on the recent softer inflation and jobs data," Lee said.
Lee said the odds of the Federal Reserve hiking interest rates at the next meeting in September have fallen to 40% from 75% two weeks ago.
“We expect easing financial conditions to be a tailwind for crypto,” he added.

title: Solana gets its first Strategy STRC product through Solstice Finance
full_text:
Solana gets its first Strategy STRC product through Solstice Finance
The Solana vault splits income from Strategy’s preferred stock into a lower-risk senior token and a higher-risk junior token.
- Solstice Finance has rolled out strcUSX on Solana, a structured product that offers DeFi users exposure to the dividend income and price risk of Strategy’s STRC preferred stock without tokenizing the shares.
- The product splits exposure into a senior token targeting a 7% annual yield and a junior token targeting more than 20% APY, with junior holders absorbing losses first if STRC’s price falls.
- Users deposit Solstice’s USX token into a vault, can redeem after a seven-day unlock or exit immediately for a fee, and receive yield via changes in the tokens’ exchange rate rather than separate distributions.
Solstice Finance rolled out a Solana-based product that gives decentralized finance (DeFi) users structured exposure to the dividend income and price risk of Strategy’s (MSTR) preferred stock (STRC).
The Zug, Switzerland-based firm, a DeFi yield infrastructure protocol built on Solana, said its new product splits the indirect STRC exposure into a senior and junior tranche, the firm said in a press release shared via Telegram.
Strategy disclosed it sold 1,690 bitcoin for $108.6 million on Monday, using the proceeds to repurchase 1,152,020 shares of its variable-rate preferred stock, STRC, for $108.6 million. The bitcoin sale reduced Strategy’s holdings to 840,447 BTC.
The product, called strcUSX, does not tokenize or give users ownership of STRC shares. Instead, users deposit USX, Solstice’s dollar-linked settlement token, into a vault and receive one of two Solana tokens tied to the economics of a portfolio holding the Nasdaq-listed preferred stock.
The senior token, SR-strcUSX, is designed to receive income first and targets a yearly yield of 7%. The junior token, JR-strcUSX, takes the residual income after senior holders are paid and targets more than 20% APY. In return, junior holders absorb losses from changes in the value of the STRC position before senior holders do.
The product is the first STRC-linked instrument on Solana, according to Solstice.
STRC, known as Stretch, is Strategy’s variable-rate perpetual preferred stock. It currently pays a 12% annual dividend in cash, with payments twice a month, but the rate is set by Strategy’s board and dividends remain subject to declaration.
STRC may continue to pay its dividend while its market price falls. The senior tranche is meant to shield holders from part of that mark-to-market risk, while the junior tranche takes on more of it in exchange for the higher yield earning potential.
Solstice said users can redeem after a seven-day unlock period or exit immediately for a fee. Yield accrues through the token’s exchange rate rather than being paid as a separate distribution.

title: Adam Back-backed H100 more than triples bitcoin holdings to 3,506 BTC in acquisition deal
summary: H100 paid for the deal with 790.5 million newly issued shares, and the company is now within striking distance of big BTC treasury players.
full_text:
Adam Back-backed H100 more than triples bitcoin holdings to 3,506 BTC in acquisition deal
Quick Take
- H100 paid for the deal with 790.5 million newly issued shares, a roughly 70% dilution.
- The company is now within striking distance of big BTC treasury players like Gemini.
We'd love your feedback.
H100 Group, a Swedish health technology company-turned-bitcoin treasury firm backed by Blockstream CEO Adam Back, more than tripled its bitcoin holdings after acquiring the Norwegian firms Moonshot and PDI.
The company added 2,455.7 BTC through the deal, bringing its total holdings to over 3,506 BTC worth roughly $226.7 million at current prices.
This vaulted H100 from the 42nd-largest to the 26th-largest public corporate bitcoin holder, putting it within striking distance of the Winklevoss-led Gemini treasury, according to Bitcoin Treasuries.
H100 paid for the acquisition by issuing roughly 790.5 million new shares to the sellers rather than using cash. The new shares were issued at SEK 1.86 each, giving them an overall value of around SEK 1.47 billion (~$155 million). H100 said the transaction left sats per basic share unchanged and increased sats per fully diluted share by about 5%.
The 790.5 million new shares issued significantly expanded H100's share count, representing an estimated 70% dilution based on the number of shares outstanding at the time of the announcement.
"This is the largest M&A transaction ever completed in the European Public Bitcoin Equity sector," H100 Executive Chairman Sander Andersen said, adding that the structure allowed the company to preserve its bitcoin-per-share exposure while growing its treasury.
This comes as some of the largest bitcoin treasury companies are moving in the opposite direction. Strategy, the largest public corporate bitcoin holder, sold 1,690 BTC for about $108.6 million last week, while MARA disclosed Friday that it sold 2,213 BTC during the second quarter, bringing its first-half sales to 23,093 BTC for roughly $1.6 billion.

title: Crypto lost $110 million to hacks in July amid rising bug bounty activity: Immunefi
summary: Crypto lost roughly $110 million to hacks in July as Immunefi said its audit competitions outperformed tier-1 audits.
full_text:
Crypto lost $110 million to hacks in July amid rising bug bounty activity: Immunefi
Quick Take
- Crypto losses from hacks reached roughly $110 million in July, according to Immunefi.
- The firm said it paid $2.32 million to researchers for confirmed bugs, while claiming its audit competitions found more serious bugs per engagement than tier-1 audits.
We'd love your feedback.
The crypto industry lost roughly $110 million to hacks in July, according to Immunefi, as the cybersecurity platform reported a rise in confirmed bug reports amid new findings on the effectiveness of crypto audits.
Immunefi said in a statement on Monday that its researchers received $2.32 million for confirmed bugs during the month, while bug bounty reports that were confirmed and paid increased 18%.
The firm’s review of 1,178 tier-1 audits found a median of zero critical or high-severity bugs, it added.
However, the review compared those audits with 58 Immunefi audit competitions, which found more serious bugs per engagement, according to the firm. Immunefi said the competitions identified an average of 6.2 serious bugs per engagement, compared with 1.5 for tier-1 audits.
Immunefi also said the cost of identifying a critical bug averaged $6,548 in an audit competition, compared with about $66,000 in a private tier-1 audit and $24.5 million when an attacker discovered the vulnerability first.
The firm said 374 threats were prevented through its bug bounty programs during the month, up from 317 in June and 339 in May. Cumulative researcher payouts reached $143.1 million, compared with $140.8 million in June.
