title: Colombia’s far-right government recognises Israeli claim over Golan Heights
summary: The South American nation is only the second country to recognise Israel's claims over the illegally annexed territory.
full_text:
Colombia’s far-right government recognises Israeli claim over Golan Heights
The South American nation is only the second country to recognise Israel’s claims over the illegally annexed Syrian territory.
Colombia has become only the second country to recognise Israel’s claim of sovereignty over the occupied Syrian Golan Heights, just days after far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella took power.
Colombia’s Foreign Ministry made the announcement on Monday, joining the United States as the only other country to recognise Israel’s annexation of the territory in 1981.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘Badge of honour’: Israeli settlers shrug off global condemnation
- list 2 of 3With Israel unleashed, there can be no peace in the Middle East
- list 3 of 3President Ahmed al-Sharaa: Syria seeking security deal with Israel
“The Government of Colombia recognises Israeli sovereignty over this territory, as well as that State’s right to protect itself against external threats,” read a statement published on X.
“Colombia recognises that maintaining Israel’s control and sovereignty over the Golan Heights is an essential component of its national defence,” it added.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar thanked his “good friend” de la Espriella for the “historic” recognition.
He said the pair had agreed on the move in the Colombian city of Barranquilla a day before de la Espriella’s inauguration.
Israel captured most of the Golan Heights from Syria during the 1967 Six-Day War, before illegally annexing the territory in 1981. The move was rejected by most of the international community, although the US formally recognised Israel’s claim in 2019 during President Donald Trump’s first term in office.
The United Nations recognises the region as a part of Syria, and last month, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres reiterated that stance, describing Israeli occupation as “totally unacceptable”.
Syria tried to regain the Golan in the 1973 Arab-Israeli war, but was thwarted. Israel and Syria signed an armistice in 1974, and the Golan has been relatively quiet since.
Colombia’s recognition of the Israeli claim comes as Israel expands its military footprint in Syria following the collapse of Bashar al-Assad’s government in December 2024. Israel has moved troops into a UN-monitored buffer zone and seized strategic territories, including the Syrian side of Jabal al-Sheikh (Mount Hermon), which overlooks the capital, Damascus.
De La Espriella, the new Colombian president, ran a bombastic campaign during which he promised close relations with the US and Israel as a way to combat armed groups in his country.
The US-backed millionaire has promised to restore Bogota’s ties with Israel after his predecessor, Gustavo Petro, criticised Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, severed diplomatic relations and halted Israeli arms imports.
De La Espriella has also cancelled Petro’s plans to open an embassy in Ramallah in the occupied West Bank.

title: Trump demands compensation from Iran as talks on Strait of Hormuz continue
summary: US president seeks payment for '50 years' of alleged damages after Iran conditions opening of Hormuz on war reparations.
full_text:
Trump demands compensation from Iran as talks on Strait of Hormuz continue
US president seeks payment for ’50 years’ of alleged damages after Iran conditions reopening of Hormuz on war reparations.
Trump to demand compensation for Tehran’s ‘conflicts’
United States President Donald Trump has demanded compensation from Iran for those he claimed were killed by the country after Tehran conditioned the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz on receiving war reparations from Washington.
Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday that his administration was going to seek payment for “50 years” of damages caused by Iran, framing the move as a direct response to Tehran’s claims.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Where does Iran stand on Saudi-Pakistan-Turkiye pact?
- list 2 of 4Who is Mohsen Rezaee; how significant is his appointment as security chief?
- list 3 of 4What’s behind Trump’s shift to economic pressure on Iran? Will it work?
- list 4 of 4Iran changed the rules in Hormuz. The Gulf is changing the rules for Iran
Tehran has said it will not open the Strait of Hormuz – through which about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas flowed before the US-Israel war on Iran – unless Washington agrees to pay war reparations and end sanctions. The Iranian demands were largely in line with the terms of an interim peace agreement signed in June, which has since broken down over a dispute on control over the strait.
Talks between Iran and Oman over the waterway, which separates the two countries, are ongoing, but Trump’s new demands risk complicating efforts to reopen the maritime passage.
“They asked for reparations, you might say. Or they asked for money for the damage that we’ve done. I said that’s a good idea,” he told reporters. “Well, we’re going to ask for money for the damage they’ve done over a 50-year period.”
The payments would cover deaths among US forces in the region as well as civilian protesters in Iran, he said, claiming that 52,000 people have been killed in Iran in the past four months. Tehran says some 3,117 people died in antigovernment protests that swept the country in January, prior to the launch of the US-Israel war.
The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) in February reported about 7,000 deaths, including 6,500 protesters.
‘Banter’
Trump also said Tehran should compensate families of the 17 US sailors killed in an October 2000 attack in Yemen on the USS Cole naval vessel, which has been blamed on al-Qaeda, not Iran.
“Also, with respect to the Iran negotiations, Iran should be responsible for the damages and death caused to the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza!” he wrote in a Truth Social post.
Since the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, Trump has repeatedly oscillated between threats of escalation and claims that a peace deal is imminent.
He threatened last week to “hit” Iran “very hard”, only to pull back, hinting a peace deal was near. This weekend, he said he was “low-keying” his approach to the conflict, suggesting that he was prepared to let economic pressure mount in place of further military strikes.
Charles Kupchan, a former special assistant to ex-US President Barack Obama, described Trump’s remarks about requiring compensation as “banter” and said both sides have strong incentives to reach a deal.
“Unfortunately, we are just looking at some back-and-forth banter here, where neither the Iranians nor the Trump administration is being serious,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Iran cannot survive if it won’t be able to export its oil”, he said, and Trump doesn’t want to go into the US midterms with high gas prices. There is also pressure on the Pentagon in light of reports that US munitions stockpiles are low, he added.
Iran-Oman talks on Hormuz
Iran earlier said it was nearing a final pact with Oman defining new shipping lanes between them through the Strait of Hormuz, but repeated that the US must meet its conditions, including an end to military threats.
The strait has been effectively blocked since the war began, pushing up oil prices and inflation.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told state media on Monday that talks with Oman were “progressing smoothly and constructively”, with an agreement reached on a shipping route map, while some technical issues remained unresolved.
Baghaei said the discussions also covered services that would normally involve payment, such as safe navigation, environmental protection, maritime services and combating crime.
He added that the US’s continued “hostile actions” in the Strait of Hormuz have made the passageway unsafe and that Tehran considers Washington’s naval blockade of Iranian ports an “act of aggression”.
US Central Command said on Monday that it has redirected 55 commercial vessels since reinstating the blockade in July and “disabled” at least two. According to Windward, a maritime intelligence firm, the blockade has resulted in a “complete halt” to Iranian oil exports from Kharg Island, located in the Gulf.
Trump on Monday described the blockade as a “steel wall” and said that “the only one that has control of the Strait of Hormuz right now is the United States Navy”.
He also claimed the waterway was open and that the US military has cleared it of mines.
Shipping data firms, meanwhile, said traffic in the waterway had dropped sharply over the weekend, with MarineTraffic reporting that crossings had gone down from 15 on Friday to 11 on Saturday, and six on Sunday.
The data showed that 17 vessels passed through the Iran-designated route, while 10 others took a route classified as “undetermined”, it said.

title: Magnitude 7.4 quake rocks western Colombia, killing at least 111 people
summary: Search teams and civilians picked through the remains of destroyed buildings in the country's third-largest city, Cali, passing large pieces of concrete and rubble down a long line of volunteers.
full_text:
Magnitude 7.4 quake rocks western Colombia, killing at least 111 people
CALI, Colombia — A powerful 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia on Monday, killing at least 111 people, damaging hundreds of buildings and leaving many trapped under debris while their loved ones and rescue workers searched through rubble.
Search teams and civilians picked through the remains of destroyed buildings in the country's third-largest city, Cali, passing large pieces of concrete and other rubble down a long line of volunteers.
"Our building has basically been left in ruins, and the building next to ours? Completely collapsed," said Álvaro López, who cradled his dog as he watched the search. The desperate scene recalled the searches still ongoing in neighboring Venezuela weeks after that country was devastated by two powerful earthquakes.
Besides Cali, the quake ravaged cities across western Colombia, including Pereira, Quibdo and Manizales, and was felt in neighboring Ecuador and Panama. The epicenter was in San Jose del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people in the Choco region about 250 miles (400 kilometers) west of Bogota, the U.S. Geological Survey said.
Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella said at least 87 people were injured and around 1,600 buildings were damaged, including at least 61 that completely collapsed. He declared an emergency to expedite funding for the quake recovery.
"We aren't going to leave people alone. They are in our hearts and we are going to tend to people with our full determination," he said.
Most powerful quake recorded in Colombia this century
Colombia's Geological Service said Monday's quake was the country's strongest recorded "in the 21st century," and that it was followed by several aftershocks.
Colombia's Pacific region around the epicenter lies along the "Ring of Fire," the line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world's earthquakes occur. The Pacific, particularly the Choco region, is one of Colombia's poorest, nestled in dense jungle. Much of Choco is only reachable by boat or plane, which may pose difficulty in assessing the wider toll.
Local authorities said the death toll included at least 40 people who were killed in the Risaralda region, where Pereira is located, and 27 people in the Valle del Cauca region, where Cali is located, including three children. Authorities also confirmed nine people killed in Choco, two in the Caldas region and a 73-year-old in the Antioquia region. It was not immediately clear where the other 32 people died.
The earthquakes left many in the Andean nation unnerved after two back-to-back quakes devastated neighboring Venezuela in late June, destroying hundreds of buildings and killing more than 6,300 people.
By Monday afternoon, people had begun reporting their loved ones missing on digital databases just as civilians did following Venezuela's earthquakes. One database had more than 2,000 people, mostly in Cali and Pereira, with the number steadily climbing.
Photos of the missing included a young mother and her baby in Pereira; another showed an 80-year-old woman in Cali whose family was desperately looking for details after her building collapsed.
Cities left devastated
Jorge Moncayo, a 64-year-old taxi driver in Cali, said he saw plumes of dust shoot up across the city as buildings collapsed. Residents and rescue workers were searching the rubble for survivors. The local government said that people remained trapped in a number of the city's 380 damaged buildings.
"My entire house shook. I've never lived through such a powerful earthquake," he said. "We're thanking God we're alive."
Little was known about the extent of the damage in Choco, a remote region where officials reported dozens of injured people and damaged buildings but few other details. Phone signals were out in many parts of the region's capital, Quibdo. The town closest to the earthquake's epicenter, San Jose del Palmar, has no airport, and is located on top of a mountain ridge along a highway linking the cities of Cali and Pereira.
In Pereira, further south in the coffee-producing mountains of Colombia, photos and videos on local media showed pieces of the airport ceiling falling onto travelers taking shelter and screaming. People ran through rubble and plumes of dust, and residents said collapsed stores, residential buildings and homes lined the city. Pereira Mayor Mauricio Salazar told a local radio station there were at least 15 collapsed buildings where people were feared trapped.
In nearby Manizales, one of the towers of the neo-Gothic cathedral collapsed and fell on the nave. Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas asked residents to stay outside in case of aftershocks. Authorities said flights were suspended at the airports in Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, Buenaventura and Pereira as they assessed damage.
Offers of aid pour in from across the Americas
Small earthquakes, known as "temblores," are common in central and western Colombia, but those above 6.0 magnitude are rare. In 1999, a 6.2 magnitude quake near the city of Armenia killed more than 1,100 people.
Response to the earthquake presents the first major challenge for de la Espriella, a Trump ally who was sworn in as president over the weekend. A divisive figure because of his pledge of an all-out crackdown on criminal groups, de la Espriella said he had personally taken charge of the government's response to the emergency.
On Monday night, the U.S. State Department announced it would provide $15.5 million for emergency shelter, food and other earthquake response aid. Governments across Latin America also lined up to help.
El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum — whose countries were among the largest providers of aid to Venezuela following its recent crisis — said they were ready to assist Colombia.
"From El Salvador, we are in communication and ready to provide immediate support with our rescue teams, medical personnel, paramedics, supplies, or any other assistance that our Colombian brothers and sisters deem necessary," Bukele said.
Chilean President José Antonio Kast said Chile, one of the region's most earthquake-prone countries, "knows the pain and the challenge left by earthquakes" and pledged help.

title: Tougher than armour, hard as diamond: China’s unbreakable crystal breakthrough
summary:
Chinese scientists have created a diamond with no Achilles’ heel – one that cannot be broken, even by a hard knock with a hammer – according to a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Synthesis.
While a diamond is the hardest natural material on Earth, it has a major weakness. It is brittle, like glass, and a sharp blow can shatter it. For years, scientists have tried to make diamonds tougher without losing their legendary hardness.
Typically, increasing one characteristic has...
full_text:
Tougher than armour, hard as diamond: China’s unbreakable crystal breakthrough
Scientists use carbon nanotubes to build an internal support structure that overcomes the brittle glasslike nature of diamonds
Chinese scientists have created a diamond with no Achilles’ heel – one that cannot be broken, even by a hard knock with a hammer – according to a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Synthesis.
While a diamond is the hardest natural material on Earth, it has a major weakness. It is brittle, like glass, and a sharp blow can shatter it. For years, scientists have tried to make diamonds tougher without losing their legendary hardness.
Typically, increasing one characteristic has meant sacrificing the other – seen as a reasonable trade-off for most applications, which include industrial uses such as in cutting and polishing tools.
The team – from the Institute of Physics at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Beihang University – found a way around this limitation, building an internal support structure to boost a diamond’s toughness by six times while leaving its hardness unchanged.
The breakthrough material is even tougher than the tungsten alloys used in armour-piercing ammunition, according to the paper, which was published online on July 9.
The secret lies in multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNT) – ultra-strong carbon fibre “cords” that are incredibly thin, about one 10,000th of the width of a human hair, yet dozens of times stronger than steel, the paper said.

Why did US defence official Colby avoid mention of Scarborough Shoal in Manila speech?
Some analysts attribute the restraint to a desire to avoid antagonising Beijing ahead of next month’s expected Xi-Trump summit
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Nayan Sethin Washington
US Undersecretary of Defence for Policy Elbridge Colby avoided naming Beijing or addressing escalating tensions in the South China Sea during a speech in Manila on Monday, adopting a measured tone weeks before an expected meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
Despite speaking in the capital of Washington’s oldest treaty ally in Asia, Colby made no direct reference to recent confrontations between Chinese and Philippine forces near the disputed Scarborough Shoal.
Instead, he sought to reassure regional allies that the United States was “definitely not disengaging from Asia”.
“We are not leaving; in fact, we are digging in, to ensure a favourable balance of power where it matters most,” Colby said during an event at a Manila think tank.
His omissions were particularly notable because two days earlier Washington had criticised Beijing for its actions over what it called a “destabilising” nature reserve at the reef and denying Filipino fishermen access to their traditional fishing grounds.
Some analysts attributed Colby’s restraint to Washington’s desire to avoid antagonising Beijing before the expected Trump-Xi meeting next month.

title: Native birds in captivity to be vaccinated against H5 bird flu as Australia prepares for more mass mortalities
summary:
Federal government also hopes to vaccinate some wild birds but admits catching them once, let alone twice for both doses, is ‘difficult’

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Vaccinations against H5 bird flu will be rolled out for Australian native bird species in captivity as the deadly virus continues to spread across the country.

The federal agriculture minister, Julie Collins, said on Tuesday that target native species in captivity would be prioritised with the first vaccinations to commence “in the coming days and weeks”.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Vaccinations against H5 bird flu will be rolled out for Australian native bird species in captivity as the deadly virus continues to spread across the country.
The federal agriculture minister, Julie Collins, said on Tuesday that target native species in captivity would be prioritised with the first vaccinations to commence “in the coming days and weeks”.
Collins said state governments would manage the program and announce the target species soon.
“We’ve been very clear that we cannot stop the H5 bird flu from spreading among wild birds, but we can take action to protect the species most at risk,” the minister said. “Vaccination is now part of that response.”
Collins warned Australians they would continue to see “more spread and larger numbers – particularly of dead birds and mass mortalities around the country”.
The vaccination program would focus on captive species such as endangered birds that were part of conservation breeding programs in zoos and other facilities.
The federal environment minister, Murray Watt, said it was difficult to vaccinate wild birds because a full course required two doses. But the commonwealth did plan to vaccinate wild birds where possible, he said.
“It does take two vaccination doses to vaccinate birds, and it is difficult enough to catch wild birds once, let alone twice. [But] where it’s possible to vaccinate wild birds, we will do so.”
Endangered birds in captivity include the orange-bellied parrot, regent honeyeater and Western Australia’s black cockatoos.
Australia’s chief veterinary officer, Beth Cookson, said the vaccination rollout followed trials examining its safety and efficacy over the past 18 months.
The government did not say which species or facilities had participated in the pilot program.
“The trials and pilots that we’ve undertaken so far have provided us with some safety data across a range of different species,” Cookson said.
She said because the vaccines already in use had been developed for poultry, the government needed to gather safety data across a range of native bird species.
“As you can appreciate, birds come in all different sizes, and the vaccines that we’ve got are made for poultry,” she said.
“So it was really important as part of the preparedness that we had that safety information. We’ll continue to gather that information and to prioritise vaccination in those species where we’ve got sufficient evidence.”
The federal government said it would move from daily updates of H5 case numbers to a focus on major events such as mass mortalities as the number of infected species continued to rise.
The first mass mortalities occurred in South Australia and Victoria last week as H5 bird flu spread to new species, including silver gulls.
The South Australian government said on Tuesday that a peregrine falcon was among 33 new suspect cases in that state.
Last week, cases were detected in the Murray-Darling region of SA and New South Wales for the first time.
Prof John Woinarski of Charles Darwin University said the plan to vaccinate priority captive species was welcomed, but more work was needed, including for mammals at risk from bird flu.
“Trials with mammals is important,” he said on Tuesday. “It’s doable, in terms of the practicality of it, with seals and seal lions that come ashore.”
Woinarski called on governments to reveal which captive bird species would be vaccinated or subject to trials. “We also need to know if they have any adverse reactions,” he said.
The conservation biologist said it should be possible to vaccinate less mobile wild bird populations, such as the little penguin population on Phillip Island in Victoria.
Cookson said on Tuesday there were “no commercially available vaccines suitable for mammals” but the federal government was working closely with other countries “to follow some of the trials that are being undertaken, including in the US”.

title: Bitcoin’s BIP-110 fork is 300 blocks behind BTC and six years from fixing itself
full_text:
Bitcoin’s BIP-110 fork is 300 blocks behind BTC and six years from fixing itself
The breakaway chain has produced two blocks since splitting off on Saturday. Bitcoin has produced more than 300 in the same stretch.
- A proposed Bitcoin rule change known as BIP-110 triggered a chain split on Saturday, but the breakaway chain has produced only two blocks and has since stalled.
- Because the forked chain inherited Bitcoin’s high mining difficulty while its coin has no market value, miners have little incentive to support it, leaving it 326 blocks behind the main network.
- The forked chain cannot lower its mining difficulty until it reaches 2,016 blocks, a milestone now estimated to be more than six years away, though some observers caution it is too early to declare the effort a failure.
A breakaway bitcoin chain is now so short of miners that its own mechanism for fixing that is six years away.
The chain that broke away from bitcoin on Saturday has not moved since. It is still sitting on block 961,633, its second. Bitcoin has since climbed to block 961,959, leaving the fork 326 blocks behind.
The split happened because of a proposal called BIP-110, which would stop people storing pictures, text and other non-payment data in bitcoin transactions for a year. Changing bitcoin's rules requires miners to agree, and they register that agreement by marking the blocks they produce. BIP-110 needed 55% of blocks over a two-week stretch. It got about 2.6% at its peak.
But rather than accept that, the proposal had a second route built into it. At block 961,632, computers running BIP-110 software began rejecting every block that did not carry the mark, regardless of what miners had decided.
Almost no blocks carry it, so those computers rejected the chain nearly all of bitcoin's mining power was building and started following one made only of blocks that did.
Bitcoin's ledger is a chain of blocks, each one a batch of transactions added by miners, firms running warehouses of specialised computers that compete to produce the next one. They are paid in newly issued bitcoin plus the fees attached to those transactions, and a block arrives roughly every ten minutes.
That ten-minute pace is not automatic. The network sets a difficulty level, which is how much computing work a miner must do to produce a valid block, and recalculates it every 2,016 blocks. If blocks have been arriving too fast, the work gets harder. Too slow, and it gets easier.
At normal speed, 2,016 blocks takes about two weeks.
Two blocks were produced on that chain. Then it stopped, because mining it costs exactly what mining bitcoin costs — as both chains having inherited the same difficulty when they parted, while paying in a coin that has no market, no exchange listing and no buyers.
It also cannot make mining easier on itself without first completing 2,016 blocks at its current pace. A live monitor now estimates that adjustment at 6.3 years away, up from 350 days on Sunday.
The number is calculated from recent block times, so every idle hour pushes it further out. Bitcoin's next adjustment is due in 12 days.
Not everyone reads this as settled, however.
"I think it is still too early to draw any firm conclusions from the initial block production," said Himanshu Sahay, co-founder of Arch, told CoinDesk in a message. Changes to bitcoin's rules depend on coordination across miners, developers and the wider ecosystem, he said, and while the gap is worth watching, "I would be cautious about describing it as a failure at this stage."

title: XRP, ether lead crypto losses as traders eye $70,000 bitcoin next
full_text:
XRP, ether lead crypto losses as traders eye $70,000 bitcoin next
Bitcoin failed to hold $65,000 for a fourth day as an oil rally revived inflation worries before Wednesday's U.S. price data.
- Bitcoin slipped below $65,000 after a fourth failed attempt to hold that level, though it remains slightly higher on the week amid weak overall crypto sentiment.
- Ether and XRP led declines among major tokens, while Solana and BNB held weekly gains and HYPE, tron and dogecoin edged higher.
- Analysts see a buildup of short positions above $65,000 and view $70,000—near bitcoin’s 200-day moving average—as the key level that could shift sentiment, as broader markets focus on rising bond yields, higher oil prices and upcoming U.S. inflation data.
Bitcoin slipped to near $64,000 on Tuesday, down over 1% on the day but still up marginally on the week, after a fourth failed attempt to hold above $65,000. It reached a 24-hour high just above $65,300 before sliding through the Asian afternoon.
Ether was the weakest major, down over 2% to $1,878, though it remains slightly higher over seven days. XRP fell almost 2% to $1.01 and is down almost 6% on the week, the worst of the group by some distance. Solana eased under 1% to $76 but leads the week at 3%. BNB slipped to $600 and holds a 2% weekly gain.
Three majors went the other way. Hyperliquid's HYPE rose almost 2% to $55, tron gained slightly to 33 cents and dogecoin was marginally higher at 7 cents.
Alex Kuptsikevich, chief market analyst at FxPro, said bitcoin has been testing $65,000 for four straight days without any surge in buying as it approaches the round number.
More telling is the absence of selling into it, which he read as "a build-up of short positions well above this level" rather than holders taking profit.
That makes $70,000 the next area to watch, another round number with the 200-day moving average sitting nearby. Clearing it would put bitcoin above the range where buyers and sellers fought through March and April, a move Kuptsikevich said would shift sentiment meaningfully.
Traders are not there yet. The crypto sentiment index sits at 30, in what is known as the fear zone, and has stayed there since mid-July with occasional dips toward extreme fear.
Bonds and oil set the tone in broader markets. U.S. 10-year Treasury yields rose six basis points on Monday to 4.71%, dragging Australian and New Zealand government bonds down with them, with no cash Treasury trading during Asian hours because of a public holiday in Japan.
Brent crude held at $87.73 a barrel after jumping 5% on Monday, when President Donald Trump made fresh demands on Iran and dimmed hopes of a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Gold rose for a third session above $4,400 an ounce.
Higher oil feeds into the inflation figures due Wednesday at 8:30 a.m. ET, which is why the rally is weighing on assets that do better when rate rises look less likely.
Fund flows had been running the other way until this week. U.S. spot bitcoin funds took in $865 million across five sessions through Aug. 7, before a provisional outflow of $91 million on Monday.

title: Luke Dashjr removed as Bitcoin Improvement Proposal editor
summary: Luke Dashjr lost his BIP editor privileges after developers raised concerns over his role in BIP 110 and its stalled minority fork.
full_text:
Luke Dashjr removed as Bitcoin Improvement Proposal editor
Luke Dashjr lost his BIP editor privileges after developers raised concerns over his role in BIP 110 and its stalled minority fork.
Bitcoin developer Luke Dashjr has been removed as an editor of Bitcoin Improvement Proposals following a dispute over his role in BIP 110.
Bitcoin developer Mark Erhardt opened the pull request on Sunday after recommending Dashjr’s removal on the Bitcoin Developer mailing list.
Erhardt said Dashjr had been “heavily involved” in creating and implementing BIP 110 and alleged that he unfairly favored the proposal while serving as an editor, including by attempting to assign it a BIP number before mailing-list discussion and quickly merging an update to it.
Bitcoin developer Jon Atack said he had verified that Dashjr no longer had editor or administrator privileges in the BIPs repository following the mailing-list discussion. Atack then merged the pull request, removing Dashjr from the list of BIP editors.
“This is just an abuse of power by Core,” Dashjr said. “They have no authority to do so.”
BIP 110 sought to temporarily restrict the amount of arbitrary data that could be embedded in Bitcoin transactions. The proposal triggered a minority chain split after nodes enforcing it rejected blocks from miners that did not signal support, but the fork quickly stalled with little hashpower support.

title: 昔日惡名昭彰紅燈區，今躋身全球頂級 AI 樞紐
summary:
昔日以毒品與性交易惡名昭彰的倫敦國王十字區，因 DeepMind 進駐引爆聚落效應，如今匯集 OpenAI、A […]

〈昔日惡名昭彰紅燈區，今躋身全球頂級 AI 樞紐〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
昔日以毒品與性交易惡名昭彰的倫敦國王十字區，因 DeepMind 進駐引爆聚落效應，如今匯集 OpenAI、Anthropic 等巨頭，租金飆漲、人才爭奪白熱化，躋身全球第三大 AI 樞紐。
（前情提要：薦讀》科技業為何集體憂鬱？當 AI 抽走你工作最後一點人味 ）
（背景補充：OpenAI 推出專用網路安全模型 GPT-5.6-Cyber：Blue 防禦、Red 攻擊雙模式迎戰 AI 威脅 ）
曾經以毒品與性交易聞名的倫敦國王十字區，如今搖身一變，成為僅次於舊金山與北京的全球人工智慧重鎮。根據《TechCrunch》報導，這片被稱為「知識特區」（Knowledge Quarter）的區域，已聚集了 Google DeepMind、OpenAI、Anthropic、Meta 等幾乎所有 AI 巨頭，昔日的都市瘡疤正上演一場戲劇性的城市翻轉。
從紅燈區到知識特區
時間拉回四十多年前，國王十字是倫敦最聲名狼藉的角落之一。
一九八○年代，古柯鹼與海洛因氾濫，讓這裡淪為毒品交易的溫床；一九八二年，「英國性工作者集體組織」更曾佔領當地教堂長達十二天，抗議警方騷擾，成為英國社運史上的著名事件。
轉機出現在二○○○年代初期。隨著大型房地產開發計畫啟動，加上聖潘克拉斯車站成為歐洲之星起訖站，這片鐵路後巷逐漸蛻變為融合歷史建築、辦公空間與休閒場所的新街區。倫敦大學學院（UCL）、大英圖書館等機構坐落於此，為日後的「知識特區」定調。
DeepMind 效應：AI 巨頭群聚
真正引爆 AI 聚落效應的，是二○一六年被 Google 收購後不久便進駐此地的 DeepMind。Hoxton Ventures 投資人 Hussein Kanji 早在二○○五年就搬到這一帶，親眼見證整場蛻變。他形容，如今的國王十字已是「英國 AI 的溫床」，並感嘆：「變化真是太大了。」
DeepMind 落腳後，新創公司如潮水般湧入，希望沾染「DeepMind 魔力」。如今方圓幾條街內，聚集了 OpenAI、Meta、藥物研發公司 Isomorphic Labs、材料科學新創 Cusp AI，稍遠處還有 AI 影片公司 Synthesia 與 Anthropic。
今年稍早，OpenAI 與 Anthropic 相繼宣布在國王十字設立新據點；其中 Anthropic 更租下約十五萬八千平方英尺的辦公室，可容納八百人，約為其倫敦現有人力的四倍，並稱倫敦是其「美國以外最重要的樞紐」。
辦公空間告急，租金三年漲近兩成
AI 公司的瘋狂擴張，直接反映在房地產數據上。根據仲量行 Knight Frank 統計，自六月以來，AI 相關企業已在倫敦承租超過一百萬平方英尺的辦公空間；國王十字的頂級租金三年內上漲百分之十八，傳統辦公空間的空置率更只剩百分之零點九。
Knight Frank 商業分析師 Chris Dunn 直言：「需求已經遠遠超過供給。」
資金面同樣火熱。根據 Dealroom 數據，倫敦目前約有三千六百家 AI 新創公司，自七月底以來，倫敦新創共募得一百四十八億美元，其中高達一百二十一億美元流向 AI 公司，占比超過八成。生技新創 BioCorteX 共同創辦人 Nik Sharma 形容：「倫敦現在非常熱鬧，大批超大規模企業正在進駐。」
薪資戰開打，本土新創壓力山大
不過，財力雄厚的美國科技巨頭大舉登陸，也讓本土新創叫苦連天。
以 Anthropic 為例，其機器學習研究工程師的年薪介於二十六萬至六十三萬英鎊之間；而根據人力顧問公司 Robert Half 的資料，倫敦同類職位的平均年薪僅約十萬二千英鎊，差距高達數倍。
這場人才軍備競賽，迫使本土公司不得不擴大募資規模，或轉向歐洲各地的遠距人才。Synthesia 人資長 Laura Gonzalez Florez 就表示，從倫敦出發，「與斯洛維尼亞到葡萄牙各地的人才合作毫無障礙」，而且這裡「離機場近，也離投資人非常近」。
歐洲的主權焦慮與真正考驗
美國巨頭壓境，也喚醒了歐洲的「AI 主權」意識。Phoenix Court 創投共同創辦人 Saul Klein 提醒：「我們最好學會照顧自己」；另一位共同創辦人 Robin Klein 則稱，近期事件是「一記雖小但尖銳的警鐘，歐洲不能只是租用 AI 能力」，必須建立自己的基礎設施與旗艦企業。
但正如 AI 法律新創 Centuro 創辦人 Zain Ali 所言，國王十字的真正考驗才剛開始：「關鍵在於，是否有更多具全球影響力的 AI 公司，能在英國創立、募資並規模化。」從紅燈區到 AI 聖地，國王十字用二十年完成第一次轉身；能否從巨頭分部聚集地升級為「孕育巨頭的搖籃」，將決定它的下一個二十年。

title: 手機漲價還沒完？三星：記憶體需求未來 1～2 年仍強
summary: 記憶體價格持續上揚，手機品牌成本壓力同步升高。台灣三星總經理陳啟蒙今（11）日表示，記憶體需求橫跨不同產業及裝 […]
full_text:
記憶體價格持續上揚，手機品牌成本壓力同步升高。台灣三星總經理陳啟蒙今（11）日表示，記憶體需求橫跨不同產業及裝置，預期未來 1～2 年需求仍將維持強勁，價格大幅下修的空間有限；從手機零組件成本來看，記憶體仍是影響成本結構的主要因素，未來手機價格也可能隨供應鏈成本持續波動。
面對成本增加，三星目前已調漲部分 Galaxy A 系列產品價格，調價幅度約落在 500 元至 3,000 元，Galaxy S 系列目前則尚未調整。陳啟蒙表示，三星在台灣市場仍會盡可能降低成本波動帶來的影響，但手機定價除了反映記憶體及零組件成本，也必須考量消費者的接受程度。
陳啟蒙指出，目前 Galaxy A 系列調價後，實際銷量並未受到太大影響；三星平板產品歷經兩次價格調整後，銷售表現同樣未出現明顯變化。她認為，消費者已逐漸意識到記憶體價格上漲帶來的影響，只要價格調整幅度合理，市場仍具有一定接受度。
近期市場也傳出蘋果可能調整舊款 iPhone 售價，手機市場後續價格走勢受到關注。陳啟蒙認為，成本上升並非單一品牌面臨的問題，未來整體手機產業價格都可能受到記憶體及零組件成本影響。除了直接調整售價，各品牌也可能減少低規格產品供應、提高高階機型比重，在銷量、毛利與消費者可接受的平均售價之間取得平衡。
對於台灣手機市場展望，陳啟蒙維持今年整體銷量年減 6% 至 8% 的預估，不過銷售金額仍有 6% 至 8% 的成長空間，反映高階旗艦手機需求仍具支撐。陳啟蒙指出，從第三方銷售數據觀察，台灣前兩大手機品牌今年上半年銷量受到的影響相對有限，在零組件成本上升下，中低階手機市場面臨的價格與銷量壓力相對更大。
（首圖來源：科技新報）

title: PM asks justice secretary to find way to keep PC Harper's killers in jail
summary: Andy Burnham is confident a solution can be found to exclude two of PC Harper's killers from an early release scheme, the BBC understands.
full_text:
PM asks justice secretary to find way to keep PC Harper's killers in jail
- Published
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told his justice secretary to find a way to exclude PC Andrew Harper's killers from an early release scheme designed to ease prison overcrowding.
Burnham is confident a solution can be found to remove Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter in 2020, from the government plan, the BBC has been told.
Downing Street had earlier warned it would not be possible to exclude "one or two offenders" convicted of manslaughter from the early release of prisoners.
PC Harper, 28, from Wallingford, Oxfordshire, died in 2019 when he was dragged behind the getaway car of three teenagers who had fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.
Under changes to the Sentencing Act made this year, Cole and Bowers, who were found not guilty of murder, will become eligible for release from custody next January after serving half of their sentences.
They are in a category of prisoners - those who have committed certain serious violent or sexual crimes - who until now would have had to serve at least two-thirds of their sentence in jail before being considered for release.
It is not yet clear how the government will prevent Cole and Bowers from being treated the same as other prisoners with similar sentences.
If ministers said, for example, that prisoners with manslaughter convictions could not be considered for the scheme, that would have an instant impact on many other inmates.
A government spokesperson told the BBC: "The prime minister has asked the Justice Secretary to work through further options to keep a greater number of the most serious offenders in prison, including the killers of PC Harper."
A source said the Justice Secretary Alex Norris would set out "in due course" how the government would exclude Cole and Bowers from early release.
The prime minister has been making daily calls while on holiday to find a solution, sources told the BBC.
Around 5,000 people are expected to be released under the sentencing changes, down from 6,000 after exemptions were previously announced for those convicted of the most serious crimes including rape, child sex offences and grooming.
The third man jailed for the manslaughter of PC Harper - the vehicle driver Henry Long - was given a longer 16-year jail term. Because he received what is called an extended determinate sentence at the time, he cannot be considered for this early release scheme.
PC Harper's widow, Lissie Harper, has been among a growing number calling for Cole and Bowers to be denied early release. She and PC Harper had been married for just a month when he was killed in the line of duty.
Lissie Harper previously led a successful campaign for Harper's Law, which introduced mandatory life sentences for anyone convicted of killing an emergency worker whilst committing a crime.
Former police dog handler Chris Bushnell, who was at the scene of PC Harper's death, said he was "shaking" when he heard that two of the officer's killers might be released early from prison.
Bushnell was waiting in a lay-by near Sulhamstead, west Berkshire, in August 2019 when the teenagers' vehicle appeared, dragging PC Harper along the ground.
The former constable gave chase until he was ordered to stop and remain where he was. He said: "I've seen people die before. I've seen suicides. This was beyond brutal. It was awful."
"To think they could be released early is absolutely outrageous," Bushnell said.
"I'm angry with them, but I'm also angry with the government. They're spitting in the face of police officers."
Aileen O'Connor, chairwoman of Thames Valley Police Federation, added: "The public are speaking loudly and clearly. They agree with us that the government are firmly on the wrong side of this."
About 900,000 people have signed O'Connor's petition to stop the killers' early release.
But ministers have said prison spaces might run out as soon as October.
Dame Vera Baird, a former victims' commissioner, told BBC Two's Newsnight that one "good thing" the government has done is invest money in victim support services, as there would be many people currenty concerned that their attackers will be walking the streets sooner than they had expected.
She said the government "need to look at the right people to be letting out more carefully than they've managed so far".
Dame Vera added that women and people jailed under controversial Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences could also be considered for early release to alleviate pressure on prisons.
IPP sentences were introduced in 2005 and allowed judges to give out sentences with no maximum tariff to perpetrators of serious crimes or repeat offenders.
The sentences were scrapped in 2012, but were not retrospectively applied. As of this year, more than 2,000 people are still in prison on IPP sentences according to the United Nations (UN),, external who have called for the end of IPP sentences.
"I think somebody has to just seize the thing and get it sorted," Dame Vera said. "There has to be a wholesale resentencing attempt, I think, and really that does need thinking through."

title: Trump says it would be 'terrible mistake' to remove Infantino

Trump says it would be 'terrible mistake' to remove Infantino
- Published
US President Donald Trump says it would be a "terrible mistake" if under pressure Fifa president Gianni Infantino was ousted from his position.
Trump's backing followed Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation issuing an open letter accusing Infantino of breaking trust "through deception" with his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal.
FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all Fifa competitions, including World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.
Trump's comments are the first time he has come out in defence of Infantino since the FFE plans came to light on 28 July.
"Fifa would be making a terrible mistake if, for any reason, they even considered replacing president Gianni Infantino," Trump wrote on social media.
"He is fantastic, having just presided over the most successful World Cup, by four times, ever presented. If he is gone, it will never be as successful or profitable again."
The 2026 World Cup was co-hosted by the US, Canada and Mexico this summer, with Spain crowned champions after beating Argentina in the final.
When addressing the FFE proposals for the first time on 31 July, Trump said he had not spoken to Infantino about the plans.
Thrive Eternal was expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE.
Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner - the brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared.

title: Jewish school heads spend more time on security than education, review finds
summary: It's one of the findings from an independent review into antisemitism in schools and colleges.
full_text:
Jewish school heads spend more time on security than education, review finds
- Published
Headteachers of some Jewish schools are spending more of their time dealing with security arrangements than on educational matters, a review into antisemitism in schools and colleges has found.
Sir David Bell, speaking for the first time about his ongoing government-commissioned independent review, told the BBC he had been struck by how many leaders of Jewish faith schools had told him security was their primary concern - and that "sometimes education takes second place to that".
The report, due in the autumn, examines the experiences of Jewish pupils and staff in faith and secular schools and colleges in England.
Sir David said he found that pupils were "subject to regular harassment and abuse".
He said Jewish children and young people "are facing a pressure - and indeed one might say even a crisis - that is not the experience of other communities in this country".
The review is likely to recommend dedicated training for all teachers and improved education about antisemitism for pupils, the BBC has been told.
The BBC has spoken to several headteachers and staff at Jewish schools. All asked not to be named because of concerns over their security and that of their schools.
One headteacher said: "In recent years [security] has become an overwhelming priority and increased a significant amount. There have been weeks where approximately 90% of my time has been spent on security-related matters.
"Security concerns can become one of the many things that headteachers carry with them beyond the school day and, quite literally, can be among the things that keep me awake at night."
Another headteacher, who has led a different Jewish school for 13 years, told the BBC: "I've never spent so much of my time and so much energy dealing with security issues, talking to governors and parents, and above all making daily decisions about how to ensure children in our school are safe."
He said it prevented him from "working on educational priorities and on improving our school - instead my focus and time has been spent on security, something that should be a given for every child in this country".
Sir David Bell, a former Ofsted chief inspector and senior civil servant at the Department for Education, is now vice-chancellor of the University of Sunderland. He has heard evidence from pupils, teachers, governors and parents across both the state and independent sectors as well as community organisations.
The Bell review has also drawn evidence from a bespoke survey of 5,000 children conducted by the universities, colleges, and admissions service, Ucas. It found about 20% had experienced or observed antisemitic behaviour in schools and colleges.
Sir David said: "When you think about antisemitism, you assume that it's going to be directed towards adults… What's been quite shocking is the extent to which antisemitism is encountered by children and young people."
'Nazi salutes became quite widespread'
Recent figures from the Community Security Trust, an organisation which provides security for the Jewish community, showed a spike in antisemitic incidents at schools.
It found in the first half of 2026, antisemitism in schools reached the highest level ever recorded for the first six months of any year. It jumped by 59%, from 112 reported incidents in the first half of 2025, to 178 recorded over the same period in 2026.
Dr Dave Rich, director of policy at the CST, said the review was timely and hopes "it will lead to practical recommendations that help educational institutions tackle antisemitism effectively."
Education Secretary Lucy Powell told the BBC the review was a "vital piece of work" and she would "carefully consider the conclusions and recommendations to ensure we do what is necessary to prevent antisemitism in our schools and colleges".
She said in a statement: "Antisemitism has no place in our society, let alone our education system. Jewish children and staff should never face hatred or prejudice, and every school and college must be equipped to tackle it when it happens."
One teenager who gave evidence to the Bell review is Jonathan Frisher, from Cheshire. Now a sixth former, Jonathan was the only Jewish student at his school. He first experienced antisemitic bullying when he started secondary school in 2020.
"Having one single lesson about modern-day antisemitism really did help," he said.
"Attitudes changed immediately and people did apologise to me. I experienced a lot less antisemitism. If it works in my school, there's no reason that it can't work in every school across the country."
Sir David said the majority of the 700 people who had responded directly to his "call for evidence" were Jewish parents and pupils at non-faith schools.
He said the evidence has led him to realise that many schools do not record antisemitic abuse in part because of a lack of understanding about how to recognise it.
When his report is published, he is likely to recommend a standardised approach to reporting and recording antisemitic incidents in schools and colleges.
Jonathan Frisher's own experiences have led him to campaign for antisemitism education to be made compulsory in schools. A petition he started has gained nearly 40,000 signatures.
He said: "People were telling me that I should be in a gas chamber. Swastikas were drawn in lots of classrooms and Nazi salutes became quite widespread. Obviously for someone whose family suffered in the Holocaust it was incredibly difficult to have to deal with comments like that."
'My car is searched with an under-car mirror'
Sir David added that pupils travelling to and from Jewish schools were "subject to regular harassment and abuse". Pupils aged 12 and 13 in one Jewish faith school in London told him they were regularly abused on the school journey and on public transport. "It's a very different experience for these children and young people to what the vast majority of children and young people in this country face when they're going to and from school and college," he said.
He said many teachers at Jewish faith schools reported that going out on school trips was more hazardous than before.
One teacher at a Jewish primary school told the BBC security had been stepped up since the spate of arson attacks against Jewish sites and the stabbing of two Jewish men in Golders Green earlier this year.
She said: "There's a security presence patrolling outside the school, inside the school, at all times of day. When I get to school in the morning and enter the car park, my car is searched with an under-car mirror."
She added that recent incidents had at times contributed to a "heavy" atmosphere.
She said: "There have been reports from parents that antisemitic comments have been made while [pupils] are walking to school. We've had children at music events and sporting events who were booed. There was a comment made about big noses at one of the events that we took the children to.
"We do what we can to shield the children from a lot of it, but also, if they approach me with their concerns, I can't ignore it. And when one of my pupils said to me, 'Why do people hate Jews so much?', that was really difficult for me to answer.
"It just goes to show what they're internalising."

title: Swimming lessons 'vital' as schools gap revealed
summary: How is your school doing on teaching pupils life-saving swimming skills in the English curriculum?
full_text:
Swimming lessons 'vital' as schools gap revealed
- Published
Children at English primary schools with more pupils on free school meals are less likely to leave able to swim 25m, BBC research has found.
While 72% of Year 6 children on average left school able to swim 25m in 2024-25, this drops to just 55% for schools with a higher proportion of disadvantaged children.
Ashley Jones, head of water safety and education at the Royal Life Saving Society (RLSS), said it was "absolutely vital" children were equipped with basic swimming and self-rescue skills.
A Department for Education (DfE) spokesperson said it was aware of the gap and it "needs to change".
The national curriculum in England, external states when they leave Year 6, all pupils should be able to:
- Swim competently, confidently and proficiently over a distance of at least 25m
- Use a range of strokes effectively (for example, front crawl, backstroke and breaststroke)
- Perform safe self-rescue in different water-based situations
A BBC Freedom of Information request to the DfE has revealed the proportion of Year 6 pupils at individual state schools, excluding special schools, who are able to meet the targets.
While 70% of 2024-25 Year 6 leavers nationally could on average perform a safe self-rescue, only half of children from schools with the highest level of free meal eligibility could do so.
A safe self-rescue includes being able to tread water for 30 seconds, children being able to float on their back for 60 seconds and swim 15m to exit the water unaided.
Most school groups only get six weeks of 30-minute sessions to learn basic swimming skills – three hours in total.
Find out how your child's school performed
School performance ranged from no pupils leaving Year 6 able to swim 25m to others meeting the target at 100%.
Only 38 schools in the highest category for disadvantaged pupils hit the swimming target. Meanwhile, it was met by nearly 400 schools with the lowest proportion of children on free school meals.
For parents, there can be several obstacles when it comes to helping their children learn to swim and become water competent.
In 2021, Swim England published its Decade of Decline report, external warning almost 2,000 swimming pools could be lost forever by 2030.
Accessibility is one of the factors Ashley Jones from the RLSS says limits children's swimming education.
"We've got some incredible public leisure facilities, just not enough of them," he said.
"That means people have got to travel further.
"Then you are dependent on public transport, which can be costly, and access to a swimming pool in terms of cost and time is still really challenging."
The RLSS works to help people stay safe in, on, and around water. A key element of its work is using education to help people become water competent.
Jones explained: "You can be a really competent pool swimmer, but we wouldn't dare put you in 6ft of surf or throw you in a raging river.
"Building competence, you've got to have knowledge, you've got to have skills, you've got to have experience, crucially, and you've got to have training."
In order to help children build water competency, Jones believes swimming lessons need to be universal, engaging and accessible.
The RLSS would like to see "a fully funded, fully supported, high-level learn to swim programme" that is supported by water safety education and then applied in an outdoor environment.
Hampshire-based swimming teacher Bethany Harris said it was "really tough" to teach a life skill in that time to children who have not had much access to swimming.
She believes school swimming lessons should start earlier in life to ensure nobody is left behind.
"Ultimately, in three hours you can't take someone from being a nervous swimmer to confidently being able to swim 25m with a stroke that is calm and is going to keep them safe," she said.
"I don't think many of us would come out of that with something that was going to save our lives potentially.
"I think it needs to come in basically as we're teaching them to read and write in the infant school."
Harris lives "on the doorstep" of Hawley Lake, where a 14-year-old died after being reported missing while swimming.
"Even being inland away from the coast you've got dangerous water all about," she said.
The bottom fifth of local authorities for the average proportion of children able to swim 25m were all urban areas.
Only four out of 31 of those council areas were coastal, with the remaining areas being landlocked.
Overall, fewer children in urban areas could swim the distance proficiently than in rural areas.
Harris would also like to see pools offer more initiatives to ensure they are accessible to all families.
She said: "Ten years ago, there used to be a summer scheme where you could swim for £1 all summer long through some leisure centres.
"I haven't heard of anything like that happening locally these days."
A spokesperson for the DfE said a new PE Partnership Network would help close the gap seen by disadvantaged children.
It will bring together schools, local clubs and national bodies like Swim England.
"This means targeted support for the areas and pupils who need it most, so that every child, wherever they live, gets the same chance to learn to swim," the spokesperson said.
Swim England is working closely with the government to support the delivery of school swimming lessons.
"Swimming is a life skill, not just a sport, and every child should have the opportunity to leave primary school able to swim and be safe in, on and around water," a spokesperson said.
"However, schools have faced significant pressures in recent years, particularly those serving disadvantaged communities, including competing curriculum demands, increasing transport costs and access to suitable swimming pools.
"These challenges are real, so it is more important than ever that there is a collective approach to helping children gain a skill that could one day save their life."
Additional reporting by Jonathan Fagg and Emily Unia

Trump’s media company reports $238m loss
Trump Media & Technology Group earns less than $2m in Q2.
US President Donald Trump’s media conglomerate has reported a net loss of $238m in the second quarter of 2026, against revenue of $1.7m.
In its latest filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Monday, Trump Media & Technology Group (TMTG) attributed most of the shortfall to $190.4m in unrealised losses on digital assets, digital assets pledged and equity securities.

Other losses included $11.7m in “accreted interest” – unpaid interest on a loan that is added to the principal – and $8.1m in “stock-based compensation”.
TMTG said revenue for the April-June quarter rose 89 percent compared with the same period last year, though losses continued to outpace earnings.
Almost all of TMTG’s revenue came from “media segments”, including $1.43m from advertising and $179,500 from subscriptions, according to the SEC filings.
The financial results bring TMTG’s net losses for the first half of 2026 to $644m, against revenue of $2.5m.
Shares of TMTG, which trades under the NASDAQ symbol “DJT”, were down 8 percent at market closing on Monday.
TMTG’s portfolio includes the social media platform Truth Social, the video streaming service Truth+ and the fintech brand Truth.Fi.
Over the past year, the company has also branched into other areas, including cryptocurrency and, as of August 1, market intelligence through the controversial subscription service Truth API.
Truth API provides investors faster access to posts on Truth Social, where Trump regularly makes market-moving announcements on policy issues such as tariffs and the US-Israel war on Iran.
TMTG interim CEO Kevin McGurn said during an earnings call on Monday that 10 companies had already signed up for the service, which has raised conflict of interest concerns, paying $60,000 to $100,000 per month in fees.
Despite the influence of Trump’s posts, Truth Social has lagged behind rival platforms such as X and Facebook in terms of users since its launch in 2022.
The New York Times reported on Monday that visitors to Truth Social in July were down by more than a third compared with the same period last year, citing data from the online tracking firm Similarweb.

title: Huge fire breaks out at Libya’s Zawiya refinery after drone attack
summary: National oil company warns it may halt operations at the country's largest operating refinery if drone attacks continue.
full_text:
Huge fire breaks out at Libya’s Zawiya refinery after drone attack
Libya’s National Oil Corporation warns it may halt operations at the country’s largest operating refinery if drone attacks continue.
Fire rages after drone strikes Libya’s largest oil refinery
Firefighters in Libya are battling a massive blaze at the Zawiya refinery following a drone attack, with the country’s national oil company warning it may declare a force majeure and shut down operations if attacks continue.
Libya’s Ambulance and Emergency Service said in a statement on Tuesday there were no “serious injuries” from the fire, with most patients treated for smoke inhalation.

- list 3 of 4Libya electricity blackout protests expose country’s failing grid

Footage verified by Al Jazeera showed huge flames and thick black smoke billowing over the facility, the largest operating refinery in Libya with a refining capacity of 120,000 barrels per day.
It is located about 40km (25 miles) west of the capital, Tripoli.
The National Oil Corporation (NOC) said in a statement on Facebook that the fire broke out on Monday evening at tank number 402-T, belonging to the Brega Oil Company.
It said the tank, which contained about 4.5 million litres (1.2 million gallons) of gasoline, was “directly targeted, resulting in a severe fire before the tank completely collapsed”.
The NOC said the attack followed drone strikes on a water desalination plant at the refinery on Sunday and on a naphtha reservoir on Saturday.
The company declared a “maximum emergency” in the region and urged authorities to launch an investigation and bring the perpetrators to justice.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attacks, and the company did not say who they believed was behind them.
In a statement hours later, the NOC said the refinery was “still being subject to sabotage attacks” with a drone targeting an oil blending and filling plant operated by the Zawiya Oil Refining Company.
It said the drone fell near its main oil tank and a pipeline network used to produce oils for the domestic market, without causing any casualties or damage.
“The company’s board of directors also confirms that if these attacks continue, it will have to declare a state of force majeure and suspend operations at the refinery,” it warned.
The Brega Oil Company, meanwhile, appealed to “all parties to stop the fighting and stay away from oil facilities and depots”. It said “oil facilities are vital infrastructure and owned by all Libyans” and that “protecting them is a national responsibility that does not tolerate any negligence”.
The attacks highlight the continuing security challenges in Libya, where rival administrations and armed groups have retained influence despite a 2020 ceasefire that halted major warfare. The country split in 2014 after a NATO-backed uprising that toppled longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.
Two governments are currently vying for power: the United Nations-recognised administration in Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, and a rival in the east backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar.
In a statement, the Tripoli-based government said Dbeibah held a meeting earlier in the day with key officials, including the interior minister and the chiefs of some armed groups in the capital, “to follow up on the latest security developments”.
Dbeibah “stressed the need to deal firmly with any transgressions or actions that threaten security or harm vital facilities and installations”, the statement said.
Separately, a Libyan parliamentary panel condemned the attack and called for stronger protection of oil installations.
“The House of Representatives’ Energy and Natural Resources Committee condemns in the strongest terms the criminal attack targeting the Zawiya Refinery, one of the most vital facilities in the oil and gas sector that is a cornerstone of the national economy,” it said in a statement.

title: Lobbying firm linked to Reformers created fake administrative assistant named ‘Jessica’, Icac hears
summary:
Consultant Jeremy Greenwood gives evidence to Independent Commission Against Corruption as it investigates allegations linked to Christian Liberal group

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A former lobbying firm which allegedly accepted illegal donations to fund factional Liberal party work created a fake administrative assistant called “Jessica”, an inquiry has heard.

Consultant and lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood gave his second day of evidence to the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s (Icac) Operation Rosny on Tuesday.

Continue reading...
full_text:
A former lobbying firm which allegedly accepted illegal donations to fund factional Liberal party work created a fake administrative assistant called “Jessica”, an inquiry has heard.
Consultant and lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood gave his second day of evidence to the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s (Icac) Operation Rosny on Tuesday.
Icac is investigating whether a Christian Liberal factional group known as the Reformers – who wanted more conservative policies on issues such as same-sex marriage, abortion and euthanasia – solicited or accepted prohibited donations for the recruitment or renewal of members to the party. The practice, known as branch stacking, is not itself illegal.
Icac is investigating whether the former registered lobbying company Beckington, set up by Greenwood and Reformer Christian Ellis in 2019, accepted payments for factional work through fake invoices to Michael O’Hara, a prohibited donor, and the schools governing body Catholic Schools NSW. Greenwood has said he cannot recall either arrangement.
On Tuesday, counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, read out 2020 correspondence from Beckington to Catholic Schools NSW with invoices, signed “Kind regards, Jessica”. “Who’s Jessica?” she asked.
“Sorry, I’m not laughing,” said Greenwood. “Jessica was a fake admin name Christian created. He just thought it was funny.”
After Dwyer said she was “not getting the joke”, Greenwood said: “We have silly humour. Sorry.”
Greenwood, a founding director of Beckington, said he could not recall if the company paid Reformers members to do factional work. He said he believed the company had made payments to Jean-Claude Perrottet, the younger brother of Dominic Perrottet. Dominic Perrottet is not named in Icac’s allegations.
“If he wanted money, we looked after him,” said Greenwood, who later admitted to a payment of $12,000 to Jean-Claude Perrottet, who he described as his “favourite friend”. Dwyer put it to him that the money was for Reformers recruitment work.
Greenwood said: “I didn’t care about the recruitment work. I felt for him. He wanted to get married. He didn’t have a job.”
He was shown an invoice to Beckington for consulting fees from Jean Claude Perrottet for $5,500. Under repeated questioning from Dwyer, he said “to the best of my knowledge”, he was not aware of Jean-Claude Perrottet ever carrying out consulting work for the company.
Ellis moved to the UK at the start of this year, and the inquiry has heard he declined to give oral evidence, but on Monday Greenwood insisted his friend did want to give evidence.
On Tuesday, the inquiry heard Ellis rang Greenwood at 6am on encrypted messaging app Signal.
Greenwood said Ellis had asked him, “‘What was the reaction to you saying I wanted to appear?’ And I said, ‘Just noted.’” He said he could not recall if he had discussed payments to Jean-Claude Perrottet with Ellis.
Greenwood defended saying in a compulsory examination prior to public hearings that he had not heard of O’Hara before Icac’s inquiry was announced. O’Hara has admitted to making payments to Beckington for factional Liberal work under fake invoices, but disputed whether they counted as political donations.
On Tuesday, Greenwood admitted to having first heard O’Hara’s name mentioned in 2019 or 2020. He said the compulsory examination had taken place immediately after a return flight following a trip to the UK in June, during which he met with Ellis at least four times, and the men had been drinking.
“We were at a pub every single time we caught up from about midday to 9pm on my days off from a conference,” he said.
Greenwood, who is named in two of the watchdog’s allegations, has repeatedly disputed being a member of the Reformers. On Monday he said there was not a “shred of evidence” that showed he was involved in the group.
On Tuesday, he told the commission that “hearing things when you’re having a beer at a pub is not actively engaging in the [Reformers] work”.
He was asked about being privy to and responding to messages in which the Reformers discussed recruitment work. Greenwood repeatedly said he was not an “active participant” in group chats.
Icac’s inquiry continues.

title: RBA interest rates: Reserve Bank holds cash rate at 4.35% but threatens more hikes if needed
summary:
In a widely expected decision, the Reserve Bank of Australia holds interest rate after three hikes earlier this year

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Reserve Bank of Australia has held the official cash rate at 4.35% but threatened to hike again if needed, as it warned falling house prices would slow income growth.

The widely expected decision comes after a steep decline in property values in Sydney and Melbourne arrived in Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide following three rate hikes earlier this year.

Continue reading...
full_text:
The Reserve Bank of Australia has held the official cash rate at 4.35% but threatened to hike again if needed, as it warned falling house prices would slow income growth.
The widely expected decision comes after a steep decline in property values in Sydney and Melbourne arrived in Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide following three rate hikes earlier this year.
Economists and financial markets were unanimous in predicting no change following the latest two-day RBA board meeting.
In a statement accompanying the decision, the RBA board said that after this year’s three rate hikes “the economy appears to be slowing as expected”, but warned that it “will continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target, including increasing the cash rate target further if upside risks materialise”.
Board members all voted in favour of holding the cash rate, even as they acknowledged that “inflation is still too high”.
At 3.8% in the year to June, headline inflation would not return towards the targeted 2.5% until late 2027 and “there are upside risks to this projection”, the board said.
“With monetary policy judged to be somewhat restrictive, the board decided to leave the cash rate target unchanged while it assesses how the economy is evolving,” the statement said.
But Stephen Smith, a partner at Deloitte Access Economics, said the statement suggested the RBA “increasingly feels its job may be done”.
“However, another rate rise in 2026 cannot be fully ruled out,” he said.
The RBA warned it was ready to hike again but markets seemed to tip against another rate rise in the aftermath of the decision. The Australian sharemarket rose, while the Australian dollar and bond yields fell, suggesting traders expected lower interest rates in future.
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said Tuesday’s decision to hold was “welcome” amid uncertainty in the global economy.
“This will come as a relief to Australians with a mortgage,” Chalmers said.
The RBA released its latest assessment of the economy’s health in new forecasts on Tuesday.
Economic growth would hold at about 1.4% over 2026, with slightly higher population growth offset by a surprisingly heavy drop in home prices, it predicted in its statement on monetary policy.
The RBA predicted household spending would be weaker than expected in 2026, as falling house prices would reduce household wealth and lead to fewer home sales.
ANZ economists on Tuesday released separate forecasts predicting capital cities’ home prices would fall at least 5% from their respective peaks early this year, with Sydney to fall 14.5% and Melbourne 12.8%.
The RBA cited research suggesting the federal budget’s tax reforms alone would leave house prices up to 5% lower in the long term. It noted prices had risen about 5% in the last year and were up 50% since 2020.
New home loans have already begun to slow. Investor loan commitments in June had fallen by roughly a quarter compared with the start of the year, as a share of total housing credit, the RBA reported.
Westpac on Monday reported a 20% fall in home loan applications since mid-May, blaming interest rate rises rather than the federal budget.
As the housing market slows, some banks have started cutting advertised mortgage rates by as much as the equivalent of an interest rate hike. The RBA said this demonstrated “continued strong competition and could reflect efforts to maintain market share”.
Mortgage holders have kept ahead on repayments as rates rise, with seven in eight borrowers holding almost a year or more worth of repayments in their offset and redraw accounts.
The RBA predicted a recovery in house prices, along with falling interest rates, could push per person economic activity back up again by 2028.
Australia’s economic growth is expected to be supported by a boom in datacentre investment. The RBA has previously warned the rapid build-out could add to inflation but its Tuesday statement said businesses were reporting no issues getting workers and materials for datacentre projects.
Underlying price pressures had risen in construction material costs and groceries, including fruit and vegetables. Service industries such as hospitality had also continued to report rising costs, with a tight jobs market adding to pressure on business.
Bullock will hold her regular press conference at 3.30pm AEST in Sydney.

full_text:
An alleged victim of Alan Jones told his older brother, after the broadcaster was arrested, that his indecent assaults weren’t “too bad” but involved Jones grabbing his penis, a Sydney court has heard.
The witness on Tuesday was asked by the trial prosecutor Georgina Wright to describe what his younger brother, known as complainant J, told him during a meeting at a McDonald’s.
Last week, J, a former student athlete, told the court he reported the indecent assaults to police in 2024 after Jones was arrested because he wanted his child to know “right from wrong”.
Jones has pleaded not guilty to 20 charges of indecent assault and two of sexual touching against six complainants.
J’s brother said J told him at McDonald’s words to the effect of: “This is the hardest thing that I’ve ever had to tell you. You’ve probably seen the news about the defendant. I’m one of the people who have come forward.”
The witness then asked his younger brother: “How bad was it?”
The witnesses told the court that J replied: “Nothing too bad, he didn’t try to fuck me or anything like that. He would grab me on the cock, he would kiss me, those sort of things.”
Complainant J told his older brother that Jones would “grab me on the cock and ask me if it was OK” and he would tell Jones he was “uncomfortable” and the older man would change the subject and become “a different person”, the court heard.
Asked by his sibling why he hadn’t told him about the abuse decades ago, J said, according to the witness: “It was hard. I didn’t want things to stop, the money, the support.”
J’s brother agreed that he told police the complainant disclosed to him that the hugs would get longer and “one time he put his hands on my shoulders and told me he loved me”.
The brother, the first of more than 70 witnesses other than the alleged victims to appear at the trial, said he met Jones on several occasions in the early 2000s, at the broadcaster’s homes at Circular Quay and Fitzroy Falls, and at the 2GB studios. He told the court he had never seen the broadcaster acting inappropriately towards his younger brother.
The witness said the first time he met Jones was when he drove his younger brother to 2GB in 2003. He said they talked about J’s athleticism and horse racing as they sat around a boardroom table.
He told the court that Jones was generous and they shared a love of sport. J’s older brother said Jones offered to help him buy his fiancee an engagement ring and later gave him a Villeroy & Boch dinner set as a wedding gift.
The witness said during a family visit to Jones’s Fitzroy Falls farm he went for a drive with Jones and his brother to “put some bets on”, played tennis and toured the property.
Under cross-examination by Jones’s barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC, the witness said his brother had never told him he was frightened of Jones.
Last week, J told the court he watched Jones’s arrest on television almost two years ago and decided to make a statement to NSW police.
Asked on Tuesday why he didn’t tell his mother about the abuse, J said he wasn’t prepared for that at the time, and she would have pushed him to report it to police. “I would be crushed in court and no one would believe me,” J said.
The trial before judge Glenn Walsh continues.

title: Clover Moore unveils 4,500 sq metre Sydney plaza design after more than 40 years of planning
summary:
Lord mayor says Town Hall square will be ‘fantastic’ – but business advocate says project’s scale of demolition presents ‘unwanted disruption’

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Sydneysiders have been given a first glimpse of a new public square set to “unify” the CBD, more 40 years after the project was initially conceived.

The City of Sydney on Tuesday released new renders of a plaza that will be built opposite Sydney town hall after the council began finalising discussions with the owners of the last of seven buildings that need to be acquired and bulldozed for the project.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Sydneysiders have been given a first glimpse of a new public square set to “unify” the CBD, more 40 years after the project was initially conceived.
The City of Sydney on Tuesday released new renders of a plaza that will be built opposite Sydney town hall after the council began finalising discussions with the owners of the last of seven buildings that need to be acquired and bulldozed for the project.
The square’s design, demolition and construction is expected to cost $150m but the lord mayor, Clover Moore, has said the proposal presents a “once-in-a-generation opportunity”.
“I’ve sat in squares in Vienna and Rome and Greece and Spain – it’s where people gather, it’s the centre of city life and it’s quite fantastic,” she said.
“This isn’t going to be like that – it’s going to be just as grand as one of those squares, but it’s going to be very Sydney and it’s going to be very Australian.”
Councils have been acquiring the land needed to build the 4,500 sq metre plaza since 1982. Demolition is expected to start in 2028, with a completion date set for 2031.
Renders of the space, created by lead design consultant and architect, JPW, and landscape architects Aspect Studios, show a semi-circular clearing with a water feature flanked by movable tables and chairs, and a grove of native trees.
The fountain will provide a misting effect to help passersby cool off on summer days, the designers said.
The surrounding trees are expected to provide shade to about 50% of the site.
“It will draw together the disjointed public places around here and gather our wonderful Victorian sandstone buildings together into a unified place,” the JPW director and lead design consultant, Matthew Morel, said.
“It will be comfortable for two friends gathering to share lunch, or for thousands coming together for a civic celebration.”
But the Business Sydney executive director, Paul Nicolaou, said the demolition of seven buildings would create “unwanted disruption” in the heart of the city.
“The area involved needs to remain a commercial hub for our city when the CBD is still recovering post-Covid,” he said.
Moore has said the council will do all it can to help businesses find other places to operate.
“These are the consequences of doing these big city projects – which the city needs, the people need – but also other people have to accommodate themselves to changed circumstances,” she said.
