full_text:
Romanian army divers used explosives to destroy two Russian-made drones found floating in the Black Sea near Romania’s largest natural gas project, according to the NATO member country’s defense minister.
Defense Minister Radu Miruță posted a Facebook video supposedly showing one of the drones being blown up in the water by explosive ordnance disposal divers of the Romanian army on August 11, as reported by Reuters and other news outlets. The drones were first spotted in the water by a ship working in the vicinity of the Neptun Deep—an offshore gas project under development in the Black Sea that will make Romania the largest gas producer in the European Union.
A Romanian Coast Guard ship that responded with army soldiers aboard found two drifting Gerbera-type drones of Russian design along with other debris. Miruță also disclosed that Romania had reached out to “Ukrainian partners who confirmed that the systems do not belong to them.”
The ongoing war in Ukraine, following the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022, has led to multiple incidents in which drones either accidentally or intentionally strayed across the borders of European countries such as Romania. Dozens of Russian drone incursions into Romanian airspace have occasionally caused damage and forced Romania to respond with costly fighter jet interceptions to shoot down some of the wayward drones.
In one of the most serious incidents, a Russian Geran-2 drone with an explosive payload struck an apartment building in southeastern Romania, injuring a child and a woman while forcing 70 people to evacuate the area on May 29. Another previous Russian drone strike damaged a workshop and an electricity pole and forced over 500 people to evacuate.

title: Chrome adopts what may be the best protection yet against account takeovers
summary: Device-bound session credentials thwart an increasingly common form of account takeover.
full_text:
Google’s Chrome browser has added a new feature that could go a long way in preventing a form of account takeover that’s grown increasingly common as users adopt two-factor authentication, passkeys, and similar protections.
The new Chrome protection is known as device-bound session credentials (DBSCs). The measure stores a unique encryption key in a silicon-resident fortress that’s built into the device running the browser. On Windows machines, this fortress is called a TPM, short for Trusted Platform Module. On macOS and iOS, it’s known as a secure enclave. Other platforms have differing names. Recently released versions of Chrome for Windows and macOS generate a key that’s stored in this fortress.
An antidote to session cookie theft
DBSCs protect against the theft of session cookies, the unique strings of characters that websites store on browsers. Session cookies greatly speed up browsing on sensitive sites that require user authentication. Instead of requiring the exchange of credentials each time a user opens a new site page, the server sets a session cookie that effectively proves the user has already successfully logged in.
The threat of session cookie theft has grown as 2FA, passkeys and similar protections have become more common. These newer protections require additional factors beyond a shared secret before a user gets access to a restricted site. Once possession of a mere password is no longer sufficient, phishing and other more traditional forms of account takeovers are no longer effective.
To compensate, attackers have increasingly relied on infostealer malware and adversary-in-the–middle attacks. Both forms of attack work by stealing session cookies. Attackers then paste the cookies into their own browser and gain the same access the rightful owner has (at least temporarily).

title: FlightAware Sues Kalshi and Seeks an Injunction to Shut Down Its Flight Cancellation Bets
summary:
The flight tracker says Kalshi settles its cancellation contracts on data it took under a free personal license that bars business use, and it is asking a New York federal court to switch the markets off.

The post FlightAware Sues Kalshi and Seeks an Injunction to Shut Down Its Flight Cancellation Bets appeared first on Unchained.
full_text:
FlightAware sued Kalshi on Monday in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, alleging the prediction market built flight cancellation betting pages on data it was never licensed to use commercially. The complaint names Kalshi Inc., KalshiEX LLC and two Kalshi Klear entities, demands a jury, and asks for a temporary restraining order plus preliminary and permanent injunctions.
Kalshi signed up for a free Personal AeroAPI account on July 14, 2022, according to the filing, under a license that permits personal use only and bars use “in furtherance of any business, whether for profit or otherwise.” Four years later, on July 14, 2026, Kalshi self-certified flight cancellation contracts with the CFTC and named FlightAware the “Primary Source Agency,” according to the complaint.
What the Betting Pages Said
According to the complaint, Kalshi’s markets told traders the outcome was “verified from FlightAware” and displayed the mark in bold, hyperlinked to FlightAware’s own site. FlightAware said in the filing that it learned of the markets “only when reporters called for comment,” adding that it cancelled the account on July 15, 2026 and that it sent a cease-and-desist letter. Kalshi later added a disclaimer saying the markets “have not been endorsed by FlightAware.” FlightAware said in the complaint that the disclaimer never told traders it had objected.
The Safety Theory
FlightAware, which tracks flights for more than 10,000 aircraft operators and service providers, also argues in the complaint that the markets create “an incentive for participants to interfere with air travel.” It pleads six counts, including breach of contract, federal trademark infringement under 15 U.S.C. § 1114(1) and unfair competition.
The case lands on a company already fighting on several fronts. States including New York, Nevada and Wisconsin have brought gambling claims against Kalshi.

title: UK prosecutors argue Tate brothers a flight risk ahead of bail hearing
summary: Andrew and Tristan Tate would attempt to evade prosecution if they are freed on bail, prosecutors argue.
full_text:
UK prosecutors argue Tate brothers a flight risk ahead of bail hearing
- Published
British prosecutors are urging a US court to deny a request by influencer Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan that they be released from jail while extradition proceedings play out, ahead of a detention hearing.
They have been held in Florida since their arrest last month after the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which prosecutes criminal cases in England and Wales, unveiled 38 charges against them. Both have denied wrongdoing.
The CPS has said the brothers are a "flight-risk", and would attempt to interfere with the witnesses in the case, according to court filings.
The hearing on Thursday will determine whether the brothers will remain in jail for the duration of their court proceedings.
The brothers, who are dual British-US citizens, were arrested in Miami on 19 July.
They are facing a total of 59 charges, including rape and counts relating to sex trafficking and indecent images of a child.
Both prosecutors and defence lawyers filed new documents on Monday in the Southern District of Florida federal court, ahead of the hearing on Thursday to decide whether they should be freed on bail.
While lawyers for the Tates acknowledged that bail in international extradition proceedings was unusual, they said the brothers had shown no reason to think they plan to evade criminal prosecution. The BBC has contacted the brothers' attorneys for comment.
Documents filed by the prosecution include a request from the British Embassy in Washington, and sent to the US Department of State, to deny bail.
Supporting documentation from the CPS was also filed highlighting alleged risks if the Tates are released on bond.
"Both Andrew and Tristan Tate have significant resources available to them, both in terms of money and in social media networks," prosecutors argued.
"All of the complainants in this case are vulnerable and in fear of Andrew and Tristan Tate because of the violence used towards them – several of the complainants describe being assaulted and threatened with weapons – and because of the resources available to Andrew and Tristan Tate, and because of their propensity to intimidate vulnerable complainants."
Prosecutors also cited social media posts made by Andrew Tate, in which he allegedly mocked prosecutors and suggested he could hide his identity to avoid arrest.
The new charges relate to four new accusers with allegations spanning from 2010-17, according to British prosecutors.
The brothers were already charged in 2025 with rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other accusers in the UK between 2012-15.
Police in Bedfordshire, in south-eastern England, secured European arrest warrants in 2024 for the brothers to have them returned from Romania to face the allegations.
The two moved to Romania in 2016, and were arrested on sex charges in 2022. The case there has not moved forward, and the brothers have been able to travel to the US since travel restrictions against them in Romania were lifted in early 2025.
- Will the Tate brothers be extradited from the US to the UK? 
  - Published21 July
Self-proclaimed "misogynist" Andrew Tate first rose to fame after an appearance on the British version of reality TV show Big Brother in 2016.
The former kickboxer now boasts more than 10.8 million followers on X. He and his brother have long maintained their controversial statements were just jokes or were taken out of context.
"It is believed that Andrew and Tristan Tate would attempt to draw upon that network to provide practical assistance or financial support to escape the jurisdiction and to avoid extradition proceedings if released," prosecutors argue.
He has appeared in countless videos, flaunting a luxurious lifestyle of fast cars, private jets and yachts. Prosecutors also pointed to his extensive international travel, as evidence of his ability to avoid trial.
If found guilty, the two could face life in prison.
Although the Tates have supported President Donald Trump, the White House has said it will not intervene in the case.
The decision on whether to extradite the brothers to the UK will ultimately be up to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, after it is first considered by US courts.

title: GB's Glave and Azu claim first and second in European 100m
summary: Great Britain's Romell Glave and Jeremiah Azu claim a sensational European 100m one-two for the hosts in Birmingham.
full_text:
GB's Glave and Azu claim European 100m one-two
- Published
Romell Glave declared "total domination" for Great Britain after leading team-mate Jeremiah Azu to a sensational European 100m one-two for the hosts, 24 hours after Amy Hunt's triumph in the women's event.
Glave made an international podium for the first time by winning 100m bronze at these championships in Rome two years ago, but the 26-year-old upgraded to gold with a dominant victory in 10.09 seconds in Birmingham.
Raising a finger to the sky in celebration, he became the sixth British man to win the European 100m title - and third in the past six editions after Zharnel Hughes (2018) and James Dasaolu (2014).
Azu, the world and European champion over 60m indoors in 2025, improved on his 2022 bronze as he followed his team-mate over the line in 10.16 to the delight of the home crowd at Alexander Stadium.
German Owen Ansah completed the podium after Italy's two-time defending champion Lamont Marcell Jacobs pulled up with an injury at halfway.
- GB's Hunt comes of age with European 100m gold 
  - Published23 hours ago
- The team behind Hodgkinson's golden rise and the hunt for a world record 
  - Published1 day ago
Three British men had qualified for the final, but Louie Hinchliffe did not contest the medal race.
"Upgrading from a bronze medal from 2024 is an amazing feeling," Glave told BBC Sport.
"The aim was to get [British] one, two, and three, but we got one-two, which is also amazing.
"I was ready for this occasion. The last week or so has been up and down with my body, but I was able to come out here regardless of how I was feeling.
On Great Britain's 100m performances, he added: "It is domination. Total domination."
Glave has made significant progress this season, breaking the 10-second barrier for the first time in legal conditions to win his first British title in June.
He has run sub-10 on six separate occasions, in all conditions, this season - including when he defeated the in-form Jacobs, a surprise Olympic champion five years ago, on his home turf in Italy.
That confidence was evident as Glave dominated his semi-final earlier in the evening, and he executed to perfection when it mattered most.
A talented junior, Glave was the fastest 17-year-old in the world in 2017 after he recorded a time of 10.21.
His progress has been disrupted by injury setbacks since, including a fracture in his back.
But, able to remain consistent with his training this year, Glave captured the gold medal he believed he was capable of winning two years ago.
The foundations of Glave's recent progress has come from a focus on sharpening the first 40 metres of his race.
After hitting the front by the 30-metre mark, he never looked back - and continued running far beyond the finish line in celebration.
After a golden 2025 season, Azu had finished fourth and fifth respectively at this year's World Indoor Championships and Commonwealth Games, with a season's best of 10.00 in Glasgow two weeks ago not proving to be enough.
While it was not gold in Birmingham, the 25-year-old was delighted to secure his return to an international podium following what he described as a "tough year".
"The most irregular [season] in terms of races, quite inconsistent," Azu said.
"When it comes to championships, I know I find my best. We always say times are irrelevant at this point. You want to go out there and race for medals.
"I want to put in my best performance in the final and I felt like I did that today. You always want to be on the podium. In the 100m there are over 100 guys that are competitive, so it is always tough."
There was a fifth-place finish for Hannah Nuttall in the women's 5,000m, as Italy's Nadia Battocletti retained her title.
Matthew Hudson-Smith, who has a stand named after him at the stadium where he trained as a junior for the duration of the championships, qualified for Wednesday's men's 400m final - although he had to settle for second place in his heat.
"I misjudged it a little bit. I thought I was clear," Hudson-Smith said.
"I was looking at the screen and I saw the guy try and surge. But he ran a PB, so he's messed up with the final ahead."
Elsewhere, Nadine Visser clinched the women's 100m hurdles by one thousandth of a second, with a photo finish required to separate the Dutch athlete and Poland's Pia Skrzyszowska.

title: Inside the Secret Service 'shell game' to hide US presidents in plain sight
summary: Elaborate deception operations and decoys are often used to deceive potential threats to the US president.
full_text:
Inside the Secret Service 'shell game' to hide US presidents in plain sight
- Published
On 8 July, US President Donald Trump boarded Air Force One in plain sight of television cameras as he departed the Nato summit in Turkey.
But when the mighty Boeing aircraft left Ankara, the president had reportedly already been secretly spirited away via a catering truck to a C-32A, a military version of the Boeing 757, which flew the president to RAF Mildenhall in the UK.
Those left on board were unwitting decoys and had no indication that Trump was no longer travelling with them.
But deception of this kind is not unusual.
"That's very common," said Ronald Kessler, an author who has written extensively on the agency. "There's a long history of strategies to mislead anybody who might be trying to harm the president."
Robert McDonald, a former high-ranking Secret Service agent with experience working on presidential security details, told the BBC that smaller-scale deceptions are used frequently during motorcade operations.
These motorcades - which often include dozens of security and support vehicles, as well as ambulances and vans carrying White House reporters - typically include two "Beasts", as the enhanced limousine carrying the president is known.
While one vehicle carries the president, the other travels nearby as a decoy, switching locations while en route to the destination.
"It's what we call a shell game," said McDonald, who drove one of the vehicles during the Bush administration. "Even in DC if we headed to Andrews [Joint Base Andrews - where Air Force One flies from], those two limousines would change position, like under a highway overpass."
"But that would happen out of sight of anybody other than those in the motorcade or in that tunnel," he added. "Different things are used to mix up the bad guy."
Similarly, Marine One - the president's helicopter - routinely flies in groups of three, changing positions so that potential threats are not sure which is carrying the US leader.
Even more elaborate deceptions are carried out for complex, high-risk trips abroad.
"I would say it does not happen often," former Secret Service agent Paul Eckloff told the BBC World Service's Newshour programme of the aircraft switch. "But it is an option that the Secret Service and others in executive protection always have."
"When the president travels to war zones, there are frequently tactics and techniques used to create doubt in an adversary of which aircraft or which movement that he's going to make," he added.
In March 2000, for example, then-President Bill Clinton flew from India to the Pakistani capital of Islamabad on an unmarked executive jet that landed after a decoy jet with all the livery of Air Force One.
Three years later, the White House claimed that President George W Bush would spend Thanksgiving in Texas, only to arrive in Baghdad in a blacked-out Air Force One.
In 2023, Joe Biden also was secretly taken to Ukraine with a slimmed down press pool of one reporter and one photographer.
In all three of those cases, the media on board was aware of the deception but had been asked to not report it in real time.
The exact nature of the perceived threat to the aircraft in this latest case remains unclear.
The Secret Service has so far not commented on the incident, while the White House has neither confirmed nor denied it, saying only that it uses every tool available to protect the president.
While contingency plans for a variety of scenarios are developed ahead of time, experts say that the Secret Service needs to maintain flexibility and remain poised to improvise in the face of new threats as they emerge, particularly overseas.
But according to McDonald, the extraordinary measure of secretly moving President Trump from the aircraft suggests that the potential danger was deemed, likely by multiple agencies, to be serious.
"That tells me that the threat level in Turkey was relatively substantial and quite high," he said, adding that the president's staff, the Secret Service and the White House Military Office were almost certainly immediately alerted.
"Those people likely got together in a room and were presented with this intelligence," McDonald explained. "And a plan was put together to negate the threat from whatever intelligence was received."
McDonald's assessment was echoed by Marc Polymeropoulos, a 26-year veteran of the CIA who served in both Iraq and Afghanistan and oversaw clandestine missions around the world.
"The key part of this is the nature of the threat, and what was so severe that the Secret Service would put forth such a deception operation," he said.
A key question going forward, according to Polymeropoulos, is whether the government and intelligence community then had a duty to warn those on the aircraft.
"Let's say the plane was blown out of the sky, and we knew about it," he said. "We don't do that…we can't. If we know ISIS is going to attack a target in Moscow, we warn the Russians. Why do we warn the Russians? Because if there's an American citizen killed in that, we can't let that happen."
How much danger those who remained on the aircraft were in - or whether they were in danger at all - remains unclear.
Journalists on board reported that they were repeatedly instructed to keep their window blinds down, a "not uncommon" practice McDonald said shows that steps were still being taken to protect the passengers.
"A large plane flying overhead where somebody could see it, with the shades up and windows illuminated, could tell somebody that it's a particular type of aircraft," he said. "I appreciate the need for transparency, but [the passengers] are also part of the roadshow. We've got to make sure that you and everybody gets home safe."
The Secret Service, he added, is under no legal obligation to inform of potential threats or detail operations being carried out to protect the president and his entourage. That decision would need to be made by the White House or other agencies.
"The Secret Service is not in the business of public relations," he said. "We're very good at keeping secrets, as our name says. Everybody doesn't need to know everything."

title: How affordable are Edinburgh's festivals?
summary: The city is no stranger to complaints about soaring prices during August - but are costs on the rise?
full_text:
How affordable are Edinburgh's festivals?
- Published
Edinburgh is home to one of the world's biggest cultural events every summer as it is transformed into a festival city.
The Scottish capital hosts the Fringe, the International Festival and the Military Tattoo alongside film, art and book festivals during August.
Complaints about soaring prices in the city are nothing new – but recent years have seen increasing concerns about the cost of attending its summer festivals.
So how affordable is the city for acts and audiences? BBC Scotland has analysed some of the main costs for festival-goers to see if they really are paying more.
Feeling the impact of rising costs
Kaitlyn Smith has attended the Fringe every year since moving to Edinburgh from Orkney 10 years ago.
She has worked handing out flyers as a way to offset the expense of seeing a range of performances over the course of a day.
The 25-year-old said the cost was the "biggest barrier" to local people getting the full festival experience.
"A full day out at the Fringe, you can spend £100 or £200 in a day," she said.
"If you are coming on holiday, you know you are coming to the Fringe. You know that you are saving up money to see it, but we're here the whole month and obviously we would like to try and do the Fringe as well.
"But you are paying £7 or £8 for a pint, £10 or £12 for food - that's one meal. And that's not even starting on your tickets for shows."
She added: "I think the shows are worth it, but if you want to see a big volume, you just can't."
What makes the city so expensive?
Darren Neale, venue director at Greenside Venue in Edinburgh, told BBC Scotland that almost every cost associated with running a Fringe venue had increased significantly over the years.
He said utilities, insurance, technical equipment, transport and other operational costs had risen for the venue - but housing had seen the most dramatic change.
"The cost of staying in Edinburgh during August has risen exponentially over the last decade, creating challenges not only for performers but also for the staff and freelancers who make the festival possible," he said.
"We have seen our accommodation cost rise on average by 300% in the last decade."
He added: "The festival's affordability is one of the reasons it has become the world's largest arts festival, and there is a real balance to be struck between paying people fairly, covering rising costs and keeping live theatre within reach of audiences."
How much have accommodation costs increased?
The price of finding somewhere to stay during August has long been an issue for the city and its festivals.
A slump in Fringe sales in 2022 was blamed on rising accommodation costs but sales recovered in the subsequent years, topping 2.6 million last year.
Earlier this year the city lost the TV festival to Manchester, with organisers citing challenges around "accessibility, affordability and sustainability".
Figures shared with BBC Scotland from commercial real estate data group Costar suggest average hotel prices have been growing year on year since 2019.
The average daily room rate in 2025 was just over £260, an increase of 9% on the previous August and 64% on pre-Covid levels. In comparison, the rate was £110 in Glasgow and £81 in Manchester.
Staying in self-catering accommodation is not much cheaper.
Figures from Visit Britain suggest renting an entire property in Edinburgh to sleep one or two people cost visitors £204.68 a day in August in 2025. The Glasgow rate was £161.67 and it was £106.92 in Manchester.
However, the price for a short-term let can vary dramatically depending on the type – such as a private or shared room within property or booking an entire home - and the number of people.
Visitors staying in Edinburgh this year will also have to pay the city's new tourist tax - an additional 5% on top of their original booking cost for the first five nights.
Due to a lack of publicly available data, we were unable to analyse festival accommodation costs at university-run establishments.
Last year 1.5 million Edinburgh residents attended the summer festivals, up from 1.4 million in 2024.
But high housing costs for those living in the city are not restricted to August. Data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS), external suggests the capital boasts some of the highest average rents in the country.
What about the price of tickets?
But what about the cost of going to shows?
We analysed the average price of the cheapest ticket at the six August festivals - nearly 600,000 shows since between 2016 and 2026 - to explore if prices have changed over the last decade.
Our analysis found average ticket prices (excluding booking fees) increased in cash terms from £10 to £12.80.
When adjusted for inflation, the price of this year's cheapest ticket has actually fallen over the last decade. The figure is £1.37 less than it was 10 years ago, when the average cost was £14.17.
Sticking with real terms, average prices of the cheapest ticket were slightly higher before the pandemic but have broadly stayed around £12.75 since 2021 - despite the rising overheads for performers, production companies and venues.
The figures also vary by festival.
Over the last decade the average lowest ticket price increased in real terms from £19.83 to £20 at Edinburgh International Festival.
However, there has been a real term decrease at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, from £14.17 to £12.80.
Real term prices have fallen from £17 to £15.50 at the Edinburgh International Book Festival and from £14.17 to £12 at the Edinburgh International Film Festival.
Due to the nature of the event, tickets for the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo are generally more expensive than other shows.
Our analysis found it saw the largest increase, with average lowest ticket prices rising by 36% from £35.41 to £48.
Lori Anderson is the director of Festivals Edinburgh, an umbrella organisation for the major city festivals.
She said that they are still seen as "incredible value for money" by residents and visitors alike.
"Costs across Edinburgh in August have risen significantly, particularly accommodation, and our festivals are actively grappling with those issues - albeit with no direct control over them," she explained.
"What we do control, however, are the events that happen every year.
"Our festivals work tirelessly to ensure tickets remain affordable for as many people as possible, putting in place ticket offers and concession prices for those who might otherwise feel excluded."
Festivals Edinburgh has estimated that the events contribute £852m to Scotland's economy, external every year
Anderson added: "We cannot be complacent - our festivals want to work with partners across the city to ensure that Edinburgh is a city where everyone can afford to live, visit and perform."
About the ticket sales data
Using official listings data from Festivals Edinburgh we analysed the median lowest publicly advertised full price ticket from 2016 to 2026.
Prices were adjusted for inflation using Office for National Statistics, external data to allow for comparisons over time.
In the absence of ticket sales data, this allowed us to consistently measure like-for-like prices for each event, while reducing the impact of different pricing structures and models across the festivals.
The analysis does not account for tickets that may have been sold at a lower price due to promotions, nor concession tickets.
Pay-what-you-can, free shows and cancelled events were excluded from the analysis, as were booking fees. The analysis only includes shows that took place in June, July or August.
Additional reporting from Isobel Cottam and James Delaney.
  - Published23 July
  - Published24 June
  - Published23 July 2025

title: Anguish of Colombian brother at rubble of building being searched for earthquake survivors
summary: BBC Mundo has gone to the site of Torres del Limonar, a collapsed building in Cali where rescue workers fight to free survivors.
full_text:
Anguish of Colombian brother at rubble of building being searched for earthquake survivors
- Published
Efraín Gallego does not lose faith that his brother will be found alive, although when he speaks about him, trapped beneath the rubble of a building, his voice breaks and he swallows hard until he regains his composure.
"You feel anguish. Every time there is an alert about someone being alive, hope is reborn that we will find him," Gallego tells me emotionally.
His 80-year-old brother was buried along with his wife when the Torres del Limonar building collapsed in Cali.
This city in south-western Colombia is one of the hardest hit by the earthquake.
The building has become a symbol of the tragedy in the country's third most populous city.
Cali has more than two million inhabitants. According to Mayor Alejandro Éder, there are at least 95 dead.
Under the scorching heat on Tuesday morning, Torres del Limonar is a shattered mountain of rubble, with mattresses, furniture, and belongings peeking out from the concrete.
On top of the remains are rescuers and volunteers: "Silence! We are firefighters. If you can hear us, shout or make any noise."
The phrase is repeated every time the teams dig deep enough to believe they may be close to a survivor.
These are the moments when Gallego regains hope, but the seconds pass and no answers come from below.
Torres del Limonar is one of more than 50 collapsed buildings in Cali.
It is located in its south, in the Capri neighbourhood. The four-storey building held dozens of apartments. The exact number of tenants who were inside when it collapsed is unknown.
Around it, apart from some cracks, the rest of the buildings seem to have escaped the fate of the Torres.
Rescuers, military personnel, volunteers, paramedics, firefighters, humanitarian workers, and journalists have come here.
There are more than 100 people waiting for news. According to Mayor Éder, as of Monday night, it was estimated that 25 people were trapped under the rubble.
Éder declared a nighttime curfew to speed up rescue operations.
The night passed. Excavations continue. A rescuer at the site said about 10 people had been saved since the collapse.
Reports in local media, such as one from Blu Pacífico radio, spoke of six survivors up until a few minutes before my arrival, including an infant only a few months old.
In the midst of tragedy, figures are often closer to estimates than definitive data.
"What I can tell you is that right now there are at least two people detected alive. Tunnels are being made to get them out. One of them has to have his leg freed," rescuer James Velasco tells me.
The magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck Colombia on Monday, 10 August, is the worst in this century, according to the National Geological Service.
In addition to Cali, it left destruction and death in other regions such as Chocó, in the north-west.
Around the remains of Torres del Limonar, unlike Gallego, many residents choose not to speak. They are visibly affected.
Some sleep exhausted on the ground or on a sofa placed in the street. Others gather together under the shade for support.
The hours are long, increasingly so, and the anguish grows.
Velasco offers hope.
"In the past I have participated in operations where we have pulled out survivors after seven days trapped."
"Those who are meant to survive, survive. Nothing is written," he adds.
"I wanted to help from the very beginning."
Amid his anguish, Gallego wants to acknowledge the work of ordinary citizens.
"We must mention all the people who have come to help with water, supplies, tools, equipment; there is a lot of collaboration. Volunteers are plentiful," he says.
Alejandro Mahecha, 19, is one of those volunteers. He decided to come after spending the night safely with his family and overcoming the initial shock.
"I wanted to help from the very beginning. The earthquake affected my city and the homes of people I know. I came to this site because there has been a lot of talk about this building and the need for help here," the young man explains.
Together with several friends, Mahecha helps remove rubble, bring water to rescuers, and clear the street to facilitate evacuation efforts.
In the background, hammers and saws can be heard creating escape routes through the destruction.
They stop only when those present raise their arms.
That means everyone must remain silent. Gallego waits. This time, too, there was no news of his brother.

title: In South Carolina, GOP Voters decide who they want to replace the late Sen. Lindsey Graham
summary: Sen. Darline Graham, who is serving out the remainder of her brother's term, faces a crowded field of candidates to replace him on the ballot as the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate in November.
full_text:
In South Carolina, GOP Voters decide who they want to replace the late Sen. Lindsey Graham
COLUMBIA, S.C.— South Carolina Republicans are voting Tuesday to decide who will be the Republican nominee to the U.S. Senate this November following the death of Sen. Lindsey Graham last month.
President Trump is backing Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed by South Carolina's Gov. Henry McMaster last month to complete her late brother's term.
Yet some GOP voters say while they respect the president's endorsement, they're choosing other candidates in a crowded field, which raises the possibility that no single candidate will win the majority of the vote. If that happens, the primary heads to a runoff between the top two vote-getters on Aug. 25.
After her appointment, Sen. Darline Graham had a busy few weeks as South Carolina's junior senator voting on key items in Washington, including the confirmation vote of Attorney General Todd Blanche and a bill long championed by her brother to sanction buyers of Russian oil and gas.
"This campaign schedule has been absolutely brutal," Graham told reporters Saturday in Florence, S.C., following a campaign event. "But you know what, I'm still standing, I'm still going and that shows you how strong I am."
At a tele-rally on Monday, President Trump said that Graham is the best candidate to support the goals of his administration.
"[She] will help us achieve our mission to Make America Great Again," Trump said. "She looks so nice, but she's actually tough and strong, and she's the perfect person to carry on Lindsey's legacy."
Sen. Darline Graham said that she would focus on cost of living concerns.
"He was more of an expert on the federal budget, like I said I know the family struggles so I'm an expert on the family budget," Sen. Darline Graham said of her brother. "While I know national security is important I'm going to be more focused on the family struggles."
A crowded race among several of South Carolina's GOP heavyweights
Several candidates running against Graham are focusing on their experience as elected leaders.
Rep. Ralph Norman, who placed third in the state's June GOP gubernatorial primary, has become a strong fiscal conservative during his time in the U.S. House, calling for cuts to the federal deficit.
"The Senate is the body where good bills die," Norman said following a campaign event earlier this month.
Norman added that he would support "the president's agenda, America first agenda, with peace through strength, the economy we have to get back on track."
In the U.S. House, where Norman has served since 2017, he is a member of the House Freedom Caucus and has been endorsed by GOP Sens. Mike Lee of Utah and Rick Scott of Florida.
Rep. Russell Fry defeated former Congressman Tom Rice in the 2022 primary after Rice voted to impeach Trump over inciting an insurrection on Jan. 6.
Now, he's fighting off claims that he isn't MAGA enough and defying Trump by running. That could jeopardize the slim House majority in what is set to be a difficult midterm election for Republicans.
Fry disagrees.
"I think that's a lot of distraction, I think more choices let the conservative movement thrive," Fry told reporters on Saturday in Florence.
Former Congressman and Gov. Mark Sanford was first elected to the House with Lindsey Graham in 1994 as part of the Republican wave. He served three terms before becoming governor in 2003. Sanford appeared to be on a trajectory for higher office when a very public extramarital affair in 2009 derailed that.
However, it didn't stop him from winning back his House seat in 2013, which he held until losing the GOP gubernatorial primary in 2018.
Sanford, who briefly ran for president in 2019 before dropping out, has consistently voiced his concern over the growing national debt and deficit.
On Aug. 6, Sanford replicated a stunt he pulled years ago as governor when he brought two piglets into the South Carolina Statehouse lobby, named Pork and Barrel.
Holding one of three pigs last Thursday he told reporters that he's made tough cuts as governor, a key difference between him and others.
"There is something very different about being an executive and being held responsible for results on the numbers that do impact people's lives here at home," Sanford said, highlighting his experience as governor.
GOP voters weigh in on candidates
Over three days last week, 61,000 Republican voters cast ballots early across the state, according to the South Carolina State Election Commission.
Oconee County is where the late Sen. Lindsey Graham cast his last ballot and on the first day of early voting on Aug. 5, divisions were on display, even though many people had previously voted for the late senator, like Robert Herron.
"I always have liked Sanford," Herron said, adding that government spending was his top issue. "He's experienced and I like his policies. He wants to cut back on things. And I like him as an individual, I think he will be good."
Herron said it was a close call between Sanford and Darline Graham, but for him, Sanford's experience as an elected official was the key factor.
Graham's debate performance earlier in the week did it for Frank Owens.
"I like her demeanor, the way she talks to people and her platform," Owens said. As for Trump's endorsement, "I think I would've gone with Darline either way but it's always nice that they're able to work with the president."
Gigi Vray, a Charleston Republican, said she's voting for Sanford because he best represents the Palmetto State.
"I think the Trump endorsement is important," Vray said. "But I think especially in the state of South Carolina we have so many people coming from the North and the East and so it's a different demographic," she added, referring to the state's transplants from other parts of the country.
"So maybe we need a different kind of candidate to support."
In Rep. Fry's 7th Congressional District, which includes the Republican stronghold of Horry County, home to Myrtle Beach and waves of northern Republican transplants, Deborah Dowd was torn.
"I had two choices: Russell Fry and Mrs. Graham and I chose Mrs. Graham," Dowd said.
"Watching the debate, I felt that I liked her answers and I think her brother did a wonderful job for all the time he's been in the Senate so I went for her."
The winner of the GOP nomination will face the Democratic Senate nominee Annie Andrews, a pediatrician. But in a state that is overwhelmingly Republican, the winner of the GOP primary will likely go on to win in November's midterm election.

title: Beyond the numbers: why China’s carrier force won’t copy the US model
summary:
Having marked its 99th anniversary on August 1, the People’s Liberation Army is now just a year away from its centenary goals, with its evolution highlighting the past, present and future of China’s military strategy. In the sixth part of a series, Gabriel Dominguez looks at Beijing’s evolving aircraft carrier doctrine.
Debate over China’s aircraft carrier ambitions has long centred on how many carriers it will build, with the Pentagon last year estimating that Beijing planned to expand its...
full_text:
In FocusBeyond the numbers: why China’s carrier force won’t copy the US model
Defence experts say PLA carrier fleet is expected to complement land-based forces and extend reach into the western Pacific and beyond
Yet behind the high-profile ship launches, experts say quieter changes in pilot recruitment, command structures and fleet integration point to a carrier doctrine distinct from the American model.
“The biggest misconception among Western analysts is the tendency to evaluate the [Chinese navy] through the doctrinal mirror of the US Navy,” said Brendan Mulvaney, director of the China Aerospace Studies Institute.
“Just because they have the same kinds of equipment doesn’t mean they will use it in the same way as the US. Their goals, missions and challenges are different than ours; they will come up with Chinese solutions to Chinese problems.”
China’s carrier force is evolving under strategic conditions unlike those that shaped the American naval doctrine of using carriers to project power thousands of kilometres from home.

title: PBS Chief Paula Kerger on the Aftermath of Federal Funding Cuts—and What People Get Wrong About Public Media
summary: Kerger discusses what people get wrong about public media and what gives her hope
full_text:
Paula Kerger is navigating arguably the most challenging period of her 20-year tenure at the helm of the Public Broadcasting Service (PBS), which has more than 330 member stations. Last spring, President Donald Trump signed an executive order calling for all federal funding to PBS and NPR to be blocked, accusing the organizations of bias. Soon after, the Department of Education notified the Corporation for Public Broadcasting (CPB) that it was terminating the 2020-2025 Ready To Learn grant for educational content, affecting PBS as well as dozens of public television and radio stations. PBS and NPR sued, and in March this year a federal judge ruled that the executive order barring the federal funding violated the First Amendment.
But the organization must still grapple with a funding shortfall created by a Congressional vote to rescind around $1.1 billion in advance appropriated federal funding for PBS and NPR, and an entirely new landscape for public media. The CPB, which was created in 1967 as a nonpartisan nonprofit to direct federal appropriations to public television and radio stations, announced in January that it would officially dissolve. PBS has since reduced its budget by 21% and cut 15% of positions, or around 100 jobs.
It’s not the first time PBS has faced such a threat, Kerger says, pointing to Newt Gingrich's “Contract with America” platform in 1994. But his idea was a “three-year glide path to zero,” she says. By contrast, the latest move gave stations just three months to find alternative funding, since they were already expecting the appropriated funds for 2026 and 2027, she says.
Since the rescission, Kerger has been touring the U.S. and speaking with affected communities. “The light bulb went off,” she says of the public’s reaction. “It's like, ‘Oh, Viewers Like You. That means us.’” Since the July 2025 rescission, PBS has seen more than a million new memberships. Philanthropy and commercial partnerships are helping. And Kerger hopes to get “some level of government funding back,” particularly to support rural communities and infrastructure, she says.
Kerger says she is most concerned about the future of content for children. “The kids' media landscape right now is really scary. A lot of kids are on YouTube, and there is some good stuff on YouTube, but kids get caught in the algorithm and they end up in places they shouldn't. Not all of it is by educators—our stuff all is, and it's rigorously tested,” she says. PBS is also working on games and content for “the significant number of kids that are not in formal pre-K, and whose family may not have access to as much technology or broadband.”
TIME spoke with Kerger on July 15 about the aftermath of the funding pullback, what people get wrong about PBS, and what gives her hope about the future for the organization.
This conversation has been condensed and edited for clarity.
You've talked before about how some people don't understand what PBS is. What do people get wrong about PBS?
Media in most countries started out as government-based, and then commercial media came second, and we were the other way around here. So commercial media was actually a growing industry, and it was the first woman FCC commissioner—a woman by the name of Frieda Hennock—who was looking at what she was anticipating as something that was going to have an enormous impact on society, but that was all rooted in commercialism in the marketplace. She worried there would be limitations, that there would be things that would be in the public interest that [the] commercial marketplace wasn't going to take up, and so she lobbied to have spectrum put aside for both TV and radio, and that's how we began.
Flash forward to Lyndon Johnson. He was particularly taken with what the BBC was able to do in terms of bringing great culture and history to the public, and he thought that our country should have that. He recognized that this loose confederation of individual stations that were mostly doing local or educational stuff wasn't exactly it, and that with some support you could create something that was more akin to the BBC, and that's when he signed the Public Broadcasting Act. Part of that was to create a network [that] could pull all these individual stations together. The second part of it was to ensure that there was federal funding available for communities that would perhaps be challenged to have their own stations. And so our funding always looked like that up until we lost the money last year. The largest percentage of most of the money went to stations, not to PBS and NPR. I think that was a confusion with some members of Congress. I'm not sure they knew exactly what they were voting on.
Those that were in smaller communities would get a larger proportion of their budget from the federal government. In Alaska, there actually is no other media except public radio and public television stations. Almost half of their budget comes from the federal government. So, it sort of played out exactly as LBJ anticipated. Our stations are all locally owned, locally operated, locally governed. I don't tell anyone what to do, but everyone pays dues to PBS. We take that money, we raise some other money, leverage some additional money. We work with producers. We pull together a full schedule that we distribute. The whole broadcast infrastructure is all managed by PBS. The digital infrastructure that was built— apps, PBS.org that a lot of stations plug into—all built by PBS. Stations’ positions on cable and on places like YouTube TV, negotiated by PBS. The work that we do in schools, which is all distributed via broadband—free, all done by PBS. Stations then contribute their content, so that it is still very much bottom up, but the glue that pulls it all together is PBS.
Can you talk me through where things stand today with the funding pullback?
So last year was quite a year, and we're still navigating through quite a few things. It started out with the FCC saying, "We think you're running commercials.” We actually are not. What we are running is sponsorship credits. We actually had worked with the FCC to define what is appropriate for public media, and we've worked closely with every Administration. Then we had the executive order that was going to make it illegal for any federal money to come to PBS and NPR. We won that suit. And the government [missed] the deadline to appeal, so it stands.
And then, of course there was the rescission. The executive order took out a program that we have managed for 30 years, which has funded our kids' content: Ready To Learn. For many years, the Department of Education would fund programming out of PBS that was all built around what the Education Department's priorities were, whether that's literacy or math skills or executive function or, in the last round—which had been re-upped under the first Trump Administration—workforce preparedness. Now, you can decide what that means for preschool, but we interpreted it as giving kids a really good start on the basics, before they entered school, as a way of just helping to make sure that we were jump-starting them in their school career that would lead to a professional career. After the executive order, that money was gone.
Then in June we lost the House vote, and this money had been advance appropriated for 2026 and 2027…I worked with the Public Media Company and within a very short period of time, we were able to raise bridge funds. That helped stabilize smaller stations that I think, some of them, would have gone dark very quickly.
PBS have been working pretty deliberately to make sure that the public is aware that the funding is gone. In the time since the rescission, we’ve picked up more than a million new members, and most of those are people that didn't just write a check, but they agreed to give every month, so they've really signed up to be part of this. It has not solved all of our problems, but we're in at least a stable position right now.

title: Xbox Elite 3 prototype pad leaks with tiny built-in screen
summary: Did a prototype Microsoft gamepad fall off the back of a truck? We can't say, but a Redditor has legit-looking photos of a prototype Xbox controller that's almost certainly the Xbox Elite Series 3. Incredibly, they claim they bought the pad for $200 on OfferUp. In May, a Brazilian regulator's leaked images revealed that Xbox […]
full_text:
Did a prototype Microsoft gamepad fall off the back of a truck? We can’t say, but a Redditor has legit-looking photos of a prototype Xbox controller that’s almost certainly the Xbox Elite Series 3. Incredibly, they claim they bought the pad for $200 on OfferUp.
Xbox Elite 3 prototype pad leaks with tiny built-in screen
Will Microsoft reveal this Elite pad at Gamescom?
Will Microsoft reveal this Elite pad at Gamescom?
In May, a Brazilian regulator’s leaked images revealed that Xbox Elite 3 would have new two new scroll wheels on the bottom edge, a second wireless mode to connect directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming servers, and a new “Pair Button” that can also switch between those servers and your console.
Where might that pair button live? Today, we have a possible answer: it might sit right next to the Xbox Elite 3’s built-in screen, a previously unrevealed feature.
The screen looks almost exactly like the leaked diagram from May showing the mode switch dialogue, with a pair button at the left:
And if I’m not mistaken, the screen on Redditor ssuberlex’s controller is displaying the little XCloud rocket ship next to an Xbox Series X.
The screen can apparently display other things, too. In another photo, it shows a URL that takes me to a Microsoft cloud resource I don’t have permission to view. That lends these images some extra credibility. Unfortunately, the Redditor says the controller doesn’t work. “It does not pair with an Xbox nor with a cable. Just the red light blinking but doesn’t do any thing wired or wireless,” they wrote.
In other photos, we can see the controller’s new scroll wheels, its four rear paddles, its battery compartment, its carrying case, and a different detachable D-pad design than we saw in the May leak. The Redditor says the triggers are clicky when you lock them to the hair-trigger position.
But beyond the screen, the most intriguing image is from inside the controller’s battery compartment. It appears Microsoft has made efforts to make this controller home repairable by including a QR code that presumably leads to a repair website, and accessible Torx T6 screws.
Still, none of these features are for certain. The controller is clearly a prototype, with “NOT FOR SALE” labels on both the pad and its removable 5.8 watt-hour battery, and many placeholder ID numbers for various regulatory bodies.
Tom Warren, The Verge’s Microsoft expert, says his sources believe this controller is still coming later this year.

title: More weather records as UK heat set to spike again
summary: Summer's record-breaking streak continues as the tally for days above 30C in the UK is broken.
full_text:
More weather records as UK heat set to spike again
- Published
The record for the number of days reaching 30C in any year has been broken, according to the Met Office.
After several locations exceeded 30C on Sunday, it has now confirmed that there have been a total of 35 days where the maximum daily temperature has exceeded this threshold - beating the 34 days set in 1995.
This tally is widely expected to be topped again on Wednesday and Thursday with temperatures peaking in the mid-to-high 30s across the Midlands and south-east of England.
A rare amber extreme heat warning has been issued by the Met Office, external for Thursday.
The hottest weather this week is expected on Thursday across the Midlands, Eastern England, London and south-east England, Yorkshire and Humber.
Temperatures could potentially reach 38C which would equal the highest temperature of the summer so far recorded at Lingwood in Norfolk on 26 June.
This would be the hottest August day since 2003, when 38.5C was recorded.
It is also likely to be the fourth calendar month this year to record 35C or more, which is unprecedented.
Amber heat health alerts also in force
The UK's Health Security Agency has also issued amber heat health alerts, which cover the whole of England.
Heat health alerts warn the public and medical professionals when periods of hot or cold weather pose a threat to health.
They warn that significant impacts are likely across social and health care, including a rise in deaths.
The alerts are in place until Friday evening.
- What does hot weather do to the body? 
  - Published22 June
- What are the signs of heatstroke in dogs? 
  - Published22 June
When will the heatwave end?
This heatwave should be shorter lived than others so far this summer with temperatures starting to feel noticeably cooler over the weekend.
Scotland and Northern Ireland will not experience the same extreme heat as southern England, although eastern parts of Northern Ireland, southern and eastern Scotland will still see temperatures well above the heatwave threshold.
They will be notably above average for mid-August and the humidity is likely to intensify on Wednesday night into Thursday.
Some places could reach the mid to high 20s Celsius on Wednesday - when a typical August daytime temperature would generally be in the high teens to low 20s.
Western Scotland and western parts of Northern Ireland are likely to remain somewhat cooler due to cloud and occasional rain moving in from the Atlantic.
While confidence in the details remains low, this could open the door for showers and perhaps some prolonged spells of rain.
To alleviate drought though, months of above-average rainfall is needed.

title: UK to get best eclipse since 1999 as Moon blocks out Sun across Europe
summary: Up to 96% of the Sun will be covered by the Moon in the UK, while parts of Spain, Greenland, Iceland, Portugal and Russia will see a total eclipse.
full_text:
UK to get best eclipse since 1999 as Moon blocks out Sun across Europe
- Published
The UK will be treated to its fullest solar eclipse since 1999 - and the best the country will see for the next 50 years - on Wednesday evening.
It will be visible across the whole of the UK, with up to 96% of the Sun's disc covered by the Moon, depending on your location.
Other parts of the world will get to witness a total eclipse. This includes northern Spain, where hundreds of thousands of people have travelled for the astronomical spectacle.
The total eclipse will also be visible in Russia, Greenland, Iceland and Portugal.
In the UK, more than 90% of the Sun will be obscured by the Moon at the peak, which will fall between 18:58 and 19.15 BST, depending on where you are in the country.
Devon, Cornwall and the western parts of Pembrokeshire in Wales are set to see the eclipse at its fullest, with 94% to 96% of the Sun obscured by the Moon.
The rest of Wales, Northern Ireland, parts of the West Midlands and the South West, and the westernmost parts of Scotland can expect to see 92% to 94% solar coverage.
People across the UK have been scrambling for eclipse glasses - the specialist glasses used to watch the eclipse safely - with a staff member at a bakery in central London saying they had sold about 100 on Tuesday morning.
But when it comes to the weather, fortunes will be mixed. In much of the UK, clear skies should give many a good view of the eclipse. However, across some parts of north Wales, northern England and especially Scotland and Northern Ireland, areas of cloud could move in between 18:00 and 19:00.
Across some parts of western Scotland and in towards the north and west of Northern Ireland, cloud could bring outbreaks of rain.
For those lucky enough to be in Spain, there will be clear skies for people to see a total eclipse in Bilbao, Valencia and Palma, Mallorca, while both Barcelona and Madrid will see more than 99% coverage.
Depending on the location, the total eclipse will peak between 20:26 and 20:33 local time (19:26 to 19:33 BST).
Crowds have been flocking from all over the world to northern Spain for the event with half a million visitors expected, according to the finance ministry.
Julie who travelled with her family from Brest, France, to the Spanish city of Burgos, said she was "very excited".
"We came from very far to see it in totality. I have seen [it] once and it was beautiful and amazing - I am so happy to have the chance to see one again."
Leonor Aguilar from Jaén, Spain, said: "During that minute and a half, what I hope to see is the grandeur of nature and to experience it with my family.
"We often spend money on trivial things instead of investing in something as beautiful as witnessing such a marvellous sight."
Martin Griffith, the director of Brecon Beacons Observatory, in Wales, described the eclipse as "one of the great phenomena of nature".
"It is going to be a fantastic eclipse in Spain, we are right on the path of totality," he said. "What they will see is about a minute and 40 seconds of totality. It will be dark, the Moon will completely cover the Sun.
"Although we know they happen quite often we're not always in the path of totality - they could be over the Pacific Ocean, but to have it over land is just incredible," he said.
The next time the Moon obscures as much of the Sun on the British Isles will be in 2081, and the next total solar eclipse in the UK will be in 2090.
A solar eclipse happens when the Earth, Moon and the Sun align - or almost align. The Moon sits between the earth and the Sun, blocking the amount of light we receive from our star.
A total solar eclipse happens somewhere on Earth roughly every 18 months.
But you have to be on the narrow path of the Moon's shadow to see it - the Moon's shadow traces a line called the path of totality as the Earth rotates and the Moon's position changes.
Anyone outside the path of totality, such as in the UK will see a partial eclipse – where the Moon blocks only part of the Sun.
Those who witness a total eclipse will first see the sky darken. Then, as the Sun is completely blocked, a pearly-white rim will appear around it. This is the Sun's atmosphere - called the corona.
It is a vast halo of superheated plasma extending millions of miles into space. The most dramatic sight of any total eclipse.
It is more than one million times fainter than the Sun's surface, which is why it is invisible in normal daylight.
And just above the visible surface sits a thin, pinkish layer called the chromosphere - only a few thousand kilometres thick.
During the first seconds of a total eclipse you see it as a narrow pink-red ring around the Moon's edge.
How to watch it safely
Watching a solar eclipse without eye protection could permanently damage your eyes.
Wearing sunglasses, welding goggles, or watching through your phone will not offer protection either.
You can only use binoculars or telescopes if they have a special solar filter.
The safest way is to use certified solar glasses or create a pinhole viewer.
Make a 3mm hole in one piece of paper or card. With your back to the Sun, you can project the eclipse as it happens on to another piece of white paper or card. Paper plates are ideal.
Other things in your kitchen can also make good eclipse viewers. A colander or a draining spoon will give you lots of mini-eclipses, with the images projected on to the ground while you stand with your back to the Sun.
Could I see a meteor during the solar eclipse?
During an eclipse, the sky darkens offering a short window to see the Perseid meteor shower, which also peaks on Wednesday evening.
But this will only be in the areas witnessing a total eclipse - like Spain - and not in the UK where only a partial eclipse will be visible.
But even there, the chances are extremely slim. "You would have to get very, very lucky to see a shooting star during the total eclipse," Royal Astronomical Society research fellow Dr Becky Smethurst said.
Remember, for a solar eclipse you must use certified solar glasses - looking directly at the Sun without proper eye protection can cause permanent eye damage.

title: Children as young as nine hurt in growing number of e-scooter crashes
summary: Three trauma centres - Liverpool, Manchester and Sheffield - say they have treated nearly 500 casualties under the age of 16.
full_text:
Children as young as nine hurt in growing number of e-scooter crashes
- Published
Some hospitals are seeing more and more children with injuries from e-scooters, a new review suggests, external.
Three trauma centres - Liverpool, Manchester and Sheffield - say they have treated 477 under-16s, with the overall numbers of cases rising from fewer than 10 in 2019 to nearly 150 in 2024.
The average age of those injured was 12, with the youngest 9. Hardly any were wearing helmets.
The emergency department doctors are calling for laws to better protect children. Currently in the UK, there is no legal age restriction, speed limit or safety equipment requirement for the estimated 1.2m, external people who own private e-scooters.
Not harmless toys
Some e-scooters have a "turbo mode" setting, meaning they can reach speeds of around 28mph.
Recently, a UK teenager using one of these crashed and killed his 14-year-old friend on a busy road - one of 59 deaths involving e-scooters in the UK to date.
Jacob Calland, who was a passenger on the back, suffered irreversible brain injuries when it was struck by a BMW car in Wythenshawe, Manchester, on 19 March 2025.
Manchester Crown Court heard the teenager driving the e-scooter also sustained serious injuries, including a bleed on the brain and numerous bone fractures.
And Det Con Steve Pennington from Greater Manchester Police's Serious Collision Investigation Unit stressed e-scooters were not harmless toys and could lead to horrific consequences when used by inexperienced riders.
Serious head injuries
Most of the incidents in Manchester, Liverpool and Sheffield involved private e-scooters, often on public roads, pavements or footpaths, despite that being illegal.
Private e-scooters are meant only for use on private land, with the owner's permission.
Half of the children injured were aged between 10 and 13. Nearly two-thirds were boys.
Most injuries were sustained by the rider - only 5% were pedestrians that had been hit by an e-scooter - and the most common cause was falling off the e-scooter.
Around 11% were collisions with a vehicle, which was often linked to more serious injuries.
Injuries to the arms and legs were the most common, followed by head or facial injuries.
The doctors say tougher laws are urgently needed. Helmet use is not mandatory in the UK, unlike some other countries.
Some have described the private e-scooter situation in the UK as the "Wild West" with few following any rules.
The researchers told the Emergency Medicine Journal that schools, local councils, youth groups and road safety campaigns all have a role to play.
"Clearly, reporting these accidents is important to influence and change policy, but there must also be an onus on retailers to clearly advise customers of the law, and policymakers to regulate private e-scooters, such as with speed limiters, or mandate helmet use," they say.
To legally rent an e-scooter in the UK, which can be used on roads and cycle lanes, you must be at least 16 and hold a full or provisional driving licence, and the rental company must provide appropriate insurance. Rental e-scooters typically have a limited top speed of around 15mph.
A Department for Transport spokesperson said: "These are concerning findings, and our thoughts are with anyone who has been injured on our roads.
"It is illegal for private e-scooters to be used on roads, pavements or in other public spaces, including by under 16s, and we're bringing forward new laws to make their use safe and legal, including consulting on requirements like helmets."

title: Sun-tanned cauliflowers and knobbly spuds - the heatwave veg that's good to eat
summary: British shoppers should expect to see more wonky vegetables due to repeated heatwaves.
full_text:
Sun-tanned cauliflowers and knobbly spuds - the heatwave veg that's good to eat
- Published
Would you buy a cauliflower that looks like it's been sunburnt or a cucumber that's curled back on itself?
Farmers across the UK are grappling with one of the driest, hottest growing seasons in decades. Repeated heatwaves after a warmer than usual spring have led to predictions of the worst harvest since records began.
The heat is not only affecting how much produce is grown, but also how it looks.
Retailers usually reject fruit and vegetables that don't meet strict guidelines on size, shape and colour. But with supplies under pressure, many are now expected to loosen those rules rather than risk empty shelves.
That means shoppers could start seeing smaller, wonkier or oddly coloured veg on the shelves in the coming weeks - and sellers and growers say it's still good to eat.
'Sun-tanned' cauliflowers
Cauliflower is one of the most affected vegetables in hot weather because it needs lots of water.
Its heads are usually shielded from sunlight by the leaves, but in this year more light is reaching them and turning them yellow.
Emilie Vanpoperingh, co-founder of Oddbox, a subscription company that sells surplus produce that supermarkets reject, said it is "purely a cosmetic defect" and the plants taste exactly the same.
She said Oddbox acquired 6,000 cauliflower heads last week that were too dark for supermarkets to sell.
Growers are reporting that their water reserves are depleted, Vanpoperingh said, which means the cauliflower and broccoli family of brassicas will experience slower growth, leading to shorter supplies.
That short supply means retailers may soon start stocking "sun-tanned" cauliflower because "their biggest nightmare is empty shelves", she said. "They want to make sure that they've got availability of produce all the time."
Curly cucumbers
Growers are also reporting cucumbers that are coming out misshapen, with some bending back into a spiral.
That is because the plants are grown in greenhouses which overheat in the high outdoor temperatures, causing the plants to become stressed, Vanpoperingh said.
"Even if they get the irrigation then it's just extreme heat, which means the plant is not able to grow anymore."
Holey pak choi
John Harper, a farmer in Worcestershire, grows pak choi for Sainsbury's, Aldi and Co-op, and has discarded more produce than usual this year because of tiny holes made by pests.
Flea beetles thrive in hot, dry conditions, and farmers are no longer allowed to use as many pesticides as before, meaning net covers are Harper's only defence.
Supermarkets' strict cosmetic rules mean "one tiny little hole can render the plant useless", he said, but some have temporarily loosened the rules.
"We've been working with them through this hot period and in general they sort of get it," he added.
Harper said the vast majority of affected pak choi is still edible - even if "it seems to be quite tasty" for the beetles too.
Knobbly potatoes
Lucy Munns, a potato farmer in Cambridgeshire, said the hot weather will stunt the root vegetable's growth, leading to oddly shaped tubers that supermarkets and chip shops, which she supplies, wouldn't normally buy.
When the weather gets cooler after a hot period, instead of the main potato tuber growing "it tends to grow a little knobble on the end".
"Trying to find people that will accept potatoes like that is very difficult. So that ultimately means a lot of wastage for us," Munns added.
"It's criminal, to be honest, to be chucking that much food away."
Those "knobbly and misshapen potatoes" however are absolutely fine to eat, she said.
"The only difficulty is peeling them, but just cut the knobbly bit off and peel it separately."
'A challenging period'
Supermarkets including Sainsbury's, Tesco, Morrisons and Waitrose already have dedicated lines for wonky vegetables.
Calum Kelly, Waitrose's produce technical manager, said in demanding weather conditions "we relax size and shape guidelines for key veg to avoid waste and provide more income to our growers and farmers".
"Baking potatoes might be a little smaller than usual this harvest if the drought continues. All these veg still taste great, but like many of us in a heatwave, they might just look a little less than perfect."
Not every gap can be filled this way though. Andrew Opie, the director of food and sustainability at the British Retail Consortium, said supermarkets are also importing more food from abroad as UK supplies run short.
"Retailers face the dilemma of supporting British farmers, but also making sure that we, as customers, have what we expect to buy when we go in the shop," he said.
"It's going to be a challenging period right through into the autumn. We're hearing potentially it could affect things like cherries as well."
British summers are getting hotter and drier as the climate changes and heatwaves like this one are becoming more frequent.
That means a season like this one may become less of a one-off, and more of a preview of what British farming has to deal with regularly.
Many farmers will either have to accept more waste, invest in better irrigation and water storage systems, or find a way to sell more wonky produce to consumers.
Munns, the potato farmer, said more people should try buying imperfect veg if they see it in the supermarket aisle this year.
People should "be a bit less picky" about fresh produce, she said. "We've been too spoilt in the UK … In other less fortunate countries we wouldn't have a choice."
