title: Colombia declares three days of mourning after deadly earthquake
summary: Hundreds are dead as rescuers race to find survivors of the magnitude 7.4 quake.
full_text:
Colombia declares three days of mourning after deadly earthquake
Hundreds are dead as rescuers race to find survivors of the magnitude 7.4 quake.
Colombia has declared three days of national mourning after a powerful earthquake killed more than 200 people as rescue crews race against time to find people trapped beneath the rubble.
The government said on Wednesday that flags would be lowered to half-staff at official buildings and Colombian embassies around the world “in honour of all the dead”.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Search for survivors underway in Colombia’s earthquake aftermath
- list 2 of 4Colombia scrambles to find survivors after deadly earthquake
- list 3 of 4On the ground in Cali, Colombia’s worst-hit city after the quake
- list 4 of 4Woman rescued after 36 hours under rubble in Colombia
Monday’s magnitude 7.4 earthquake was the strongest to hit the country in a century. It flattened buildings and damaged roads across western Colombia. More than 100 aftershocks had been recorded by Tuesday afternoon.
The disaster is also an early test for President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office just three days before the earthquake. The first-time president came to power after a divisive election and is now facing the first major crisis of his presidency.
Government figures put the number of injured at 2,595 and the number officially missing at 195 although civilian-run databases suggested the number of people unaccounted for could be closer to 4,000.
The search for survivors has become increasingly urgent as the disaster enters its third day. Aid agencies said the first 48 to 72 hours are generally the most critical for finding people alive beneath collapsed buildings although people can survive longer if they have access to water and food.
Crews worked through the night in some of the hardest-hit cities, including Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Quibdo. In Pereira and Cali, rescuers used cranes, search dogs and heavy machinery while volunteers formed human chains to clear debris by hand.
In Cali, entire neighbourhoods appeared flattened with piles of rubble where blocks of homes and apartment buildings once stood and cars crushed beneath concrete and fallen walls. Residents have joined firefighters in searches for survivors, digging with picks, shovels and their bare hands and stopping periodically to listen for signs of life.
But the full scale of the destruction is still unclear, particularly in rural areas where little information has been coming out.
That includes Choco near the earthquake’s epicentre and one of the poorest regions in the country. Many communities there can only be reached by boat, through the jungle or by air. The region has also long been affected by violence between armed groups, making it even harder to reach remote areas.
The earthquake has put parts of Colombia’s health system under enormous strain. Part of the Hospital Universitario del Valle in Cali collapsed, forcing doctors to move patients into a parking lot and treat some people outside.
Colombians have mobilised to help. Thousands have brought food, water and other supplies to affected neighbourhoods while long lines have formed outside blood donation centres.
De la Espriella has declared a state of emergency and promised rent subsidies for families who lost their homes.
International help has also started to arrive. The United States has announced $15.5m in emergency aid, and the State Department announced on Wednesday that following a request from de la Espriella’s government, it was deploying urban search-and-rescue technical teams from Fairfax County, Virginia, and Los Angeles County, California, to help with the search effort.
The European Union has also pledged $2.3m, while Mexico has offered hundreds of search and health workers, and El Salvador said it would send two planes carrying 100 tonnes of aid.
But for rescue crews, the immediate focus remains searching the rubble.

title: WHO chief says Trump vaccine push goes against ‘decades of evidence’
summary: The US health secretary has spent years saying the MMR vaccine caused autism despite no medical evidence.
full_text:
WHO chief says Trump vaccine push goes against ‘decades of evidence’
The US health secretary has spent years saying the MMR vaccine caused autism despite no medical evidence.
The World Health Organization (WHO) chief has accused United States President Donald Trump of ignoring “decades of evidence” with his push to overhaul US childhood vaccination policy.
The warning from WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus on Wednesday comes days after Trump signed an order calling for a rethink of school vaccine mandates and renewed calls for the split of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three separate doses.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Could the HPV vaccine eliminate cervical cancer deaths?
- list 2 of 3US records 2,318 measles cases, already surpassing 2025 total
- list 3 of 3DRC’s Ebola outbreak began months before it was officially declared, says WHO
Trump’s Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has long promoted a disproven link between the MMR shot and autism.
But Tedros said the science is “unequivocal” and that “vaccines including the MMR vaccine are safe and do not cause autism”.
“Vaccination policy should be guided by rigorous, independent and transparent review of the best available science, not by political influence,” he wrote in a post on X.
“That evidence is reviewed continuously as new data emerge from across the globe,” he added.
The WHO chief also warned that “delaying vaccines or separating doses unnecessarily does not make vaccination safer and can leave children unprotected.”
Since joining the Trump administration, Kennedy has launched a sweeping review of longstanding vaccines, rewritten the childhood immunisation schedule, and slashed funding for new vaccine development.

title: Iran remains defiant as it vows to fight US until demands met
summary: IRGC advisers say Iran has replaced more missiles and drones than it used, and cite falling US munition stocks.
full_text:
Iran remains defiant as it vows to fight US until demands met
Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) advisers say Iran has replaced more missiles and drones than it used, and cite falling US munition stocks.
War on Iran: Phase II: Day 32
Tehran, Iran – Shortly after meeting China’s ambassador, Iran’s new security chief left no room for doubt about Tehran’s position after nearly six months of war with the United States.
“Iran’s message is clear: The Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until the US ends the war and blockade, releases Iran’s frozen assets, and agrees to a region-wide ceasefire, including in Lebanon and Gaza,” Mohsen Rezaei said in a social media post late on Tuesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Top Iranian commander visited Iraq to discuss disarmament plan: Source
- list 2 of 3Oil prices rise as attacks dent hopes for Strait of Hormuz reopening
- list 3 of 3Iran rejects Trump’s claim to ‘control’ Hormuz: What’s the latest in talks?
“Until all conditions are met, the Strait will remain closed,” added the former wartime commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
His defiant message was in line with conditions emphasised by his predecessor, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, and by newly appointed commanders as Iranian authorities maintain that they are willing and capable of continuing to stand up to their opponents in the US-Israel war on Iran.
In his first meeting as secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Rezaei sat down with a delegation led by China’s envoy to Tehran, Cong Peiwu, on Tuesday. State media said he pushed for closer ties with China, praised its unwillingness to go along with US-backed resolutions targeting Iran at the United Nations, and said any potential deal with Oman over the Strait of Hormuz is separate from Washington.
But an arrangement with Oman, which Tehran said last week had been finalised and was awaiting confirmation at the top, still does not appear imminent, with military action continuing in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
A merchant ship appeared to have been hit by a projectile off the coast of Oman on Sunday night, when Rezaei’s appointment was announced. The Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen launched their deadliest recent maritime attack on Tuesday, hitting an Egyptian-owned ship in the Red Sea in an attack that killed six people, according to the Houthis’ rival, Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
The US military reported an overnight attack on Tuesday, saying a US Navy helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles at a Panama-flagged vessel in order to enforce its naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports. This marked the 12th vessel attacked by US forces since April, and the third since the blockade resumed almost a month ago after the collapse of a memorandum of understanding (MoU) that was signed by Iran and the US in June.
With the 60-day period of the repeatedly violated MoU approaching next week, mediators such as Pakistan and Qatar have said they are continuing efforts to bring the two sides closer to a diplomatic solution.
Yet the rhetoric from Tehran has only hardened over the past week, with the IRGC indicating that it aims to take threats from the administration of US President Donald Trump, including to further strike Iran’s power plants and civilian infrastructure, more seriously.
“If Iran is threatened again, hundreds of thousands of miles of energy lines, thousands of power plants, all the American and non-American systems, and even global infrastructure connected to the internet will be exposed to threat,” IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said on Wednesday.
“The US had about 30 to 40 war vessels in the region before the war, but today not even a single US warship is present in the Persian Gulf,” he said, adding that the declining level of key air defence missiles and precision munitions in the Pentagon’s arsenal was a “big threat” facing US decision-makers.
Mohammad Reza Naqdi, an adviser to the IRGC’s chief commander, claimed on state television on Tuesday night that the force has continued to produce more ballistic missiles and drones during the war than it has been firing across the region, relying predominantly on native know-how and capabilities.
“Even if the war takes several years, our ballistic missiles would still descend on our enemies,” he said.
Military integration
In appointing six new figures to leading military posts this week, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei consolidated a small circle of trusted officials, including longtime ally Hossein Taeb as the new head of the paramilitary Basij force of the IRGC.
Khamenei also selected Ali Abdollahi, head of the Khatam al-Anbiya joint wartime command, to lead the General Staff of Armed Forces.
Abdollahi is tasked with integrating the Khatam headquarters, which was formed during the eight-year war with Iraq in the 1980s to coordinate operations between the then-nascent IRGC and Iran’s regular army, with the general staff overseeing all armed personnel.
In his post-appointment message, Abdollahi emphasised upgrading capabilities across missiles, drones, naval, ground, cyber and asymmetric warfare, in addition to closer inter-service coordination and naval readiness to take action around the Strait of Hormuz.
IRGC commander-in-chief Ahmad Vahidi said he would cooperate with the other military leaders in order to resist the “Zionist-American arrogance”.
Battling an exacerbating economic crunch, President Masoud Pezeshkian suggested on Wednesday that the opponents of the Islamic Republic may be looking to defeat it by banking on another round of nationwide protests on the back of public discontent.
“The current war is more complex than before, and the enemy is pursuing collapse from inside the country,” he said during a speech.
Ali Akbar Javidan, head of the police border guard in the western province of Kurdistan in Iran, said on Wednesday that US claims that Iraq-based separatist Kurdish fighters could potentially launch a ground assault on Iranian soil were “delusional”.
“The country’s borders are fully safe and impenetrable through the vigilance of border personnel and the backing of people living in border areas, including the brave people of Kurdistan, Sistan and Baluchistan, and Khuzestan,” he was quoted as saying by state media.
In the meantime, most of Iran’s population of about 90 million people continues to weather the worsening impact of war and uncertainty, as well as a tightening security grip at home.
“I have given up on predicting what’s going to happen,” Jamshid, a 36-year-old resident of central Tehran, told Al Jazeera.
“I don’t expect anything to get better this year, or maybe even next year,” he said. “I just hope this situation doesn’t last a lot longer than that, because most of our youth is already gone dealing with these things.”

title: US consumer inflation slows in July as energy prices briefly retreat
summary: Energy prices declined 1.5 percent in July but remain 14.7 percent higher compared with a year ago.
full_text:
US consumer inflation slows in July as energy prices briefly retreat
Energy prices declined 1.5 percent in July but remain 14.7 percent higher compared with a year ago.
United States consumer inflation has slowed in July amid a short retreat in energy prices and hopes that the Strait of Hormuz would reopen.
Shipping continues to be severely disrupted since Iran established a maritime “toll booth” in the strait shortly after the US and Israel launched a war against the country in late February.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Paramount CEO may remove operations from California over stalled merger
- list 2 of 4Oil prices rise as attacks dent hopes for Strait of Hormuz reopening
- list 3 of 4Why have several nations raised red flags over Indian farm exports?
- list 4 of 4Taiwan’s Foxconn reports 35 percent rise in profit on AI demand
Consumer inflation rose by 0.1 percent compared with this time last month but was 3.4 percent higher than this time a year ago, according to data released by the Department of Labor’s Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) on Wednesday.
Inflation has been largely driven by fuel prices, which, despite a temporary reprieve, are rising. While energy prices declined 1.5 percent from this time last month, they are up 14.7 percent for the year.
“Energy prices have gone down in July because people thought perhaps the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz would end, but it didn’t. If you look at the past 12 months, energy prices are now much higher than they were a year ago,” Michael Klein, professor of international economic affairs at The Fletcher School at Tufts University, told Al Jazeera.
Brent crude fell 7 percent last week but has jumped this week as hopes that the Strait of Hormuz would reopen faded. Brent crude oil futures rose 0.3 percent to $89.19 per barrel on Wednesday.
Petrol prices dropped 2.9 percent from last month but surged 39.1 percent from a year ago.
At the petrol pump, prices are rising after tumbling 9 cents last week.
The average price for a gallon (3.78 litres) of petrol is $4.03, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices. By comparison, it was $4.00 on Monday, $4.08 this time last week, $3.87 a month ago, and $2.98 per gallon on February 28 , when the US and Israel first struck Iran.
Food prices rose marginally in July by 0.1 percent for the month but were 3 percent higher than this time last year.
Growing economic pressures
The inflation comes amid a lacklustre jobs report last week, where the US economy lost 23,000 jobs, with most losses in retail trade, local government (particularly in education), and hospitality, while healthcare made gains, according to the BLS.
Days earlier, the Jobs and Labor Turnover Report (JOLTS), also from the BLS, showed little change in the number of people leaving their jobs for new ones, continuing a so-called low-fire, low-hire environment.
These combined factors have put pressure on the Federal Reserve as it gauges the path forward to reach its goal of 2 percent inflation. In July, the central bank kept interest rates at 3.50–3.75 percent.
Economists are divided on whether rates will rise or remain unchanged during the next policy meeting slated for September 16, which would be the third under the new chairman, Kevin Warsh, who took over from Jerome Powell in May.
CME FedWatch, a tool that tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, forecasts a 61.6 percent chance of maintaining rates, while 38.4 percent believe that rates will increase to 3.75–4.00 percent.
US markets are responding. The tech-heavy Nasdaq is up 0.7 percent, the S&P 500 rose by 0.3 percent, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average is 0.05 percent higher since the market opened.
Gold prices, which are generally considered a safe investment during times of economic uncertainty, are up by 1.4 percent to $4,428 an ounce.
The inflationary pressures are overshadowed by the upcoming midterm elections. There are only two more inflation reports before the election.
Meanwhile, Americans are divided on which party is better suited to handle the economy. Slightly more Americans, or 37 percent, believe that Democrats are better at handling the economy, as opposed to 36 percent who believe that Republicans are, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released last week.

title: As Strait of Hormuz transit drops, Trump again says US has ‘control’
summary: Just eight vessels crossed strait on Tuesday, down from 130 to 140 prior to the war as peace talks stall.
full_text:
As Strait of Hormuz transit drops, Trump again says US has ‘control’
Just eight vessels crossed strait on Tuesday, down from 130 to 140 prior to the war as peace talks stall.
United States President Donald Trump has doubled down on claims the United States maintains “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz, even as transit through the arterial waterway fell to a one-week low amid the US-Israel war with Iran.
Trump made the statement in a Truth Social post on Wednesday, reiterating a similar claim he made to reporters the day before as diplomatic efforts to end the conflict and fully re-open the strait have continued to stall.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Six killed in Houthi attack on Bab al-Mandeb ship, Yemen’s government says
- list 2 of 3Oil prices rise as attacks dent hopes for Strait of Hormuz reopening
- list 3 of 3Trump says his decoy plane faced ‘greater risk’ in secret flight change
“The U.S.A. has total control over the Strait of Hormuz. I THINK WE WILL KEEP IT!” Trump said.
He went on to claim the ongoing US blockade of Iranian ports “is being called, by everyone, “A WALL OF STEEL,” and there is nothing Iran can do about it”.
“Iran is all talk and no action, the Bully of the Middle East No Longer,” Trump said, ending his message with, “Praise be to Allah!”
Despite the statement, Iran has continued to assert its influence over the strait as it has pursued talks with Oman on future management. Wider peace talks with the US have been largely paused amid the Iran-Oman talks, which do not include Washington.
Iran has said it will not allow full traffic in the strait until the US naval blockade is lifted, sanctions are lifted, and its assets are unfrozen.
While ships can still transit through the strait, they face several obstacles and heightened threats. That has caused the volume of traffic to drop dramatically.
Reuters news agency reported that just eight ships transited through the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, far below the 130 to 140 ships pre-war rate. That was down from the previous ten-day average of about 12 ships, according to trade analytics platform Kpler data.
The US and Israel launched the war with Iran on February 28. The US and Iran signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) aimed at ending the conflict in June, but the agreement dissolved in mid July with both sides renewing attacks.
Fighting between the US and Israel has been mostly in recent days, with sporadic incidents. That included a US Navy military helicopter striking a Panama-flagged cargo vessel on Tuesday.
The Yemen-based Houthis have also opened a new front in the war, with attacks on vessels in the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Six people were killed in a Houthi attack on an Egyptian-owned ship on Tuesday, in the first deaths from such an attack.
Stalled peace efforts
Speaking on Wednesday, Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Tahir Andrabi, said Islamabad was working to “bring the two parties to the negotiating table” and prevent efforts to undermine the peace process.
He added that Pakistan’s deputy prime minister and deputy foreign minister held talks with officials from Iran, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait on August 10, and that Pakistani Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi is also visiting Tehran.
Despite the lack of progress, the Trump administration has continually signalled its desire for an off-ramp in the war, which remains politically unpopular in the US ahead of midterm elections in November.
Some analysts saw Trump’s latest statements as part of a concerted effort to frame the conflict as a victory, despite falling short of stated goals of ending Iran’s nuclear programme, ending its influence in the region and fomenting wider regime change.
“Unfortunately, the determination to demonstrate that the United States is ‘winning’ at all costs is creating a virtual reality that prevents both the administration and the president from making decisions based on the actual situation on the ground,” Dennis Citrinowicz, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies, wrote in a post on X.
“The United States does not control the Strait of Hormuz. Despite everything that has happened, Iran retains sufficient capabilities to disrupt maritime traffic through the strait,” he added.
Others have questioned US Energy Secretary Chris Wright’s statement on Tuesday that “the seven-day average for oil leaving the Strait of Hormuz is currently up to almost 9 million barrels per day”. Wright said that, when combined with upgraded land delivery infrastructure, fossil fuel deliveries from the region were close to pre-war levels.
In a post on X, Brett Erickson, an analyst at Obsidian Risk Advisors, said there is “zero evidence that 9Mbpd is exiting the Strait of Hormuz per day”.
“Zero. Not ‘maybe’, not ‘potentially’,” he added.

title: Zhu Rongji: reformer who led China’s economic transformation through ‘minefield or abyss’
summary:
“Regardless of what lies ahead – be it a minefield or a deep abyss – I will forge ahead unswervingly, dedicating my entire life and energy to the country until my dying day.”
Those words, spoken at the dawn of his premiership, came to define Zhu Rongji, China’s towering economic reformer who died in Beijing on Wednesday. He was 97.
His remarks at a press conference in 1998 came as China was undertaking sweeping state-owned enterprise (SOE) reforms that caused widespread job losses, even as it...
full_text:
ObituaryZhu Rongji: reformer who led China’s economic transformation through ‘minefield or abyss’
China’s bold economic tsar who drove sweeping SOE reforms and secured WTO entry has died aged 97
“Regardless of what lies ahead – be it a minefield or a deep abyss – I will forge ahead unswervingly, dedicating my entire life and energy to the country until my dying day.”
His remarks at a press conference in 1998 came as China was undertaking sweeping state-owned enterprise (SOE) reforms that caused widespread job losses, even as it reeled from the 1997 Asian financial crisis.
Zhu, dubbed China’s economic tsar by the media, was known for his determination to steer the country through the rough waters of reforms and external shocks during his tenure as vice-premier and premier between 1991 and 2003.
He shook up the centrally planned economy, overhauled the state-owned business sector, fought corruption, revamped the tax system and secured China’s entry to the World Trade Organization – changes that some economists say brought about a historic transformation in China’s economic system, ushering in a modern state and making it an integral part of the world economy.
His straight-talking, no-nonsense style earned him a host of nicknames – including “iron-face Zhu”, “no-nonsense leader”, “problem solver”, “fire-brigade captain”, “crisis manager” and “troubleshooter”.

title: What’s behind Sydney airport’s heavy delays and near-miss incident?
summary:
Air traffic controllers are short-staffed and exhausted – and new recruits face a difficult aptitude test and must train in Melbourne

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Travellers flying in and out of Sydney airport had already been dealing with heavy delays even before a Jetstar plane narrowly avoided colliding with a Qatar Airways plane on the tarmac early on Sunday.

The day before, more than 150 flights passing through Sydney were delayed as the airport grappled with a lack of air traffic controllers, highlighting how just how delicate the rostering situation is.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Travellers flying in and out of Sydney airport had already been dealing with heavy delays even before a Jetstar plane narrowly avoided colliding with a Qatar Airways plane on the tarmac early on Sunday.
The day before, more than 150 flights passing through Sydney were delayed as the airport grappled with a lack of air traffic controllers, highlighting how just how delicate the rostering situation is.
While Sunday’s incident is under investigation – an air traffic controller and a tug driver were temporarily stood down for mandatory drug and alcohol testing – the issue has shone a spotlight on the severe staffing shortages of those in charge of managing air traffic, and takeoffs and landings.
‘Doing the work of two people’
While air traffic controllers are entitled to unlimited sick leave under their terms of employment, Scott Nugent, the president of the air traffic controllers’ union Civil Air, says the issue “is that we do not have enough controllers just to fill the base roster before we have any sick leave at all”.
“In practice, the only way you fill the roster is with overtime, and it relies on overtime just to do business as usual,” says Nugent.
The experienced air traffic controller says workers are getting to the point where they’ve done so much overtime that they’re exhausted. Some staff are working 10 days on and then having one day off.
“The reason you’ve seen these delays in the last week is because we increased the spacing between aircraft to maintain safety when we have less people,” he says.
“If you’re doing the work of two people, you can only take half as many planes.”
Much of the problem is tied to a pandemic-era program that incentivised a significant number of experienced staff to leave Airservices Australia, the commonwealth-owned organisation responsible for the management of the country’s skies, in 2021.
With most planes grounded due to pandemic restrictions, 140 employees aged 56 or older accepted a redundancy.
Soon after, the organisation embarked on a large recruitment drive but hirings have failed to keep up with demand.
Gaps in rosters
Despite the starting salary for a qualified air traffic controller post-training being $116,990 a year – an experienced supervisor can earn a base salary of almost $300,000 – Airservices has struggled with recruitment ever since the pandemic.
In February 2024, two air traffic controllers who didn’t show up for work at Sydney airport caused cascading flight delays and cancellations across the country. Airservices narrowly avoided a similar incident in September last year.
At the same time it has been trying to plug roster gaps, Airservices has been preparing for a once-in-a-generation transformation to a new flight-tracking computer system, as well as managing past allegations of workplace bullying.
A review into workplace culture, conducted by the former sex discrimination commissioner Elizabeth Broderick’s firm, found 27% of staff in 2023 had experienced bullying in the past 12 months, up from 23% in 2020.
From July 2022 to 2026, Airservices says it endorsed 245 controllers, most of whom qualified in 2025-2026. Over the same four-year period, 86 controllers left the organisation.
Airservices says it now has a record number of controllers across Australia. There were 985 controllers in December 2020 and 1,073 as of July this year, according to the organisation.
However, the organisation says the demands on its workforce have also grown significantly, citing the new Western Sydney airport and its recent takeover of the airspace at Ballina in northern New South Wales.
There still aren’t enough controllers at Sydney, Australia’s busiest airport.
Tough tests and training demands
A newly qualified controller can’t just fill the gap left by a retiring veteran.
After 18 months of training, a newly qualified controller may be able to work in one position at a Sydney tower, such as helping organise the taxiways around the domestic airport.
That person wouldn’t be qualified, for example, to work on the taxiways around the international airport, or runways, which require additional training, making newer employees less able to fill urgent vacancies.
Airservices acknowledges there’s a problem. It says training experienced controllers for Sydney airport is its “top priority” but it can’t say when it will have recruited a sufficient number.
It takes about two years to train a controller, and that’s only if someone can get past the initial screening, which includes a difficult online aptitude test as one of the first hurdles.
“Only a very, very small number of people get through the application process,” says Nugent. “We’re usually talking about 2,000 people who might apply, and you hire 15 of them.”
Additionally, applicants must move to Melbourne for the mandatory training. Only offering training at one location is seen as an impediment, because some applicants don’t want to relocate given there’s a risk they don’t pass.
Airservices says it is considering different training locations, and says it has a new simulator in Sydney.

title: ABC changing editorial policy after Rinehart furore prompts concerns of overreach from academics and advocates
summary:
Managing director says guidelines will ensure no individual will ‘be the subject of comedy that is violent in its description in our programming’

The four-minute film, titled A Very Relaxing Video, ran on documentary-reality show Race Around the World on 12 July and sparked a furore over comments made about the billionaire.

Continue reading...
full_text:
A pledge by the ABC managing director, Hugh Marks, to change editorial guidelines on satire and violence after the broadcaster aired a program featuring offensive comments about Gina Rinehart, has sparked concerns about overreach.
The four-minute film, titled A Very Relaxing Video, ran on documentary-reality show Race Around the World on 12 July and sparked a furore over comments made about the billionaire.
The segment concluded with the film-maker, Kate McGuinness, stating: “When the revolution comes will you hide under the bed or will you know exactly how to shove a stick right up Gina Rinehart’s butthole, stirring it round, mixing her guts up nice and smooth, to make one big sausage roll to make something out of nothing?”
After sustained backlash in News Corp and The West Australian, and threats of legal action from Rinehart, Marks issued an apology last Thursday.
He said while the ombudsman, Fiona Cameron, had found that the film didn’t breach editorial policies on harm and offence, it fell short of “community expectations”, and the ABC would change its editorial guidance.
On ABC Radio North Queensland last Thursday, he said the ABC’s guidelines will now demand that “no individual should be the subject of comedy that is violent in its description in our programming”.
“And I think the ABC has to hold itself to a higher standard and I think it’s really important we make that change.”
Journalist and professor of communication at Deakin University, Matthew Ricketson, said it was poor satire but once McGuinness had apologised for the joke, as she did on 30 July, that should have been “the end of it”.
“It’s a very ill-advised move,” he said of the promised change. “It’s virtually unenforceable … and it’s literally throwing fuel on to the News Corp fire. They will bank that and they will move straight on to the next demand which will be a curtailing if not the abolition of the ABC.”
The ombudsman initially received eight complaints about the program in the week after was broadcast. A further 988 complaints were made after criticism from “several media outlets”, it said in its report.
News Corp’s major mastheads have published 46 articles critiquing the program since it aired, and The West Australian has published 15.
The ombudsman found “a reasonable audience member would be likely to understand the remarks as part of a satirical and exaggerated commentary” rather than encouragement of violence.
The former editorial director of the ABC, Alan Sunderland, agreed with the ombudsman’s findings, which didn’t discount that the joke was in “poor taste”.
He said he wasn’t “perturbed” by the ABC reviewing its guidance, which could help program makers interpret editorial principles if it wasn’t enforceable. But he said “if it’s more elaborate than that then you start to get into problems”.
“You wouldn’t be able to put much [satire] to air,” he said, pointing to Aunty Jack in the 1970s, who threatened to “rip yer bloody arms off” if viewers didn’t watch the next week.
Sunderland said it was a “repeated pattern” to see ABC content picked up and “amplified” by some media and politicians, thereby giving it a “second life”. “Broadcasters can and do apologise without the world coming to an end,” he said.
Journalist, author and academic, Dr Margaret Simons, said Marks was right to apologise but rewriting editorial policies “wasn’t necessary”.
“The problem here is that either somebody didn’t make a judgment call or they made the wrong one,” she said. “I would have thought it was self-evident that a threat of violence, even a satirical threat, is a pretty serious matter.”
Simons said the ABC’s editorial policies required carefully judged decisions, and explicitly stated that contentious decisions should be upwardly referred to an appropriate level.
“My main question is, were the ABC policies followed in the sense of upward referral? Did anybody actually stop to look at this before it was broadcast?” she said.
“If it wasn’t … that in itself is arguably a breach of editorial policy. If editorial policies are substantially rewritten in the light of what I suspect is a failure of the ABC’s internal processes … that’s not good.”
An ABC spokesperson confirmed the changes would be amended “soon”, with approval by the ABC board. It didn’t respond to questions on whether the program had been upwardly referred.
On Saturday, Hancock Prospecting said it would “wait to see long overdue changes to the ABC’s ‘editorial standards’” and accused it of normalising “violent torture against a woman till death”.
“Satire needs to be funny, what the ABC approved to be aired for 25 days, in its violent torture until death content, was not,” it said. “We await a detailed account in relation to who approved this unacceptable piece to be aired, and who approved the long delay in its removal. The buck stops with the heads of the ABC.”
The president of ABC Friends, Cassandra Parkinson, said the ABC had “overreacted in trying to appease Ms Rinehart”.
“I can understand that the ABC issued an apology to avoid a costly legal action, but it’s difficult to understand the rationale for this new rule,” she said.
“Regardless of our views about the ‘joke’ in question, it’s important that the process that follows involves close scrutiny. It’s essential that the ABC hold firm against this sort of external pressure and that it uphold the independence laid out in its charter.”
McGuinness has also apologised over the segment, saying it wasn’t her intention to promote violence.
“My writing is cartoonish and always satirical. Unfortunately, jokes do not land with everyone. Its purpose was never to be taken literally,” she said in a statement uploaded to the ABC’s website.

title: Victorian police investigate allegation a car drove deliberately at speed towards anti-racism protester
summary:
Exclusive: ‘Peaceful community rally’ of more than 150 people was walking in Broadmeadows when car travelling in same direction allegedly approached

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Victorian police are investigating allegations that a car was deliberately driven at speed towards a protester taking part in an anti-racism rally in Melbourne last month.

More than 150 people gathered in the outer-north suburb of Broadmeadows on 25 July for what organisers described as a “peaceful community rally”.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Victorian police are investigating allegations that a car was deliberately driven at speed towards a protester taking part in an anti-racism rally in Melbourne last month.
More than 150 people gathered in the outer-north suburb of Broadmeadows on 25 July for what organisers described as a “peaceful community rally”.
After speeches, the group marched to Broadmeadows Town Park, occupying one lane of Tanderrum Drive, a two-lane road.
While the group was walking on the road, a car travelling in the same directionsounded its horn.
Protesters alleged that as the car approached the group, a passenger flung open the door twice, as if trying to push people out of the way.
Video of the incident, seen by Guardian Australia, shows a protester walking on the edge of the group in the lane where the car was attempting to pass. The video shows him turning as the car approaches and appearing to kick at it.
The car then clips the man on the legs and accelerates away.
Witnesses said it did not slow down as it attempted to pass the group.
The protester, who asked not to be identified, alleged that he heard an occupant of the car shout racial abuse before the car struck him.
The comments were not audible in the video, but Guardian Australia spoke to two others at the march who claim to have heard the alleged remarks. Several participants, including the man in the video, said they separately reported the incident directly to police within hours and in the following days.
“It felt surreal. I did not have the chance to even feel anything but shock,” the 43-year-old said.
Merri-bek Socialist Alliance councillor Sue Bolton, an organiser of the event, said the incident contradicted the rally’s purpose, which was to support community members who were “feeling really intimidated” by a recent rise in anti-immigration rhetoric.
Bolton said the group had been in contact with police in the days before the event to make them aware of the rally and received confirmation over the phone that officers would attend, but none did so.
Athiya Zameer, the member of the group designated to liaise with police, said she believed the incident would not have occurred if police had been present.
In a formal complaint to police on behalf of the group, Zameer called for action against the driver, claiming the alleged incident had caused trauma to the person hit by the car, children present and the wider community.
“We want to make sure that people feel safe to do these actions, to raise their voices,” she said. “We live in a community [of people from] migrant backgrounds who are already traumatised by wars and the police … and to have an incident like that just traumatises them even more … that’s really unfortunate.”
In a response to the complaint, seen by Guardian Australia, police confirmed they had been aware of the planned event. The response said the incident was “being actively investigated” and police were “committed to ensuring that allegations are thoroughly assessed”.
They declined to answer questions from Guardian Australia about why officers did not attend the protest.
The Greens state MP Anasina Gray-Barberio, who attended the rally but did not witness the car incident, said “the community expects an urgent and robust response”.
“The community deserves answers … Communities of colour deserve to know that when they’re subjected to violence or racism, those incidents will be treated with the seriousness they deserve,” she said.

full_text:
A Coalition plan to abolish compulsory energy standards for new homes that help reduce people’s exposure to heat and cold has been criticised by advocates as a “cost-of-living timebomb” that would deepen inequality.
The opposition’s housing and environment spokesperson, Andrew Bragg, said a Coalition government would cut the National Construction Code from more than 2,000 pages to 80, and strip away all requirements for new homes beyond demanding they were “basic and safe”. Longstanding compulsory energy and accessibility measures would become “optional extras”.
Speaking at the National Press Club, Bragg said house construction regulation was a “nightmare” and accused the Albanese government of making it “illegal to build a cheap house in Australia”.
“We will cut building costs,” he said.
Asked about the policy on ABC Radio National, the Liberal treasury spokesperson, Tim Wilson, said in some cases people could put “a jumper on in winter rather than spending huge amounts of money” on improving housing quality.
The Energy Efficiency Council said minimum standards were “not some extraneous bauble”, but made sure homes were safe, comfortable and affordable to run.
“Australians deserve to live in decent housing, not leaky shacks with paper thin walls,” the council’s chief executive, Luke Menzel, said. “This proposal is a cost-of-living timebomb … I never thought I’d see an Australian politician out and about advocating for higher energy bills, but here we are.
“If you’re a renter living in western Sydney you had better hope you don’t land in a home that has been built without energy efficiency measures. You’re going to need to run your air-conditioners like the clappers to try to keep yourself cool in summer and your energy bills are going to be through the roof.”
The chief executive of the Australian Council of Social Service, Cassandra Goldie, said governments should remove unnecessary regulation but needed to strengthen energy performance and accessibility rules that were “fundamental to health, safety and wellbeing”.
“Stripping out energy efficiency and accessibility standards would shift costs on to households, deepen inequality and leave future generations with homes that are expensive to run and difficult to live in,” she said.
Industry groups argued at a recent Senate inquiry that a range of changes to the construction code over the past seven years had added significantly to the cost of a new home, estimated between $3,600 and $33,000.
Government analysis found increasing the minimum residential energy rating from six to seven stars – the current standard – would increase the average capital cost of building a home by less than 1%. The Reserve Bank and CSIRO separately found constructions costs barely changed, and in some cases decreased, after previous increases in energy efficiency requirements.
Asked to respond to Goldie’s comments, Bragg said “I love energy efficiency” and that he was “really passionate” about electrification. But he said “we should be for choice” and “people just want to get access to a roof over their head”.
“Why do we have to make it compulsory for everyone? I just think it’s punitive for people on lower incomes,” Bragg said.
He said under the Coalition’s proposal, the states would enact their own building codes, given “it’s very different to live in Tasmania compared to Western Australia, so the conditions are different”.
Menzel said states and territories already had their own rules. He said the standardised national approach helped lower industry compliance costs, made homes cheaper for buyers, and the national code was already designed to take account of regional differences, incorporating eight different climate zones.
“[Bragg’s] comments suggest a pretty fundamental misunderstanding of how the code works,” he said.
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, told the ABC the government had already paused changes to the code as it was too hard to navigate and too costly, and was working with the states to streamline it.

title: How to Tell If You’re Trauma Dumping or Just Venting
summary: Plus, how to seek support without silencing yourself.
full_text:
You won’t find the term “trauma dumping” in a psychology textbook, but it’s gained popularity online to describe the act of unloading overwhelming feelings onto someone else without their consent. It’s like an extended, one-sided version of venting, says Cheryl Groskopf, an anxiety and trauma therapist in Los Angeles.
It’s also treated as one of the worst social sins you can commit—which can make people afraid to talk about their grief, trauma, or anything else too painful to package neatly. Yet social support is one way people cope with hard experiences. Conversations about tough topics don’t have to be concise, comfortable, or perfectly balanced to be healthy.
“It’s not about not talking about problems,” says Stephanie Mahalec, a therapist in Los Angeles. “Talking about problems is a very important part of relationships. It’s just how you talk about it.”
Here’s how to tell when trauma dumping might be reaching unhealthy levels in a friendship or relationship, according to therapists—and how to repair.
There’s no room for the other person to set a boundary
Asking whether someone has time to listen is considerate. It can be as simple as: “Do you have a minute? Can I vent about something?”
Dr. Hans Watson, a psychiatrist in South Jordan, Utah, recommends taking into account the time, place, and audience. Is this a workable moment? Is this an appropriate setting? Is this someone you ordinarily talk to about personal things?
With some relationships, that understanding is already in place. If you and a close friend routinely call each other when life falls apart, you probably don’t need to renegotiate the terms every time. And if you forget to ask permission during an especially painful moment, that alone does not make the conversation a trauma dump. “One conversation or one trauma dump is not a problem,” Groskopf says. “We’re all human.”
The larger concern is whether the other person has a meaningful way to say “not now,” slow the conversation down, or stop it—and what happens when they do. If every limit is ignored, negotiated away, or treated as proof that they don’t care, the relationship has lost room for one person’s boundaries.
The listener has a responsibility, too. Someone who’s overwhelmed may not notice shorter replies, broken eye contact, or glances at the clock. “If you’re that dysregulated, you’re not going to notice how someone else is feeling,” Mahalec says. That’s not necessarily selfishness; it can be part of what happens when a person is emotionally flooded. Rather than expecting them to decode subtle cues, the listener may need to say plainly: “I care about you, but I can’t give this conversation my full attention right now. Can we talk later today?”
Only one response will do
Wanting reassurance is normal. So is asking someone to listen, offer advice, sit beside you, or remind you that you’re not alone. The warning sign isn’t that you want comfort; it’s that the other person becomes responsible for producing one exact response that will make the feeling disappear.
If you need them to agree with you, reassure you repeatedly, or validate you in one very specific way, “you’ve unintentionally handed them the responsibility for changing your emotional state,” Groskopf says. That’s not reasonable to expect from anyone.
You might notice yourself explaining the story again, adding more context, or calling someone else because the first person didn’t say the thing that finally made you feel better. “It’s easy to start believing that one more detail or one more piece of context will finally make the other person understand the situation enough to change how we feel,” Groskopf says. “The strategy isn’t working, so the brain keeps trying harder and harder.”
That doesn’t mean there’s something wrong with telling a painful story more than once. Grief and trauma often need to be spoken about repeatedly. The question is whether you’re inviting someone to witness what you’re feeling—or making them responsible for ending it.
The friendship has become one permanent emergency
All close relationships go through periods of imbalance. When someone is grieving, ill, traumatized, or otherwise struggling, they may need far more support than they can give. People who love them often want to provide it.
So don’t judge the relationship by one conversation—or even one very difficult stretch. Look at the broader pattern. Do you contact this person only when something has gone wrong? Are they expected to be available whenever you become overwhelmed? Is there room for them to talk about their own life? Do the two of you still know each other outside of distress?
Groskopf says that when the same person repeatedly becomes the only place you go for emotional relief, both people can settle into roles without realizing it: One is always in crisis, and the other is always expected to steady them. Eventually, “the friendship starts to revolve around emotional crises,” she says.
How to seek support without silencing yourself
None of this means swallowing your pain, waiting until you can discuss it calmly, or saving every difficult thought for a therapist. “The urge to get it all out is so incredibly healthy,” says Jenny Martin, a psychologist and founder of Gemstone Wellness, a trauma-informed practice in Chicago. “The urge is correct.”
Some relationships can hold the full story. When enough trust and intimacy exist, Martin says, even an intense account of “real trauma and pain” can make sense and be welcomed. Mahalec also points to the value of co-regulation: Being with someone calmer can help an overwhelmed nervous system begin to settle. You don’t always have to regulate yourself before reaching for another person.
A few strategies can make that connection easier—without requiring you to communicate perfectly.
Say what you need
Before or during the conversation, tell the other person what would help. You might say: “I don’t need advice; I just need someone to listen.” Or: “I’m overwhelmed and don’t know what I need yet. Can you stay with me for a few minutes?”
Naming what you want relieves the listener of having to guess. It also makes room for an honest answer about what they can offer.
Ask about timing
Groskopf suggests asking: “Do you have the bandwidth for something really heavy right now?” Martin offers another option: “How much energy do you have for holding space for hard stuff right now?”
Think of these questions as tools, not tests you have to pass before you’re allowed to speak. If you’re too overwhelmed to ask gracefully—or only realize afterward that you never checked in—you haven’t committed some unforgivable relational offense. Watson points out that everyone occasionally gets difficult conversations wrong. What matters is being willing to listen, adjust, and repair.
Give your pain more than one place to go
Needing more support than one friend can provide doesn’t mean your story is too much or that it belongs only in therapy. It means you deserve more than one place where you can tell it.
Depending on what feels right, that might include several friends or relatives, a support group, a faith community, or a therapist. Different people may be able to offer different things: company, practical help, lived experience, distraction, advice, or space to tell the entire story.
The goal isn’t to protect everyone else from your feelings. It’s to keep you from becoming isolated—or dependent on one person being available every time the pain surges.
Use a private voice memo as a bridge
When you want to get your thoughts out in private, Martin recommends opening your phone’s voice recorder and saying everything you need to say. She uses the strategy herself. On one recent evening, after a particularly difficult day, she retreated to her hammock and let herself unload.
“I sat out in my hammock under the moon, and I just cried and talked into an audio memo,” Martin says. “It allows me to purge and wring out so much that is simmering in my body. It organizes and releases

title: Should You Let Your Dog Lick Your Face? 9 Animal Hygiene Questions, Answered
summary: From dog kisses to cat scratches, here’s what’s harmless—and what warrants a call to the doctor.
full_text:
You might be surprised to learn that Dr. Daniel Griffin, chief of infectious diseases at Island Infectious Disease Medical in Long Island, N.Y., lets his two dogs lick him.
He’s not delusional. “We know how dogs greet each other,” he says. “We know where that tongue has been.” But he lets his expertise take over afterward. Griffin diligently washes his hands after his dogs lick them, especially before picking up a slice of pizza.
That’s more or less the expert consensus: love the pet, wash your hands. Living closely with pets brings you closer to germs, but for most people, ordinary contact is low-risk. There are exceptions, however. Here, experts answer the face-licking question and eight others about hygiene and animals you might encounter.
Should you let your dog lick your face?
First, forget the thing you may have heard your whole life. “I used to hear, ‘Oh, dogs’ mouths are like 10 times cleaner than people’s mouths,’” says Kelley Steury, a veterinarian and clinical associate professor at the University of Nevada, Reno School of Public Health. “I don’t think that’s based in science.”
A dog’s mouth, like a person’s, is full of bacteria. One species commonly found in dogs, Capnocytophaga canimorsus, can occasionally cause serious illness in people. Most of the time, though, nothing happens. “It doesn’t really pose a problem,” Steury says. The trouble starts when saliva gets past the body’s defenses—through a bite or into an open cut, for example. In rare cases, the infection can progress to sepsis and become fatal.
The risk also depends on who’s getting licked. People being treated for cancer or taking immune-suppressing drugs are more vulnerable to severe C. canimorsus infection. So are people without a spleen and those with alcohol-use disorder. But for healthy kids and adults, the occasional lick is fine, experts say.
Official guidance takes the cautious route, though: Keep dogs away from your mouth and face, and don’t let them lick open wounds. Saliva is more of a concern when it reaches broken skin or a mucous membrane, such as the mouth or eyes. If your dog gets you anyway, wash the area afterward. And if you’re immunocompromised or don’t have a spleen, ask your doctor what precautions make sense. But the fact that dogs, like so many of our daily exposures, can carry germs is not “a reason to not own a dog,” she says.
What if your cat licks you?
A cat lick is usually a non-event, too, provided your skin is intact. Cats commonly carry Pasteurella multocida, but on unbroken skin, Steury says, it “pretty much will not be a problem at all.”
Experts are more concerned about bites. A cat’s teeth are narrow and sharp, so they often puncture instead of scraping the surface. “The tooth acts kind of like a needle,” Steury says, “and it’ll inject that bacteria into your deep tissues.” What looks like a pinprick can be a deeper wound than it appears.
If a cat bite breaks the skin, wash it immediately with soap and running water and see a medical provider, Steury says.
What should you do about a cat scratch?
“I definitely respect the claws of cats,” says Dr. Peter Chin-Hong, an infectious disease specialist at the University of California, San Francisco.
If a claw catches you, wash your skin right away with soap and running water. The goal is to rinse the bacteria away before it settles in, not to disinfect. “Disinfectants don’t kill everything,” he says. “Running things are better than stagnant things in general.”
After that, pay attention to the area. Increasing redness, pus, or a fever over the next several days are all reasons to see a medical professional. So is a swollen lymph node on the same side of your body as the scratch, which can signal cat-scratch disease, a bacterial infection most common in kids. Location matters, too. Chin-Hong is extra cautious when a bite or scratch lands directly over a joint, where an infection can be harder to treat.
What if you have a fresh surgical site?
Coming home from surgery might be when you most want your furry friend on your bed. It’s also when experts want you to put a little distance between your pet and whatever is healing.
Dr. Ashley Drews, an infectious disease specialist at Houston Methodist, has seen patients develop infections after a pet licked an incision or surgical drain. “That’s not a good idea,” she says. Keep the site covered and your pet away from it.
Do you need to worry about the litter box?
Yes. Cats can shed Toxoplasma gondii in their poop, and the parasite can travel from the box to your hands to your mouth.
Yet the litter box isn’t the only way to get toxoplasmosis. The parasite can also turn up in soil, unwashed produce, contaminated water, and undercooked meat—especially pork, lamb, and venison.
“I think people are aware of the cat litter thing,” says Jill Roberts, a molecular epidemiologist and professor at the University of South Florida College of Public Health. Meat gets less attention. Roberts is so wary of undercooked pork that she skips thick cuts, which she worries are harder to bring to a safe temperature. “All I can see is Toxoplasma,” she says. You don’t have to give up pork chops, but you should use a food thermometer: Whole cuts of pork should reach 145°F. Once they come off the heat, wait at least three minutes before cutting or eating them; the meat’s temperature holds steady or continues to rise during that time, helping destroy pathogens.
While the pork chop may deserve more attention, the litter-box rule still stands. If you’re pregnant or immunocompromised, hand off the scooping if you can. If you have to do it yourself, wear disposable gloves and wash your hands afterward. Change the litter daily, too: The parasite takes one to five days after being shed to become infectious.
Can you catch your dog’s parasites?
Sometimes, but your dog’s diagnosis doesn’t automatically mean the whole household is next. When Griffin’s dogs had giardia, an intestinal illness caused by a microscopic parasite, he wasn’t panicking about catching it himself. “In general, it’s a different giardia that we get vs. dogs,” he says. The type that usually makes people sick isn’t the same type that usually infects dogs and cats.
Pay special attention during cleanup. Giardia can travel through tiny traces of feces on soil, water, fur, surfaces, and objects. Clean up dog poop promptly; keep up with veterinary care and parasite prevention; and clean the bowls, bedding, crates, and toys of a pet being treated for giardia. Your veterinarian may also recommend a bath to remove contaminated feces from its fur.
Always use actual soap and water after handling a sick pet or cleaning up poop. Sanitizer is helpful when it’s all you have, but it doesn’t remove dirt or every kind of germ.
Are your pets bringing ticks into the house?
Quite possibly. Your dog can come inside alone and still bring company. Dogs and cats can carry ticks indoors, where the ticks may disembark and choose a human for their next meal. Dr. Heidi Torres, an infectious disease physician and assistant hospital epidemiologist at Weill Cornell Medicine in New York, takes the possibility seriously enough to pack fine-tipped tweezers for overnight trips to the country.
Ticks are remarkably good at hiding in plain sight. On people, they tend to hide under arms, behind knees, around the waist, and in the hair. On dogs, check the ears, under the front legs, and between the toes. Torres says many people who develop Lyme disease or another tickborne illness “have no recollection of ever being bitten by a tick or ever seeing a tick.”
After spending time in tall grasses or woods, make sure everyone gets inspected. “Check yourself, check your partner, check your kids, check your dogs,” Torres says. If you find a tick attached to your skin, remove it then and there; waiting for a doctor only gives it more time to feed and potentially transmit disease. title: Introducing OlmoEarth embeddings: Custom embedding exports from OlmoEarth Studio for downstream analysis
full_text:
Introducing OlmoEarth embeddings: Custom embedding exports from OlmoEarth Studio for downstream analysis
OlmoEarth Studio, our platform for building Earth observation models, now lets you compute and export embedding vectors—compact numerical representations of Earth-observation data produced by our open source OlmoEarth foundation models. The source code and model weights are publicly available alongside the research paper, so the community can inspect exactly how these embeddings are generated.
Embeddings are a fast, cost-effective entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they support a wide range of downstream tasks, from similarity search to segmentation to unsupervised exploration. Locations with similar surface characteristics end up with similar vectors; locations that differ land far apart. OlmoEarth embeddings have shown strong performance in our own benchmarking and in independent evaluations. The exported Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (COGs) are lightweight and easy to share. Choose your area of interest, time range, encoder variant, resolution, and imagery sources via the Studio UI or API, and get back a COG you can use however you like. If your application requires higher performance, Studio also supports supervised fine-tuning (SFT).
Custom-computed embeddings are now available for users of OlmoEarth Studio. Reach out if you're interested in gaining access. Instructions for using the publicly available OlmoEarth models to compute your own embeddings are available here.
Computing embeddings in Studio
Global structure in OlmoEarth embeddings from seasonal Sentinel-2 imagery across 1.1M samples. Colors indicate 15 k-means clusters in a PCA-reduced embedding space.
Computing embeddings follows the same workflow as any other prediction in Studio. First configure a model and run it, and then download the results. Several parameters tailor the output:
- Area of interest: Draw or upload any polygon; Studio handles imagery acquisition and tiling.
- Time span: 1-12 monthly periods.
- Encoder variant: Nano (128-dim, 1.4M params), Tiny (192-dim, 6.2M params), or Base (768-dim, 89M params).
- Spatial resolution: 10 meter, 20 meter, 40 meter, or 80 meter per pixel.
- Imagery sources: Sentinel-2 L2A, Sentinel-1 RTC, or both.
Different visualization options applied to the same embedding raster.
Studio delivers a COG with one band per embedding dimension. Vectors are stored as signed 8-bit integers (int8). Values range from -127 to +127, with -128 reserved for nodata. To recover floating-point vectors, see dequantize_embeddings in olmoearth_pretrain.
Because everything is computed on demand rather than pulled from a pre-computed global archive, your embeddings reflect exactly the conditions you care about. You can generate monthly embeddings to capture seasonal dynamics, not just annual snapshots.
What you can do with OlmoEarth embeddings
The examples below all use OlmoEarth-v1-Tiny (192-dim) embeddings at 40-meter resolution with Sentinel-2 L2A composites (annual for most examples; monthly for change detection). Tiny is a lightweight encoder but still highly performant; for your own applications, you can swap it for a larger variant at the cost of higher compute and storage.
Similarity search: Finding "more like this"
Pick a query pixel, extract its embedding, and compute cosine similarity against every other pixel. The result is a heatmap showing where the landscape looks most and least like your query pixel.
This query sits near the Merced urban center in California. Urban fabric and road corridors light up coherently while agricultural parcels stay dark. The model distinguishes built-up surfaces from cropland without any labels.
Switching the query to a small agricultural window, we define the query vector as the mean of the embedding vectors over that window, then pull Sentinel-2 imagery at the highest- and lowest-similarity locations to see what the model treats as similar and dissimilar.
The most similar patches (0.89 and above) are all agricultural parcels with irrigated fields. The least similar (around zero) are an airport with surrounding bare ground, a reservoir with dry terrain, and arid rangeland. No training data, no labels, just a dot product in embedding space.
Few-shot segmentation: Labeling the landscape
Similarity search tells you "where is it like this?" but sometimes you need discrete labels across a region. Because the representations are already rich, a simple linear classifier can produce a wall-to-wall land-cover map from very few labeled pixels.
To test this, we labeled just 60 pixels (20 per class) over Ca Mau, Vietnam, a coastal mangrove region. Using ESA WorldCover 2021 as the label source for three classes (mangrove, water, other), we randomly sampled 20 pixels per class, trained a logistic regression with per-feature standardization, and predicted every pixel in the region.
From 60 labeled pixels, the classifier produces a coherent map with weighted F1 = 0.84. Mangrove stands, tidal channels, and open water are delineated across the entire region. The classifier saturates quickly: increasing from 30 to 300 labels barely changes accuracy, because the embeddings are doing most of the heavy lifting.
The core of the analysis is a few lines of Python:
import rasterio
import numpy as np
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
# Load the 192-band embedding COG exported from Studio
with rasterio.open("embeddings.tif") as ds:
    emb = ds.read().astype(np.float32)  # (192, H, W)
C, H, W = emb.shape
X = emb.reshape(C, -1).T  # (H*W, 192)
# Train on labeled pixels, predict everywhere
clf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))
clf.fit(X[train_idx], labels[train_idx])
prediction = clf.predict(X).reshape(H, W)
This is a linear probe, a standard evaluation for foundation models. The fact that a logistic regression over 192 dimensions recovers land-cover boundaries from so few labels means the Tiny encoder has organized these ecological distinctions during pretraining. Larger variants (Base, 768-dim) encode even richer representations.
If you have ground-truth polygons, field survey points, or a coarse existing map, you can train a similar classifier and produce a wall-to-wall map for your own region of interest.
Change detection: Spotting what shifted
Because Studio can generate embeddings at any temporal resolution (monthly through annual), you can compare two time periods directly to identify where surface conditions have changed. Below, we computed monthly Sentinel-2 embeddings for the same region in September 2023 and September 2024 and measured per-pixel cosine distance. The Park Fire (July-September 2024) burn scar in Butte County, California lights up immediately.
No labels or training required—just two embedding COGs and a few lines of Python.
Unsupervised exploration: Seeing what the model sees
Sometimes you have no query location or reference labels. You just want to understand what structure exists in the embeddings. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a clean way to do this: reduce to three dimensions, map to R/G/B, and display as a false-color image. Similar embeddings get similar colors automatically.
Flevoland, in the Netherlands, is a reclaimed polder landscape with a regular grid of agricultural parcels. The PCA false-color image reproduces those boundaries with high fidelity. Different crop types, water bodies, and urban areas each get distinct hues. The embedding has internalized landscape structure without ever being told what a parcel or crop is.
This kind of unsupervised view is a quick way to see what structure the model has picked up across your area of interest.
From export to insight
Similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA exploration are simple operations on standard raster data that run in seconds. The power comes from the embeddings: learned representat

title: Guitar company D’Addario admits that AI music was used in a promotional video
summary: After weeks of controversy and speculation, music company D'Addario has admitted that AI, specifically Suno, was used as part of a recent promotional video. For nearly two weeks, the company has denied the allegations, even as evidence piled up against it. It offered various explanations, from low-quality exports, to combinations of plugins like Autotune introducing […]
full_text:
After weeks of controversy and speculation, music company D’Addario has admitted that AI, specifically Suno, was used as part of a recent promotional video. For nearly two weeks, the company has denied the allegations, even as evidence piled up against it. It offered various explanations, from low-quality exports, to combinations of plugins like Autotune introducing digital noise, and the use of AI-assisted mastering tools from LANDR and Logic. But now the company has edited its original Instagram post denying the use of generative AI to say it was wrong.
Guitar company D’Addario admits that AI music was used in a promotional video
After initially denying it, the company now admits that its string demo video was made with Suno.
In a lengthy update to its post from July 29th (embedded at the bottom), it said:
We got this wrong. We’ve completed a full review and confirmed that Suno Studio was used to regenerate the original track. We shared inaccurate information, and we’re truly sorry … We do not support AI-generated music, and our process will reflect that going forward. We’ll require our employees and creative partners to disclose any use of generative AI, and we’ll more closely review everything we put into the world.
The post also apologizes for heavy-handed comment moderation, which saw posts from critics deleted and those users blocked. Rather than issue a new statement, it appears the company simply edited its original post five days ago, ten days after it was originally posted.
The original video was a demo for a new set of strings designed for extended-range guitars and low tunings. People immediately flagged the recording as suspicious. Things only got worse when D’Addario posted a clip of what it said were the Logic recording sessions of the demo track in question. But there were some very noticeable melodic and rhythmic differences between what people heard in the finished track and the Logic session.
Guitarist and YouTuber Rhett Shull managed to get his hands on the original Logic files directly from D’Addario, and it actually only added more fuel to the fire. Even in his rather generous assessment, Shull concluded that Suno was probably used at some point in the process, most likely to regenerate an original recording.
D’Addario has now admitted that Suno Studio was used to regenerate the track. This is just the latest AI controversy to shake the guitar world following the Fender CEO’s comments comparing bandmates to analog AI.

title: Goldman Sachs leaps into bitcoin income ETFs with $2.25 billion NEOS buyout
full_text:
Goldman Sachs leaps into bitcoin income ETFs with $2.25 billion NEOS buyout
The $2.25 billion deal expands Goldman’s derivative platform to $130 billion in total ETF assets, taking direct aim at BlackRock's rival BITA fund, according to an analyst.
- Goldman Sachs agreed to acquire NEOS Investments, the manager of the $1.1 billion BTCI bitcoin synthetic ETF, in a cash-and-equity deal valuing NEOS at up to $2.25 billion, with closing expected in early 2027 pending regulatory approval.
- BTCI, which does not directly hold bitcoin, uses a covered-call strategy on bitcoin ETPs to generate a yield of about 27% but has fallen roughly 43% over the past year and charges a 0.99% expense ratio.
- The acquisition gives Goldman a $30 billion options-based ETF platform across 19 funds and, combined with prior deals, will lift its ETF assets above $130 billion as it races rivals like BlackRock in the fast-growing derivative income ETF market.
Goldman Sachs is acquiring NEOS Investments, the firm behind BTCI, a $1.1 billion bitcoin synthetic exchange-traded fund (ETF) that yields roughly 27%, according to a senior ETF analyst at Bloomberg.
The acquisition deal in cash and equity puts NEOS at a valuation of up to $2.25 billion, is subject to performance targets and is expected to close during the first quarter of 2027 pending regulatory approval, Goldman Sachs said Wednesday in a statement detailing the agreement.
BTCI launched in October 2024 and has crossed $1 billion in assets in under two years, Eric Balchunas, a senior ETF analyst at Bloomberg, said in an X post. He also said it holds spot bitcoin exchange-traded products (ETPs) and sells call options against those positions to generate monthly distributions. It does not directly hold bitcoin, and investors receive the yield from the product but forfeit some of the upside when bitcoin rallies, he said..
That trade-off is exactly what Goldman filed to build itself four months ago, Balchunas added.
On April 14, Goldman registered the Goldman Sachs Bitcoin Premium Income ETF with the SEC, proposing a structurally similar covered-call product. Balchunas was blunt about what Wednesday's deal means for that filing.
"Nowww I get why GS never launched the BTC covered call product they filed months ago," Balchunas wrote. "Better to leapfrog BlackRock's $BITA vs me too?"
One senior ETF analyst, who asked not to be named, said the deal reflects Goldman's push to build out its ETF business broadly, noting that BTCI is one of almost 20 funds in the NEOS lineup. "If anything, it shows that bitcoin is just part of the financial world, alongside stocks, bonds, etc." As of June 30, 2026, Goldman Sachs Asset Management, Innovator from Goldman Sachs Asset Management and NEOS manage more than $130 billion in ETF assets under supervision (AUS), according to the Wall Street bank’s statement.
BlackRock released its own bitcoin income ETF, BITA, on Nasdaq on June 16, about two months ahead of Goldmine’s filing. BITA targets a 15-25% annual yield and sells covered calls on 25-35% of its IBIT holdings. Its expense ratio is 0.65%.
BTCI charges 0.99% and is down 42.55% over the past year, with shares falling from a 52-week high of $65.87 to around $28.40, according to Bloomberg terminal data shared by Balchunas on X. According to the fund's SEC prospectus, BTCI's distributions may in part represent a return of capital rather than net investment income, a distinction income investors should weigh.
Goldman's NEOS acquisition doesn't just hand it BTCI. It also grants it access to a $30 billion options-based ETF platform across 19 funds, one of the fastest-growing in the industry, the Wall Street giant’s statement said. Combined with Goldman's existing $40 billion in options-based ETF assets and the Innovator Capital Management acquisition it announced in December, Goldman will control more than $130 billion in total ETF assets, which is enough to rank it eighth among active ETF managers globally, it said.
NEOS co-founders Troy Cates and Garrett Paolella will join Goldman as partners after closing.
The derivative income ETF category has grown to roughly $180 billion in assets industry-wide, compounding at more than 70% annually since 2021, according to Morningstar. Goldman is buying into that growth rather than trying to organically replicate it.
